california.html:
How a California injury claim is valued

A California injury claim pays two kinds of loss. Economic damages are the bills and lost income you can prove with paper: medical care, future treatment, wages, and the cost of replacing things like a car. Non-economic damages pay for pain, emotional distress, lost enjoyment of life and disfigurement. Insurers and juries add the two, cut the total by your share of the blame, and the at-fault side’s insurance limit usually sets how much can actually be collected.

California is friendlier to injured people than most states on two points: it uses pure comparative fault, so partial blame never wipes out a claim, and it has no cap on pain and suffering outside medical malpractice. It is stricter on two others: past medical damages are measured by what was actually paid, not the full bill, and a driver who had no insurance at the time of the crash generally can’t recover pain and suffering at all. Each of those rules is covered below, with the statute or case behind it.

To run your own numbers, use the California personal injury calculator or, after a crash, the California car accident calculator. Both open with the rules on this page already applied.

A California claim, worked through

Here is an example, not a prediction. A driver is rear-ended on a freeway on-ramp and treats for a neck and shoulder injury for five months. The providers billed $24,600, but the driver’s health plan paid $9,800 and the providers accepted that as full payment. The driver missed $7,400 of wages. The insurer argues the driver braked suddenly and was 20% at fault.

  • Economic damages, using the amount actually paid: $9,800 medical plus $7,400 wages = $17,200.
  • Pain and suffering at two to three times the economic losses, a common range for a moderate soft-tissue injury: $34,400 to $51,600.
  • Claim before fault: $51,600 to $68,800.
  • After a 20% fault reduction: $41,280 to $55,040.

Three California rules move that range. If the claim were valued on the full billed amount, the pre-fault range would be $96,000 to $128,000, but California’s Supreme Court has held that past medical damages are limited to what was paid, so insurers start from $9,800, not $24,600. If the driver had been uninsured at the time of the crash, Proposition 213 would remove pain and suffering, leaving about $13,760 after fault. And if the at-fault driver carried only the state minimum, $30,000 would be the most that policy pays, whatever the claim is worth.

Fault: pure comparative negligence

California adopted pure comparative fault in Li v. Yellow Cab Co. (1975). Your award is reduced by your percentage of fault and never drops to zero because of it. At 20% fault you keep 80% of the value. At 70% fault you still keep 30%. That is different from the many states that bar recovery once you reach 50% or 51%, and it changes negotiation: in California the fight is over how many points of fault you carry, not whether you cross a cliff.

Fault arguments come from the police report, photos, vehicle damage, witness statements and, more and more, dashcam and phone data. An insurer that can move you from 10% to 30% fault takes 20% off the value of the whole claim, so it is worth answering each point with evidence rather than letting it stand.

When more than one party is at fault

Proposition 51, now Civil Code section 1431.2, splits liability in two. For economic damages, every at-fault defendant is responsible for the full amount, so you can collect your medical bills and lost wages from whichever defendant can pay. For non-economic damages, each defendant pays only its own percentage. If an uninsured driver was 60% at fault and a city was 40% at fault for a badly designed intersection, the city can be made to cover all of your economic losses but only 40% of your pain and suffering. Use the comparative fault calculator to see how a fault split changes your number.

California filing deadlines

Missing a deadline ends a claim no matter how strong it is. These are the main ones:

  • Personal injury: two years from the date of injury (Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1).
  • Wrongful death: two years, usually counted from the date of death (§ 335.1).
  • Damage to a vehicle or other property: three years (§ 338).
  • Medical malpractice: three years from the injury or one year from when you discovered it, whichever comes first (§ 340.5). Before suing a health care provider you must give 90 days’ notice of intent to sue, and a notice served near the end of the period can extend it (§ 364).
  • Claims against a city, county, school district or the state: six months to file a written government claim for an injury (Government Code § 911.2). If the claim is rejected in writing, you generally have six months from the rejection to file suit (§ 945.6). A late-claim application can be made within one year of the injury in limited cases (§ 911.4).
  • Injured children: the two-year period usually doesn’t start until the child turns 18 (§ 352), but the six-month government-claim deadline still applies, so a claim against a public agency can’t wait.

The California filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury date. Treat its result as a reminder to act early, because tolling rules and the date you discovered an injury can change the count.

Car insurance in California

California is an at-fault state: the driver who caused the crash, through their liability insurer, pays the injured person’s claim. Since January 1, 2025, every policy must carry at least $30,000 per injured person, $60,000 per crash and $15,000 for property damage, written 30/60/15 (Vehicle Code § 16056). Those minimums were 15/30/5 for decades. The same 2022 law, SB 1107, raises them again to 50/100/25 for policies starting January 1, 2035.

A $30,000 limit is small next to a serious injury, which is why the at-fault driver’s policy limit often decides a California settlement. Your own coverage can add to it:

  • Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage (UM/UIM). Policies include it unless you rejected it in writing. California UIM is reduced by what the at-fault driver’s insurer pays: with $100,000 of UIM and a $30,000 policy on the other side, your UIM can add up to $70,000 (Insurance Code § 11580.2).
  • Medical payments coverage (MedPay). Optional. It pays medical bills regardless of fault, usually in small amounts such as $1,000 to $10,000.

The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how much of a claim the available coverage can actually pay.

Uninsured drivers lose pain and suffering: Proposition 213

Voters passed Proposition 213 in 1996, and it is now Civil Code section 3333.4. If you owned an uninsured vehicle involved in the crash, or were driving without the insurance the law requires, you can’t recover non-economic damages from the at-fault driver. The same bar applies if you were convicted of driving under the influence in connection with the crash. You can still recover economic damages: medical bills, lost wages and property damage.

There is an exception that matters: if the at-fault driver was convicted of DUI for that crash, Proposition 213 does not stop an uninsured driver from recovering pain and suffering. The rule also doesn’t reach passengers in someone else’s car or pedestrians, unless they owned the uninsured vehicle involved. Because Proposition 213 can remove the largest part of a claim, insurers check coverage at the time of the crash early. Buying a policy after the crash does not fix the problem.

Medical bills: what was paid, not what was billed

In Howell v. Hamilton Meats & Provisions (2011), the California Supreme Court held that an injured person can’t recover past medical expenses above the amount actually paid or owed. When a health plan pays a negotiated rate and the provider writes off the rest, the written-off portion is not recoverable. In the example above that cut the medical figure from $24,600 to $9,800. The collateral source rule still applies in other ways, so the jury is not told that health insurance paid; the limit is on the amount, not on mentioning insurance.

Different rules apply if you had no health insurance or chose to treat on a lien, where a doctor waits to be paid from the settlement. A later Court of Appeal decision, Pebley v. Santa Clara Organics (2018), allowed a plaintiff treating on liens to present the full billed amount as evidence of reasonable value, subject to challenge by the defense. Expect insurers to dispute lien-based bills hard, often with a billing expert.

Damage limits: MICRA and punitive damages

California does not cap damages in ordinary injury cases. Car crashes, falls, dog bites and product cases have no limit on pain and suffering. The exception is medical malpractice, governed by the Medical Injury Compensation Reform Act (MICRA) as rewritten by AB 35 in 2022:

  • Injury cases: the non-economic damages cap is $470,000 for 2026. It started at $350,000 in 2023 and rises $40,000 each January 1 until it reaches $750,000.
  • Death cases: the cap is $650,000 for 2026. It started at $500,000 and rises $50,000 a year until it reaches $1,000,000.
  • Up to three caps can apply in one case: one for all health care providers, one for all health care institutions such as hospitals, and one for unaffiliated providers or institutions whose separate negligence caused harm (Civil Code § 3333.2).
  • Lawyer fees are capped too: 25% of a recovery that settles before a lawsuit is filed and 33% after filing, unless a court allows more after trial (Business and Professions Code § 6146).

Economic damages in malpractice cases, such as lifetime care costs and lost earnings, are not capped. The malpractice calculator applies the 2026 California caps.

Punitive damages (Civil Code § 3294) require clear and convincing evidence of malice, oppression or fraud. They are uncommon in injury cases, but drunk driving and deliberate safety violations are where they come up. California sets no fixed cap on them; courts review large awards for constitutional limits.

When the injured person dies

Two claims can follow a death. A wrongful death claim belongs to the family (spouse or registered domestic partner, children, and in some cases others who depended on the person) and pays for the loss of financial support, household services, love, companionship and guidance, plus funeral costs (Code of Civil Procedure § 377.60). California does not pay for grief itself, but the loss of the relationship is compensable. A survival claim belongs to the estate and recovers what the person could have claimed had they lived.

The survival rules changed on January 1, 2026. A 2021 law, SB 447, temporarily let estates recover the person’s pain and suffering before death in cases filed from 2022 through 2025. That provision expired at the end of 2025 and an extension bill did not pass, so survival claims filed in 2026 are back to economic losses and, where proven, punitive damages (§ 377.34). Cases already pending may raise arguments about which version applies. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Claims against a city, county or the state

Public agencies are liable for injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property they knew or should have known about (Government Code § 835), and for the negligence of employees acting on the job, such as a city bus driver. The process is stricter than a claim against a private person:

  • File the agency’s written claim form within six months of the injury. Each agency has its own form, often on its website.
  • The agency has 45 days to act. Silence counts as a rejection.
  • After a written rejection you usually have six months to sue.

Dangerous-condition cases also need proof that the condition created a substantial risk of injury and that the agency had notice of it, so photographs and early records requests matter.

Dog bites, drunk drivers and other California rules

Dog bites. Civil Code section 3342 makes owners strictly liable when their dog bites someone in a public place or lawfully on private property. It doesn’t matter whether the dog had bitten before. The statute covers bites; injuries from a dog knocking someone down fall under negligence rules. See the California dog bite calculator.

Bars and party hosts. California largely shields bars and social hosts from claims by people hurt by a drunk guest (Civil Code § 1714 and Business and Professions Code § 25602). The main exceptions are selling alcohol to an obviously intoxicated minor (§ 25602.1) and an adult host knowingly serving a minor who then causes harm. The claim is usually against the driver alone.

Falls on someone else’s property. Owners must keep property reasonably safe and warn of hidden dangers (Civil Code § 1714). Your own carelessness, such as looking at a phone, reduces the claim under pure comparative fault rather than ending it. The California slip and fall calculator applies that rule.

Medical liens and who gets paid from a settlement

A settlement check is rarely all yours. Before it reaches you, these usually come out:

  • Lawyer’s fee and case costs, often 33⅓% before suit and 40% after, outside malpractice cases.
  • Hospital liens. Under the Hospital Lien Act a hospital that gave you emergency and ongoing care can claim part of the recovery, but hospital liens under the Act can’t take more than 50% of the money due to you (Civil Code § 3045.4). Hospitals often accept less when the settlement is small.
  • Medi-Cal. The state can recover what it paid, reduced for attorney fees and costs (Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 14124.72 to 14124.76).
  • Medicare and employer health plans, under federal rules that California law doesn’t control.

The medical lien calculator shows what a settlement leaves after fees and liens.

Settlement offers, interest and timing

California’s offer-to-compromise statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 998, puts pressure on both sides. If a defendant rejects a plaintiff’s reasonable 998 offer and the plaintiff then does better at trial, the defendant can owe the plaintiff’s expert fees and 10% annual interest on the judgment from the date of the offer (Civil Code § 3291). If a plaintiff rejects a defense 998 offer and does worse, the plaintiff loses post-offer costs and can owe the defense’s. These offers often come once medical treatment is finished and the claim can be valued.

Most car crash claims settle without a lawsuit, often several months after treatment ends. A claim with surgery, disputed fault or a public agency takes longer, and a lawsuit adds one to three years. Settlements for children need court approval (Probate Code § 3500). The settlement timeline calculator gives a stage-by-stage estimate. Small claims court can handle claims up to $12,500 for individuals, without lawyers on either side.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Report a crash involving injury or more than $1,000 of damage to the DMV within 10 days on form SR-1, even if police came (Vehicle Code § 16000).
  • Tell your own insurer promptly so UM, UIM and MedPay are available if you need them.
  • If a public agency may share fault, calendar the six-month government claim date now.
  • Keep bills and the explanations of benefits from your health plan. Under Howell, what was paid is the number that matters.
  • Don’t give a recorded statement to the other driver’s insurer before you know the extent of your injuries.

faqs.question: Can I get a settlement in California if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes. California uses pure comparative fault, so your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault but never eliminated by it. At 30% fault you keep 70% of the claim’s value.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in California?
faqs.answer: Two years from the injury in most cases (Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1). Claims against a city, county or state agency need a written government claim within six months, and malpractice claims have their own one-year discovery rule.

faqs.question: Can I recover pain and suffering if I didn’t have car insurance?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Under Proposition 213 (Civil Code § 3333.4), an uninsured driver can recover medical bills, lost wages and property damage but not non-economic damages, unless the at-fault driver was convicted of DUI for the crash.

faqs.question: Does California cap pain and suffering damages?
faqs.answer: Only in medical malpractice. For 2026 the MICRA cap is $470,000 in injury cases and $650,000 in death cases, and up to three caps can apply. Other injury claims have no cap.

faqs.question: Will my settlement include the full amount my doctors billed?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Under Howell v. Hamilton Meats (2011), past medical damages are limited to the amount actually paid or owed, such as the rate your health plan paid. Bills on a lien are treated differently and are often disputed.

faqs.question: Can my family recover my loved one’s pain and suffering before death?
faqs.answer: Not in survival claims filed on or after January 1, 2026. The SB 447 provision that allowed it for cases filed from 2022 through 2025 expired. The family’s wrongful death claim for loss of support and companionship is unaffected.

texas.excerpt: Texas bars recovery once you are more than 50% responsible, limits medical damages to what was paid, and gives you only two years to sue. It also doesn’t cap pain and suffering outside malpractice. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
texas.html:
How a Texas injury claim is valued

A Texas injury claim is built from two kinds of damages. Economic damages are the provable money losses: medical care already received and still needed, lost wages and lost earning capacity, and property damage. Non-economic damages pay for physical pain, mental anguish, physical impairment and disfigurement, which Texas juries consider as separate categories. Your share of responsibility then reduces the total, and above 50% it ends the claim.

Three Texas rules shape the number more than anything else. First, the 51% bar: if you are found more than half responsible, you recover nothing. Second, Texas limits medical damages to the amount actually paid or owed, not the full bill. Third, the defense can point to people who aren’t in the lawsuit at all, called responsible third parties, and the jury can assign them a share of the fault. Each is explained below with the statute behind it.

To test your own figures, use the Texas personal injury calculator or, for a crash, the Texas car accident calculator. Truck crashes, which often involve higher federal insurance minimums, have their own Texas truck accident calculator.

A Texas claim, worked through

This is an example, not a forecast. A driver is hit in a Houston intersection and needs physical therapy and two injections for a back injury. The providers billed $31,000. Health insurance paid $12,400 and the providers wrote off the rest. The driver lost $5,800 in wages. The other driver says the light was yellow and argues the injured driver was 40% responsible.

  • Recoverable medical expenses under Texas law: the $12,400 paid, not the $31,000 billed.
  • Economic damages: $12,400 plus $5,800 = $18,200.
  • Non-economic damages at two to three times the economic losses for a moderate injury: $36,400 to $54,600.
  • Claim before fault: $54,600 to $72,800.
  • At 40% responsibility the award drops by 40%: $32,760 to $43,680.

If the jury instead found the injured driver 51% responsible, the recovery would be zero. That cliff is why fault evidence, such as signal timing, video and witness statements, carries so much weight in Texas negotiations. A ten-point shift from 45% to 55% doesn’t trim the claim, it erases it.

Fault: the 51% bar and proportionate responsibility

Texas calls its system proportionate responsibility (Civil Practice and Remedies Code chapter 33). The jury assigns a percentage to every claimant, defendant, settling person and designated responsible third party. Your damages are reduced by your own percentage, and you can’t recover at all if your percentage is greater than 50% (§ 33.001). At exactly 50% you still recover half.

Responsible third parties

A defendant can ask the court to designate a responsible third party, someone who allegedly caused or contributed to the harm but isn’t being sued (§ 33.004). That can be an unknown hit-and-run driver, a company that went out of business or a person you chose not to sue. The jury can assign that person a percentage, which shrinks the defendants’ shares even though the third party pays nothing. Expect this argument whenever another driver, a property owner or a contractor was involved.

When one defendant pays for others

A defendant is responsible for the whole judgment, jointly and severally, only if the jury puts its share above 50%, or if it acted with others in certain serious crimes (§ 33.013). Otherwise each defendant pays only its own percentage. If a trucking company is 40% responsible and an uninsured driver 60%, the trucking company pays 40% of the damages and the rest may be uncollectable. The comparative fault calculator shows how a split changes the result.

Texas filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the day the claim accrues, usually the injury date (§ 16.003).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (§ 16.003).
  • Property damage, such as a car: two years (§ 16.003).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the treatment or the end of a course of treatment, with an outer limit of ten years (§ 74.251). You must give written notice and a medical records authorization at least 60 days before filing, which pauses the deadline for 75 days (§ 74.051).
  • Claims against a city, county or the state: written notice within six months of the incident, describing the injury, time and place (§ 101.101). A city charter can require notice even sooner, so check the city’s own rules the same week.

The two-year lawsuit deadline is short by national standards. A claim that is still in negotiation in month 20 is a claim the insurer knows is close to the line. The Texas filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Car insurance and PIP in Texas

Texas is an at-fault state. The at-fault driver’s liability insurer pays the injured person, and the minimum policy is $30,000 per person, $60,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage (Transportation Code § 601.072). Many Texas drivers carry only the minimum, so the at-fault driver’s limit often caps a serious-injury settlement. The policy limits calculator shows how much coverage is actually available.

Two coverages on your own policy can fill gaps:

  • Personal injury protection (PIP). Every Texas auto policy includes at least $2,500 of PIP, which pays your medical bills and part of lost income regardless of fault, unless you rejected it in writing (Insurance Code § 1952.152). Because Texas isn’t a no-fault state, using PIP doesn’t stop you from making a claim against the at-fault driver.
  • Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage (UM/UIM). Insurers must offer it, and it applies unless you rejected it in writing (§ 1952.101). It pays when the at-fault driver has no insurance, can’t be identified, or has too little to cover your damages, up to your own UM/UIM limit.

The PIP calculator estimates what your PIP pays and what is left for the liability claim.

Medical bills: paid or incurred

Since 2003, Texas has limited recovery of medical expenses to the amount actually paid or incurred by you or on your behalf (§ 41.0105). In Haygood v. De Escabedo (2011), the Texas Supreme Court held that amounts a provider has no right to collect, such as insurance write-offs, aren’t recoverable and that only evidence of recoverable amounts can go to the jury. In the example above that cut the medical figure by $18,600.

Texas also has a shortcut for proving bills. Under § 18.001 an injured person can serve an affidavit from each provider stating that the charges were reasonable and the care necessary. If the defense doesn’t serve a proper counteraffidavit from a qualified person by the deadline, the bills come in without live testimony. Insurers often serve counteraffidavits to push down the value of treatment, particularly when care was given on a letter of protection, where the provider waits to be paid from the settlement.

A 2025 bill, SB 30, would have tightened these rules further and changed how juries hear evidence on non-economic damages. It failed when the regular session ended in June 2025, so the rules above still apply.

Caps on damages in Texas

There is no cap on compensatory damages in ordinary injury cases. Car, truck, premises and product cases can recover the full value of medical costs, lost earnings, pain and mental anguish. The caps that do exist are narrower:

  • Exemplary (punitive) damages. They require clear and convincing proof of fraud, malice or gross negligence and a unanimous jury (§ 41.003). They are capped at the greater of $200,000 or twice the economic damages plus up to $750,000 of non-economic damages (§ 41.008). The cap doesn’t apply to harm from certain felonies, such as intoxication assault.
  • Medical malpractice, non-economic damages. $250,000 for all doctors and other individual providers together, plus up to $250,000 per health care institution with a $500,000 limit for all institutions, for a maximum of $750,000 (§ 74.301).
  • Medical malpractice deaths. A separate limit on total damages other than medical expenses, set at $500,000 in 1977 dollars and adjusted for inflation since (§ 74.303).
  • Government defendants. Claims under the Texas Tort Claims Act are capped at $250,000 per person, $500,000 per incident and $100,000 for property damage against the state and cities, and lower amounts against other local units (§ 101.023).

Malpractice claims also need an expert report served within 120 days of each defendant’s answer, or the case can be dismissed with fees (§ 74.351). The malpractice calculator applies the Texas caps.

Truck and rideshare crashes: more insurance, more defendants

Commercial vehicles change the math because they carry far more coverage than a family car. A truck carrying general freight across state lines must carry at least $750,000 of liability insurance under federal rules, and more for some hazardous cargo (49 CFR § 387.9). Claims against a trucking company can also reach the carrier’s own negligence, such as hiring an unqualified driver or ignoring hours-of-service limits, and federal driver logs, electronic logging data and inspection records become evidence. That data can be overwritten, so a letter asking the company to preserve it should go out early.

Rideshare crashes have their own coverage tiers under Insurance Code chapter 1954. While a driver is logged into the app and waiting for a request, the company’s coverage must provide at least $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $25,000 for property. From the moment a ride is accepted until the passenger gets out, at least $1,000,000 of liability coverage applies. Which tier was active at the moment of the crash often decides how much a serious claim can recover. The rideshare accident calculator and the truck accident calculator use these limits.

The Stowers doctrine and policy-limit demands

Texas has a long-standing rule that pushes insurers to settle within limits. Under G.A. Stowers Furniture Co. v. American Indemnity Co. (1929), if an injured person makes a clear demand within the policy limits that offers a full release, and the insurer unreasonably refuses it, the insurer can be responsible for a later judgment above the limits. A well-drafted Stowers demand, with medical records, a deadline and an offer to release all claims against the insured, is one of the main tools in a Texas claim with serious injuries and low coverage. A careless one can be rejected on a technicality, so the details matter. The demand letter generator covers the structure.

When the injured person dies

Texas allows a wrongful death claim only by the surviving spouse, children and parents of the person who died (§ 71.004). Siblings and other relatives can’t recover under the statute. The family can recover lost financial support and household services, loss of companionship and mental anguish. If none of them sues within three months of the death, the executor or administrator can bring the claim unless the family asks them not to.

A separate survival claim (§ 71.021) belongs to the estate and recovers what the person could have claimed for their own injuries before death, including medical costs, pain and mental anguish, and funeral costs. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Claims against government in Texas

Government entities in Texas are immune from suit except where the Tort Claims Act waives that immunity. The main waivers cover injuries caused by an employee’s use of a motor vehicle, by a condition or use of tangible property, and by premises defects (§ 101.021). Many other claims, such as most claims about police decisions, are excluded. Within the waiver, the six-month notice rule and the damage caps above apply. A government claim is often the right claim to pursue alongside a claim against a private driver, for example when a city vehicle or a road hazard the city knew about was involved.

Dog bites, bars and other Texas rules

Dog bites. Texas has no dog bite statute. An owner is liable if they knew the dog was dangerous, often called the one-bite rule, or if they were negligent, for example by breaking a leash ordinance (Marshall v. Ranne, 1974). See the Texas dog bite calculator.

Bars and restaurants. The Dram Shop Act makes an alcohol seller liable when it was apparent the customer was obviously intoxicated to the point of presenting a clear danger to themselves and others, and the intoxication caused the harm (Alcoholic Beverage Code § 2.02). A seller whose staff completed approved training and who didn’t encourage the violation can avoid liability for employee mistakes. A bar’s policy is often much larger than a driver’s, which makes this claim worth checking after a drunk driving crash.

Seat belts. Since Nabors Well Services v. Romero (2015), a jury can hear evidence that you weren’t wearing a seat belt and assign you a share of responsibility if it made your injuries worse.

Falls on property. For a customer or other invitee, the owner must have known or should have known of the dangerous condition and failed to fix it or warn of it. Proving how long a spill was on the floor is often the whole case. The Texas slip and fall calculator applies the fault rules.

Interest, settlement offers and timing

Prejudgment interest in Texas injury cases starts on the earlier of the 180th day after the defendant receives written notice of the claim or the day suit is filed, and runs until the day before judgment (Finance Code § 304.104). The rate tracks the prime rate, with a floor of 5% and a ceiling of 15%. Sending a written notice of claim early starts that clock.

Texas also has an offer-of-settlement procedure (Civil Practice and Remedies Code chapter 42 and Rule 167). If a party rejects a qualifying offer and the judgment is significantly less favorable to them, they can owe some of the other side’s litigation costs. For a claimant, that means a judgment below 80% of a rejected defense offer.

Many crash claims settle within months after treatment ends. Lawsuits often take one to three years, and cases seeking $250,000 or less can use the expedited trial rules in Rule 169. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage.

What comes out of a Texas settlement

  • The lawyer’s contingency fee and case costs, commonly 33⅓% to 40%.
  • Hospital liens. A hospital or emergency provider that treated you can hold a lien on the claim for its reasonable charges, if it filed the lien properly (Property Code chapter 55).
  • Health plan and Medicaid or Medicare reimbursement, under the plan’s terms and federal and state rules.
  • PIP generally doesn’t have to be repaid from a liability settlement, but check your policy.

The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Get the police crash report (form CR-3) from the Texas Department of Transportation’s online crash report system.
  • If a city or county vehicle or road was involved, send the written notice of claim within the charter or six-month deadline.
  • Keep your explanations of benefits. In Texas, what your health plan paid is the medical number that matters.
  • Send the at-fault insurer a written notice of claim to start the 180-day interest clock.
  • Don’t sign a medical authorization giving the other driver’s insurer your full medical history.

faqs.question: Can I recover in Texas if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as your share of responsibility is 50% or less. Your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 51% or more you recover nothing (Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 33.001).

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Texas?
faqs.answer: Two years from the injury in most cases, and two years from the death for wrongful death (§ 16.003). Claims against a city, county or the state need written notice within six months, or sooner if a city charter says so.

faqs.question: Is Texas a no-fault state?
faqs.answer: No. The at-fault driver’s insurer pays. Texas policies include $2,500 of PIP unless you rejected it in writing, and PIP pays your medical bills regardless of fault without stopping a claim against the other driver.

faqs.question: Does Texas cap pain and suffering?
faqs.answer: Not in ordinary injury cases. Caps apply to punitive damages, to non-economic damages in medical malpractice ($250,000 for doctors plus up to $500,000 for institutions) and to claims against government entities.

faqs.question: Will I recover the full amount my doctors billed?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Texas limits medical damages to the amount actually paid or incurred (§ 41.0105). Insurance write-offs aren’t recoverable, and the defense can challenge bills with a counteraffidavit.

faqs.question: What is a Stowers demand?
faqs.answer: A written offer to settle within the at-fault driver’s policy limits in exchange for a full release. If the insurer unreasonably refuses a proper Stowers demand, it can be liable for a later judgment above the limits.

florida.title: Florida Personal Injury Claims: PIP, the 51% Rule and HB 837
florida.metaTitle: Florida Personal Injury Laws 2026: PIP, Fault and Deadlines
florida.metaDescription: How Florida’s PIP, permanent-injury threshold, 51% fault bar, two-year deadline, HB 837 medical evidence rules and $200,000 government cap shape a claim.
florida.excerpt: Florida is a no-fault state that doesn’t require bodily injury coverage, and since 2023 it bars recovery above 50% fault and gives you two years to sue. Here is how PIP, the injury threshold, HB 837 and Florida’s damage limits work, with the statute behind each.
florida.html:
How a Florida injury claim is valued

Florida injury claims follow the same basic arithmetic as other states: economic losses (medical care, lost income, property damage) plus non-economic losses (pain, suffering, mental anguish, inconvenience and loss of enjoyment of life), reduced by your share of fault. What sets Florida apart is everything around that arithmetic. It is a no-fault state for car crashes, so your own insurance pays first. Drivers aren’t required to carry bodily injury liability coverage at all. And a 2023 law, HB 837, rewrote fault, deadlines, medical evidence and insurer bad-faith rules for claims that arose after March 24, 2023.

This guide walks through those rules in the order they usually affect a claim, with the statute for each. To run your own figures, use the Florida car accident calculator, which applies PIP and the injury threshold, or the Florida personal injury calculator for other injuries.

A Florida car crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is hit while changing lanes in Orlando and is diagnosed with a herniated disc that a doctor says is permanent. Medical care, valued under Florida’s evidence rules, comes to $26,000, and the driver lost $9,000 in wages. PIP paid the first $10,000 of benefits. The other driver’s insurer argues the injured driver was 30% at fault for not checking a blind spot.

  • Total economic losses: $26,000 medical plus $9,000 wages = $35,000.
  • Losses PIP already paid can’t be claimed again from the other driver, so the economic claim is $25,000.
  • Pain and suffering is available because the injury is permanent. At two to three times the economic losses: $70,000 to $105,000.
  • Claim before fault: $95,000 to $130,000.
  • After a 30% fault reduction: $66,500 to $91,000.

Change two facts and the picture changes completely. If a jury found the driver 51% at fault, the recovery from the other driver would be zero under the post-2023 rule. If the doctor couldn’t say the injury was permanent, Florida’s tort threshold would block the pain and suffering claim and leave only the unpaid economic losses. And because Florida doesn’t require bodily injury coverage, the other driver may have no liability insurance at all, which makes your own uninsured motorist coverage the real source of payment.

Fault after HB 837: the 51% bar

For negligence claims that arose after March 24, 2023, Florida moved from pure comparative fault to a modified system. A claimant found more than 50% at fault can’t recover any damages; at 50% or less, damages are reduced by the claimant’s percentage (§ 768.81(6)). Medical malpractice claims are the exception and still use pure comparative fault. Claims that arose on or before March 24, 2023 follow the old pure comparative rule.

Fault is apportioned among all parties, including people who aren’t in the lawsuit if the defense proves their share. Florida also lets a jury consider not wearing a seat belt as evidence of comparative negligence (§ 316.614(10)), so expect that argument in any crash where belt use is in question. Use the comparative fault calculator to see how a fault split changes your number.

Florida filing deadlines

  • Negligence, including most car crash, fall and injury claims: two years for claims that arose after March 24, 2023. Earlier claims kept the old four-year period (§ 95.11).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (§ 95.11).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from when the injury was or should have been discovered, with an outer limit of four years in most cases (§ 95.11). Before suing, you must send a notice of intent and allow a 90-day investigation period (§ 766.106).
  • Claims against the state, a county or a city: written notice to the agency, and in most cases to the Department of Financial Services, within three years, and a lawsuit within four years (§ 768.28).

The two-year deadline is new enough that many people still hear “four years” from friends or old websites. For a crash in 2026, plan on two. The Florida filing deadline calculator counts the dates.

No-fault insurance and PIP

Every Florida driver must carry $10,000 of personal injury protection (PIP) and $10,000 of property damage liability (§§ 627.736 and 324.022). After a crash, your own PIP pays first, whoever caused it:

  • 80% of reasonable medical expenses and 60% of lost income, up to $10,000 in total, plus a $5,000 death benefit (§ 627.736).
  • You must get initial treatment within 14 days of the crash, or PIP doesn’t pay medical benefits.
  • The full $10,000 is available only if a doctor, dentist, physician assistant or advanced practice nurse finds you had an emergency medical condition. Otherwise medical benefits stop at $2,500.

Repeal of PIP has been debated for years. A repeal passed the Legislature once, in 2021, and was vetoed, and repeal bills died again in the 2025 and 2026 sessions. As of November 2026, PIP is still required. Some websites have claimed otherwise; they’re wrong. The no-fault and PIP calculator estimates what PIP pays.

The tort threshold: when you can claim pain and suffering

Because PIP pays the first losses, Florida limits who can sue the at-fault driver for non-economic damages. You can claim pain, suffering and inconvenience only if the crash caused one of these (§ 627.737(2)):

  • Significant and permanent loss of an important bodily function
  • A permanent injury, within a reasonable degree of medical probability, other than scarring or disfigurement
  • Significant and permanent scarring or disfigurement
  • Death

Economic losses that PIP didn’t cover, such as the 20% of medical bills and 40% of wages PIP leaves unpaid, and anything above $10,000, can be claimed without meeting the threshold. Whether an injury is permanent is usually a medical opinion question, which is why imaging, specialist records and an impairment rating often decide the value of a Florida crash claim.

Pedestrians, cyclists and rideshare passengers

PIP follows people, not just cars. A pedestrian or cyclist hit by a car is usually covered by PIP on a policy in their own household. A Florida resident with no household auto policy can usually claim PIP from the vehicle that hit them (§ 627.736(4)). That means a person on foot still goes through the 14-day treatment rule and the emergency medical condition rule before the claim against the driver begins, and still has to meet the permanent-injury threshold for pain and suffering.

Rideshare crashes have their own coverage levels under § 627.748. While an Uber or Lyft driver is logged into the app and waiting for a request, the company’s coverage must include at least $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $25,000 for property, plus PIP. From the moment a ride is accepted until the passenger gets out, at least $1,000,000 of liability coverage applies. That is often the largest policy in a Florida crash and the reason it matters exactly what the app showed at the moment of impact. The rideshare accident calculator and the pedestrian accident calculator apply these rules.

Trucks are similar. Interstate freight carriers must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, so a serious truck crash claim is less likely to be capped by insurance than a crash with a car insured only for PIP. The Florida truck accident calculator uses those limits.

Bodily injury coverage isn’t required, so check UM

Florida is one of very few states that doesn’t require drivers to carry bodily injury liability insurance in the first place. Many do, but plenty carry only PIP and property damage. Bodily injury coverage becomes mandatory only in certain cases, such as after a crash causing injury or a DUI conviction, when the financial responsibility law requires proof of coverage going forward (chapter 324).

That makes your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage unusually important. Insurers must offer UM equal to your bodily injury limits, and you have it unless you rejected it in writing or chose lower limits (§ 627.727). Stacked UM lets you combine limits for each vehicle on the policy. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how much coverage can actually pay a claim.

Medical bills: what Florida juries now see

HB 837 created § 768.0427, which controls what evidence of medical expenses a jury hears in injury cases:

  • Bills already paid: only the amount actually paid, from any source.
  • Unpaid bills, if you have private health insurance: what that insurance would pay, plus your share, even if you treated outside insurance on a letter of protection.
  • Unpaid bills, if you have no insurance or have Medicare or Medicaid: 120% of the Medicare rate, or 170% of the Medicaid rate if no Medicare rate exists.
  • Future care: valued the same way, based on your coverage.

If you treated under a letter of protection, where a provider waits to be paid from the settlement, you must disclose the letter, itemized coded bills, whether the bill was sold to a factoring company and for how much, and whether a lawyer referred you to the provider. Damages for medical care can’t exceed the amounts admitted under these rules. In practice this has pushed Florida medical values down, especially for claims built on full billed charges.

Insurer bad faith and settlement deadlines

Florida’s bad-faith law (§ 624.155) lets an insured or injured person sue an insurer that fails to settle a claim when it could and should have. HB 837 added a safe harbor: an insurer can’t be held in bad faith if it tenders the policy limits, or the amount demanded if lower, within 90 days after receiving notice of the claim with enough evidence to support it. The law also says negligence alone isn’t bad faith and that a jury can consider whether the claimant acted in good faith, for example by giving the insurer the information it needed.

The practical effect is that a well-documented demand gives the insurer a 90-day window, and many limits tenders now arrive within it. The demand letter generator helps assemble one. HB 837 also ended most one-way attorney fee awards against insurers, which used to make an insurer pay the policyholder’s lawyer after losing a coverage suit.

Proposals for settlement. Under § 768.79, if a defendant’s formal offer is rejected and the judgment is at least 25% less than the offer, the plaintiff can owe the defendant’s attorney fees from the offer date. If a plaintiff’s offer is rejected and the judgment is at least 25% more, the defendant pays the plaintiff’s fees. These offers carry real risk for both sides.

Damage limits in Florida

Florida has no cap on non-economic damages in ordinary injury cases, and its Supreme Court struck down the medical malpractice caps (Estate of McCall v. United States, 2014, for death cases, and North Broward Hospital District v. Kalitan, 2017, for injury cases). The limits that matter are these:

  • Government defendants: $200,000 per person and $300,000 per incident (§ 768.28(5)). Anything above that needs a claims bill passed by the Legislature. A 2026 bill, HB 145, would have raised the limits to $350,000 and $500,000, but the Governor vetoed it on June 30, 2026.
  • Punitive damages: generally the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000. Higher limits apply when the conduct was driven by unreasonable financial gain, and there is no limit when the defendant specifically intended to cause harm (§ 768.73).

The malpractice calculator reflects that Florida has no malpractice cap, but see the wrongful death limit below.

Wrongful death, and the medical malpractice exception

Florida’s Wrongful Death Act (§§ 768.16 to 768.26) lets the personal representative bring one claim for the estate and the survivors. Survivors can recover lost support and services; a spouse can recover lost companionship and mental pain and suffering; children under 25 can recover lost parental companionship and mental pain; and parents of a minor child can recover their mental pain. The estate recovers medical and funeral costs it paid and lost earnings and net accumulations.

One exception is unique to Florida. In medical negligence deaths, adult children 25 and older can’t recover non-economic damages for a parent’s death, and parents can’t recover them for the death of an adult child (§ 768.21(8)). When the person who died had no spouse and no children under 25, that can leave no non-economic claim at all. The Legislature voted to repeal this rule in 2025, but the Governor vetoed it, so it still applies. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites, bars and security

Slip and fall in a business. If you fall on a transitory substance, such as a spill, you must prove the business knew or should have known about it and failed to fix it, for example because it was there long enough or happened regularly (§ 768.0755). See the Florida slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable for bites in public places or where the victim was lawfully on private property (§ 767.04). A clearly displayed “Bad Dog” sign can limit liability, except for victims under six. Your own negligence reduces damages. See the Florida dog bite calculator.

Bars. Florida’s dram shop law is narrow. A seller is liable only for willfully and unlawfully serving someone under 21 or knowingly serving a person habitually addicted to alcohol (§ 768.125).

Negligent security. HB 837 added rules for claims against property owners over crimes by third parties. Fault is apportioned to the criminal as well as the owner, and owners of apartment and condominium properties that meet listed security measures get a presumption against liability (§§ 768.0701 and 768.0706).

Liens and what you keep

  • Florida Medicaid recovers from a settlement using a formula: after 25% for attorney fees and taxable costs, Medicaid takes half of what remains, up to the amount it paid. You can ask an administrative judge to reduce it if the settlement doesn’t fully cover your damages (§ 409.910).
  • Hospital liens are set by county or city ordinance in Florida, not one statewide law, so the rules vary.
  • Collateral sources that don’t have repayment rights, such as some health benefits, can be deducted from a verdict after trial (§ 768.76).
  • Settlements for children above $15,000 need court approval (§ 744.387).

The medical lien calculator shows the take-home amount after fees and liens.

What to do in the first weeks

  • See a doctor within 14 days of a crash, or you lose PIP medical benefits.
  • Ask the treating doctor whether you had an emergency medical condition, which unlocks the full $10,000 of PIP.
  • Find out whether the other driver carries bodily injury coverage, and report the claim to your own insurer for PIP and UM.
  • If you have private health insurance, use it. Under § 768.0427 the jury will hear what it would have paid anyway.
  • Calendar the two-year deadline. For claims against a public agency, the three-year notice deadline applies too.
  • If a provider treats you on a letter of protection, keep the letter and the itemized coded bills. You will have to disclose them under § 768.0427, and gaps invite a fight over value.
  • After a rideshare crash, ask the company in writing which coverage tier applied and save screenshots of the trip from the app.

faqs.question: How long do I have to sue after a Florida car accident?
faqs.answer: Two years for negligence claims that arose after March 24, 2023 (§ 95.11). Claims that arose before that date kept the old four-year period. Claims against a government agency also need written notice within three years.

faqs.question: Can I get a settlement in Florida if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you were 50% or less at fault; your damages are reduced by your share. Since HB 837, a claimant more than 50% at fault recovers nothing, except in medical malpractice cases, which still use pure comparative fault.

faqs.question: Can I sue for pain and suffering after a Florida car accident?
faqs.answer: Only if the crash caused a permanent injury, significant and permanent scarring or disfigurement, significant and permanent loss of an important bodily function, or death (§ 627.737). Unpaid economic losses can be claimed without meeting that threshold.

faqs.question: Did Florida repeal PIP no-fault insurance?
faqs.answer: No. Repeal bills died in the 2025 and 2026 sessions, and the only repeal that passed, in 2021, was vetoed. Drivers must still carry $10,000 of PIP and $10,000 of property damage liability.

faqs.question: What happens if the driver who hit me has no bodily injury insurance?
faqs.answer: Florida doesn’t require it, so this is common. Your own uninsured motorist coverage is usually the source of payment for injuries beyond PIP. You can also pursue the driver personally, but collecting from an individual is often difficult.

faqs.question: How much can I recover from a Florida city or county?
faqs.answer: Up to $200,000 per person and $300,000 per incident under § 768.28. A bill to raise those limits was vetoed on June 30, 2026. Amounts above the cap need a claims bill from the Legislature.

new-york.title: New York Personal Injury Claims: No-Fault, Serious Injury and Deadlines
new-york.metaTitle: New York Personal Injury Laws 2026: No-Fault and Deadlines
new-york.metaDescription: How New York’s no-fault $50,000 PIP, serious injury threshold, pure comparative fault, three-year deadline, 90-day notice and Scaffold Law affect a claim.
new-york.excerpt: New York doesn’t cap damages and never bars recovery for partial fault, but car crash claims run through no-fault and the serious-injury threshold, and claims against cities need notice within 90 days. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
new-york.html:
How a New York injury claim is valued

New York pays injured people for economic loss (medical care, lost earnings, household help and other out-of-pocket costs) and non-economic loss (pain and suffering, including the loss of enjoyment of life). There is no cap on either in ordinary injury cases, and partial fault never wipes out a claim. Those are generous rules. The catch, for car crashes, is the no-fault system: your own insurer pays the first $50,000 of economic loss, and you can sue for pain and suffering only if the injury meets the statutory definition of a “serious injury”.

Outside car crashes, other New York rules do the heavy lifting: the Scaffold Law for construction falls, very short notice deadlines for claims against cities, and a wrongful death statute that still limits families to financial losses. Each is covered below with the statute behind it. To run your own figures, use the New York car accident calculator or the New York personal injury calculator.

A New York crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A delivery driver is broadsided at an intersection in Queens and fractures a wrist that needs surgery. Medical costs reach $38,000 and the driver loses $21,000 in wages. The other driver’s insurer says the delivery driver was speeding and argues for 25% fault.

  • Total economic loss: $38,000 plus $21,000 = $59,000.
  • No-fault pays the first $50,000 of economic loss, whoever was at fault. The remaining $9,000 can be claimed from the at-fault driver.
  • A fracture is listed as a serious injury, so pain and suffering is available. At two to three times the economic loss: $118,000 to $177,000.
  • Claim against the other driver before fault: $127,000 to $186,000.
  • After a 25% reduction under pure comparative fault: $95,250 to $139,500.

Without the fracture, the outcome could be very different. A soft-tissue injury that doesn’t meet the serious-injury definition would leave only the $9,000 of economic loss above no-fault. That is why so many New York car cases are fought over medical proof of the threshold rather than over who caused the crash.

Fault: pure comparative negligence

Under CPLR 1411, your own culpable conduct reduces your damages in proportion but doesn’t bar recovery. A person 60% at fault still recovers 40%. New York also lets a jury consider not wearing a seat belt, but only to reduce damages for injuries the belt would have prevented, not as fault for causing the crash (Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1229-c(8)).

When several parties share fault

CPLR 1601 limits a defendant who is 50% or less at fault to its own share of non-economic damages; it still owes all economic damages. The limit doesn’t apply in several important situations listed in CPLR 1602, including claims arising from the use of a motor vehicle, Labor Law construction claims and defendants who acted with reckless disregard. In a multi-car crash, every at-fault driver can be held responsible for the whole award. The comparative fault calculator shows the effect of a fault split.

New York filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (CPLR 214(5)).
  • Property damage: three years (CPLR 214(4)).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (Estates, Powers and Trusts Law § 5-4.1).
  • Medical malpractice: two years and six months from the act or the end of continuous treatment for the same condition (CPLR 214-a). For a missed cancer diagnosis, Lavern’s Law (2018) starts the clock when you knew or should have known, with an outer limit of seven years.
  • Claims against a city, county, town, village or school district: a notice of claim within 90 days (General Municipal Law § 50-e), then a lawsuit within one year and 90 days (§ 50-i). In New York City, the notice goes to the Comptroller’s office. The city can examine you under oath before you sue (§ 50-h).
  • Claims against the State of New York: file a claim, or serve a notice of intention to file one, within 90 days in the Court of Claims (Court of Claims Act § 10).
  • No-fault benefits: a written application within 30 days of the crash, with medical bills submitted within 45 days of treatment (11 NYCRR § 65-1.1).

The 30-day no-fault deadline and the 90-day notice of claim are the two that people miss most. A court can allow a late notice of claim in some cases, but it is discretionary. The New York filing deadline calculator counts these dates.

No-fault benefits: what your own policy pays

New York requires every car policy to provide personal injury protection that pays “basic economic loss” up to $50,000 per person, regardless of fault (Insurance Law § 5102(a)). It covers:

  • Necessary medical and rehabilitation expenses, paid at the state fee schedule
  • 80% of lost earnings, up to $2,000 a month, for up to three years
  • Up to $25 a day for other reasonable expenses, such as help at home, for up to a year
  • A $2,000 death benefit

Pedestrians and cyclists hit by a car are usually covered by the no-fault policy of a car in their household or, if there is none, the car that hit them. Motorcycle riders are not covered by no-fault, and because they aren’t “covered persons” the serious-injury threshold generally doesn’t limit their claims either. Many drivers buy optional additional PIP above $50,000. Disputes over denied no-fault bills usually go to arbitration rather than court. The no-fault calculator estimates what the policy pays.

The serious-injury threshold

You can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering, and for economic loss above $50,000, only if you suffered a “serious injury” (Insurance Law §§ 5102(d) and 5104). The statute lists:

  • Death, dismemberment or significant disfigurement
  • A fracture
  • Loss of a fetus
  • Permanent loss of use of a body organ, member, function or system
  • Permanent consequential limitation of use of a body organ or member
  • Significant limitation of use of a body function or system
  • A medically determined injury that kept you from performing substantially all of your usual daily activities for at least 90 of the first 180 days after the crash

Courts require objective medical evidence for the limitation categories, such as imaging and measured loss of range of motion compared with normal, not just reports of pain (Toure v. Avis Rent A Car Systems, 2002). Gaps in treatment and prior injuries to the same body part are the defense’s usual arguments. Economic loss above $50,000 can be claimed whether or not the injury is serious.

Car insurance minimums and SUM coverage

New York requires liability coverage of at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per crash for injury, $50,000 and $100,000 for death, and $10,000 for property damage (Vehicle and Traffic Law § 311). Uninsured motorist coverage of at least $25,000/$50,000 is mandatory too (Insurance Law § 3420(f)(1)).

Because $25,000 is a low limit next to a surgery or a long recovery, supplementary uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage (SUM) on your own policy is often what pays a serious claim. SUM is optional, can be bought up to your own liability limits, and applies when the at-fault driver’s coverage is too small (§ 3420(f)(2)). Check your declarations page soon after a crash. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how the coverages stack up against a claim.

Who pays: owners, permissive drivers and rental cars

New York makes the owner of a vehicle liable for the negligence of anyone driving it with permission (Vehicle and Traffic Law § 388). If a friend borrowed a car and caused the crash, the owner’s policy is on the hook as well as the driver’s own coverage, which can add a second source of insurance. Permission is presumed, and the owner has to prove it wasn’t given. Rental and leasing companies are the main exception: a federal law, the Graves Amendment, shields them from owner liability unless the company itself was negligent, for example by renting a car with known defects.

Employers are liable for employees driving in the course of work, which is why delivery, contractor and company-car crashes often involve a commercial policy with much higher limits than the personal minimum. Truck crashes add federal minimums of at least $750,000 for interstate freight carriers and records such as driver logs that should be preserved early. The New York truck accident calculator uses those limits.

Construction injuries and the Scaffold Law

New York gives construction workers unusual protection. Labor Law § 240(1), the Scaffold Law, makes property owners and general contractors absolutely liable for injuries from gravity-related accidents, such as falls from a height or being struck by a falling object, when they didn’t provide proper safety devices like scaffolds, harnesses, hoists or ladders. The worker’s own carelessness doesn’t reduce the award; the main defense is that the worker’s own conduct was the sole cause of the accident. Labor Law § 241(6) adds liability for violations of specific Industrial Code safety rules.

These claims run alongside workers’ compensation, which can’t be sued for directly but can assert a lien on the third-party recovery. The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Damages: no caps, but limits on what families recover

New York doesn’t cap compensatory or punitive damages in injury cases, including medical malpractice. Jury awards are reviewed on appeal and can be reduced if they “deviate materially” from reasonable compensation (CPLR 5501(c)), so prior verdicts for similar injuries matter in negotiation.

Wrongful death is the big exception. Under EPTL § 5-4.3, families recover only pecuniary losses: lost financial support and services, the value of a parent’s care and guidance for children, and medical and funeral costs. Grief and loss of companionship aren’t compensable. The Grieving Families Act, which would change that, has passed the Legislature four times and been vetoed four times, most recently in December 2025, so the old rule still applies. The estate can still recover the person’s conscious pain and suffering before death in a separate survival claim. The wrongful death calculator reflects these limits.

Medical malpractice in New York

Besides the 2½-year deadline, malpractice cases need a certificate of merit stating that a lawyer consulted a doctor and believes the case has a reasonable basis (CPLR 3012-a). There is no cap on damages, but lawyers’ contingency fees are capped on a sliding scale: 30% of the first $250,000, 25% of the next $250,000, 20% of the next $500,000, 15% of the next $250,000 and 10% of anything above $1.25 million (Judiciary Law § 474-a). Large future damages are often paid over time under CPLR article 50-A. The malpractice calculator applies New York’s rules.

Dog bites, bars and falls

Dog bites. For decades New York allowed a claim against an owner only if the owner knew or should have known the dog was vicious. In Flanders v. Goodfellow (April 2025), the Court of Appeals changed that: an injured person can now sue for ordinary negligence too, for example when an owner fails to restrain a dog, as well as or instead of the vicious-propensity claim. Medical costs are recoverable without proof of fault if the dog had already been declared dangerous (Agriculture and Markets Law § 123). See the New York dog bite calculator.

Bars. The Dram Shop Act lets a person injured by an intoxicated person sue a seller who unlawfully sold alcohol to someone visibly intoxicated or under 21 (General Obligations Law § 11-101).

Falls. A property owner is liable if it created the dangerous condition or had actual or constructive notice of it. In New York City, owners of most buildings are responsible for keeping the sidewalk next to their property in reasonably safe condition, so a fall on a cracked sidewalk is often a claim against the building owner rather than the city. Owner-occupied one-, two- and three-family homes used only as residences are an exception. For streets and many other defects, the city generally can’t be liable unless it had prior written notice of the defect, which is why a pothole map or a 311 complaint record can decide a claim. The New York slip and fall calculator applies the fault rules.

Liens, health insurance and what you keep

  • Health insurers generally can’t take a share of your settlement. General Obligations Law § 5-335 bars most health insurers from seeking reimbursement from a personal injury settlement. Statutory liens such as Medicaid, Medicare and workers’ compensation are excepted, and self-funded employer plans governed by federal law may not be covered.
  • Collateral source reduction. After a verdict, the court reduces economic damages by amounts paid by collateral sources such as health insurance, unless the source has a lien or reimbursement right (CPLR 4545).
  • Settlements for children need court approval through an infant compromise order (CPLR 1207 and 1208).

The medical lien calculator shows what a settlement leaves after fees and liens.

Interest, offers and how long claims take

Most New York injury claims settle, either before a lawsuit or after one has been filed and the parties have exchanged records and testimony. After a lawsuit, the plaintiff files a note of issue when the case is ready for trial, and in busy courts such as those in New York City the wait for a trial date can be long. That delay is one reason insurers settle cases with strong serious-injury proof and clear liability before trial.

Interest works differently than in many states. In injury cases, interest at the statutory rate of 9% a year generally runs from the date of a liability verdict, not from the date of the injury (CPLR 5002 and 5004), so there is little interest pressure while a case is pending. New York’s offer-of-compromise rules (CPLR 3221) shift only modest court costs, so they carry less weight than offer rules in states such as Florida. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage, and the settlement offer checker compares an offer with your estimate.

Before you accept, add up what comes out: the lawyer’s fee, usually one third outside malpractice cases, case costs, and any Medicaid, Medicare or workers’ compensation lien. A settlement of a no-fault case also should not release your right to unpaid no-fault benefits unless that is intended.

What to do in the first weeks

  • File the no-fault application (form NF-2) with the right insurer within 30 days, and make sure providers bill within 45 days.
  • If a city, county, school district or public authority may be involved, serve the notice of claim within 90 days.
  • Get an X-ray or MRI where symptoms persist. Objective findings decide the serious-injury question.
  • Check your own policy for SUM coverage and report the claim.
  • Keep a diary of daily activities you can’t do. It is the evidence for the 90/180-day category.
  • If you can’t work, get a letter from your employer and keep pay stubs. No-fault pays lost earnings only with proof, and the same records support the claim above $50,000.
  • Be careful what you post online during the claim. Insurers look at social media when they argue that an injury didn’t limit your usual activities.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury lawsuit in New York?
faqs.answer: Three years from the injury (CPLR 214(5)). Wrongful death claims have two years, malpractice claims two and a half years, and claims against a city or other municipality need a notice of claim within 90 days.

faqs.question: What counts as a serious injury in New York?
faqs.answer: The list in Insurance Law § 5102(d): death, dismemberment, significant disfigurement, a fracture, loss of a fetus, permanent loss of use or significant or permanent limitation of a body part or function, or an injury that kept you from substantially all usual activities for 90 of the first 180 days.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in New York?
faqs.answer: Yes. New York uses pure comparative fault, so your damages are reduced by your percentage but never eliminated. Not wearing a seat belt can reduce damages for injuries a belt would have prevented.

faqs.question: What does New York no-fault insurance pay?
faqs.answer: Up to $50,000 per person for medical bills, 80% of lost earnings up to $2,000 a month, and up to $25 a day for other expenses, whoever caused the crash. You must apply within 30 days.

faqs.question: Can I recover pain and suffering in a New York wrongful death case?
faqs.answer: The family can’t recover for grief or lost companionship; New York limits wrongful death damages to financial losses. The estate can recover the person’s own conscious pain and suffering before death in a survival claim.

faqs.question: Can I sue a dog owner in New York if the dog never bit before?
faqs.answer: Since Flanders v. Goodfellow (2025), yes, if the owner was negligent, for example by failing to restrain the dog. The older claim based on the owner’s knowledge of the dog’s vicious tendencies is still available too.
