north-carolina.metaTitle: North Carolina Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault and Deadlines
north-carolina.metaDescription: How North Carolina’s contributory negligence rule, three-year deadline, 2025 insurance changes (50/100/50), Rule 414 and 50% lien cap affect a claim.
north-carolina.excerpt: North Carolina can bar your claim if you were even slightly at fault, so the exceptions matter. It gives you three years to sue and, since July 2025, higher insurance minimums and better UIM coverage. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
north-carolina.html:
How a North Carolina injury claim is valued

A North Carolina injury claim pays for medical expenses, lost earnings and other financial losses, plus pain and suffering, scarring, and permanent injury. There is no cap on those damages outside medical malpractice. On paper, the math looks like any other state’s.

The difference is fault. North Carolina is one of only a handful of jurisdictions that still use contributory negligence: if you were even slightly at fault for your own injury, you can be barred from recovering anything. That single rule shapes every North Carolina negotiation, and the exceptions to it, especially last clear chance and gross negligence, are where many claims are won or lost. This guide explains it, along with North Carolina’s three-year deadline, the insurance changes that took effect on July 1, 2025, and the state’s limits on medical bills and liens, with the statute or case behind each.

Run your own figures with the North Carolina car accident calculator or the North Carolina personal injury calculator.

A North Carolina claim, worked through

An example, not a forecast. A driver is hit by a car pulling out of a parking lot in Charlotte and treats for a neck injury, including injections. Providers billed $30,000; health insurance paid $17,500 and the providers accepted it. Lost wages are $7,000.

  • Medical expenses under North Carolina’s evidence rule: the $17,500 actually paid, not the $30,000 billed.
  • Economic damages: $17,500 plus $7,000 = $24,500.
  • Pain and suffering at two to three times the economic damages, and the claim before any fault issue: $73,500 to $98,000.

Now suppose the insurer finds a witness who says the injured driver was going a few miles over the limit. In most states that might cut the claim by 10%. In North Carolina, if a jury finds that the driver’s speed was a proximate cause of the crash, the recovery is zero. That is why North Carolina insurers deny claims over small fault arguments that adjusters elsewhere would simply discount, and why the evidence that you did nothing wrong deserves as much attention as the evidence of your injuries.

Contributory negligence

Under North Carolina common law, a plaintiff whose own negligence contributed to the injury, even slightly, can’t recover from a defendant whose negligence was ordinary rather than gross. The defense has to plead contributory negligence and prove it; the injured person doesn’t have to disprove it (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-139). Common contributory negligence arguments include speeding, following too closely, not keeping a proper lookout, walking outside a crosswalk, and for falls, failing to watch where you were going.

Exceptions that keep a claim alive

  • Last clear chance. If you were negligent and put yourself in a position of peril you couldn’t escape, and the defendant saw or should have seen your danger in time to avoid the harm but failed to use that chance, you can still recover. This doctrine comes up often in pedestrian cases.
  • Gross negligence or willful conduct. Ordinary contributory negligence isn’t a defense when the defendant’s conduct was grossly negligent or willful and wanton, such as racing or driving while heavily impaired. The plaintiff’s own gross negligence can still bar the claim.
  • Children. Very young children are presumed incapable of negligence, and older children are judged by what a child of the same age, experience and capacity would do.

North Carolina also keeps joint and several liability, the companion rule: when two or more defendants are at fault, each can be made to pay the whole judgment. That helps when one defendant has little insurance. The comparative fault calculator shows how North Carolina’s all-or-nothing rule compares with other states.

Seat belts

Not wearing a seat belt generally can’t be used as evidence of negligence, including contributory negligence, in a North Carolina civil case (§ 20-135.2A(d)). The insurer can’t use it to bar your claim.

Pedestrians and cyclists

Contributory negligence weighs heavily on people outside a car. A pedestrian crossing outside a marked or unmarked crosswalk must yield to vehicles (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-174), and the insurer will often argue that a pedestrian who didn’t yield was contributorily negligent. The same statute also requires every driver to use due care to avoid hitting a pedestrian, and the last clear chance doctrine was developed for cases like these: a driver who saw, or should have seen, a pedestrian in a helpless position and had time to stop can still be liable. Cyclists are treated as vehicle operators and must follow the rules of the road, including lighting requirements at night, so a missing headlight can become the defense. Photos of the scene, lighting conditions and the driver’s line of sight matter more here than in most states. The pedestrian accident calculator and the bicycle accident calculator apply North Carolina’s fault rule.

North Carolina filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-52(16)).
  • Property damage: three years (§ 1-52).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (§ 1-53(4)).
  • Medical malpractice: three years from the last act of the provider, with up to one more year if the injury wasn’t discovered right away, and a four-year outer limit in most cases (§ 1-15(c)). The complaint must certify that a qualified expert reviewed the care and is willing to testify that it fell below the standard (Rule 9(j)).
  • Claims against the State: three years, filed with the North Carolina Industrial Commission under the State Tort Claims Act (§ 143-299).
  • Children: the deadline generally doesn’t run until the child turns 18 (§ 1-17), with special limits in malpractice cases.

Three years is longer than many states allow, but the two-year wrongful death period is shorter, and a claim that starts as an injury claim becomes a death claim with a different clock if the person dies. The North Carolina filing deadline calculator counts the dates.

Car insurance after July 1, 2025

North Carolina is an at-fault state. A 2023 law raised the minimum liability limits for policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025 to $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $50,000 for property damage, up from 30/60/25. Older policies keep their old limits until renewal, so for a crash in late 2025 or 2026 it matters when the at-fault driver’s policy last renewed.

The same law changed underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage in a way that helps injured people. Before, UIM was reduced by what the at-fault driver’s insurer paid. For policies issued or renewed since July 1, 2025, UIM is no longer offset by the liability payment, and whether a driver is “underinsured” is measured against your total damages rather than your own UIM limit. With $50,000 of liability coverage on the other side and $100,000 of your own UIM, a claim worth $200,000 can now recover up to $150,000 from the two coverages combined, instead of $100,000 under the old offset rule. New and renewed policies must include UM and UIM at least equal to the new minimums. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how the coverages combine.

Medical payments coverage is optional and pays medical bills regardless of fault, which matters in a contributory negligence state: MedPay pays even if your own fault would bar a liability claim.

Medical bills: what was paid

Since 2011, North Carolina Rule of Evidence 414 limits evidence of past medical expenses to the amounts actually paid to satisfy the bills, plus the amounts actually necessary to satisfy bills that remain unpaid, regardless of who paid them (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 8C-1, Rule 414). Write-offs aren’t part of the claim. In the example above, that kept the medical figure at $17,500 rather than $30,000. For unpaid bills, the question becomes what amount would actually satisfy them, which can be disputed when care was given on a lien. Future medical costs are proven through testimony and aren’t limited by past discounts.

Damage limits in North Carolina

  • Ordinary injury cases: no cap on compensatory damages.
  • Medical malpractice: non-economic damages are capped at an amount adjusted every three years; the figure for 2026 is $712,847, per the state budget office (§ 90-21.19). The cap doesn’t apply when the injury involves permanent injury, disfigurement, loss of use of a body part or death and the provider’s conduct was reckless, grossly negligent, fraudulent or malicious.
  • Punitive damages: require fraud, malice or willful or wanton conduct proven by clear and convincing evidence, and are capped at three times compensatory damages or $250,000, whichever is greater (§ 1D-25). The cap doesn’t apply to injuries caused by a driver impaired by alcohol or drugs in certain circumstances (§ 1D-26).
  • The State: claims under the State Tort Claims Act are limited to $1,000,000 per person (§ 143-299.2).

The malpractice calculator applies the 2026 North Carolina cap.

Claims against government

Claims for negligence by State employees go to the Industrial Commission rather than to a jury, and the State can raise the claimant’s contributory negligence there too. Cities and counties have governmental immunity for governmental functions, such as police and road maintenance, but waive it to the extent they buy liability insurance (§§ 160A-485 and 153A-435). Whether a function is governmental or proprietary, and what the policy covers, often decides whether a claim against a local government can go forward. School buses and other specific programs have their own statutes. Get the government’s insurance information early.

Wrongful death claims

North Carolina’s wrongful death statute is broad on damages. The personal representative can recover medical and funeral expenses, the person’s own pain and suffering before death, the present value of the person’s net income, the services, protection, care and assistance they would have provided, and the family’s loss of society, companionship, comfort, guidance and advice, plus punitive damages in a proper case (§ 28A-18-2). The money is distributed under the intestate succession rules rather than the will.

The catch is contributory negligence: if the person who died was contributorily negligent, the death claim can be barred the same way an injury claim would be. The deadline is two years from the death. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. North Carolina owners owe all lawful visitors reasonable care to keep the premises safe, after Nelson v. Freeland (1998) did away with the old distinction between invitees and licensees. Contributory negligence is the usual defense: an owner will argue the hazard was obvious and the visitor should have seen it. See the North Carolina slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable for injuries caused by a dog that has been declared dangerous (§ 67-4.4) and by dogs over six months old running at large at night (§ 67-12). Otherwise, the owner is liable if they knew or should have known of the dog’s dangerous tendencies. See the North Carolina dog bite calculator.

Bars. The Dram Shop Act allows claims against a permit holder that negligently sold alcohol to someone underage who then caused a crash while impaired, with damages capped at $500,000 (§§ 18B-121 and 18B-123). North Carolina courts also recognize a common-law negligence claim against a seller who served a visibly intoxicated person who it knew would be driving.

Hurt at work in North Carolina

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer for most workplace injuries, and it pays regardless of fault, which removes contributory negligence from the comp claim. A lawsuit against the employer is allowed only in narrow cases where the employer intentionally engaged in misconduct knowing it was substantially certain to cause serious injury or death (Woodson v. Rowland, 1991). A claim against a third party, such as a negligent driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and contributory negligence does apply there. When the third-party claim recovers money, the employer or its insurer has a lien for the benefits it paid, and a superior court judge can reduce that lien in some circumstances (§ 97-10.2). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Medical liens: the 50% limit

North Carolina caps how much of a settlement medical providers can take. Under §§ 44-49 and 44-50, liens of doctors, hospitals and other providers attach to the recovery, but all of them together can’t exceed 50% of the amount recovered after attorney fees. For example, on a $60,000 settlement with a one-third fee of $20,000, the providers’ combined liens can’t exceed $20,000, even if they claim $22,000. Providers usually share that amount in proportion to their bills. The limit doesn’t control Medicare, Medicaid, workers’ compensation or self-funded employer health plans governed by federal law, which have their own repayment rules.

The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you. Settlements for children need court approval.

Interest, offers and timing

When an injury case goes to judgment, North Carolina adds interest at the legal rate of 8% a year on the compensatory damages from the date the lawsuit was filed (§§ 24-1 and 24-5(b)). A defendant can make a formal offer of judgment under Rule 68; if the plaintiff rejects it and then does no better at trial, the plaintiff bears the costs incurred after the offer. Claims up to $10,000 can be filed in small claims court before a magistrate. Most crash claims settle with the insurer months after treatment ends, and the contributory negligence defense is the main reason some don’t. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage.

Trucks, rideshare and other commercial vehicles

Interstate trucking companies must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and a claim against the company can rest on its own failures in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance as well as on the driver’s conduct. Rideshare companies carry much higher limits once a ride has been accepted than while a driver is only logged into the app. In these cases, a defendant’s gross negligence, such as a driver far beyond hours-of-service limits, can also take contributory negligence off the table. The North Carolina truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Collect the evidence that you weren’t at fault: photos, video, witnesses, the police report and, after a crash, the vehicle data. In North Carolina this evidence is the claim.
  • Don’t give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement without advice. Small admissions about speed or attention are how contributory negligence defenses start.
  • Check when the at-fault driver’s policy last renewed, and your own UIM limits. The July 2025 changes depend on renewal dates.
  • Use MedPay if you have it. It pays regardless of fault.
  • Keep the explanations of benefits for every bill. Rule 414 makes the amounts paid the medical number that matters.
  • If the other side claims you were partly at fault, write down exactly what happened while you still remember it, including where you were looking, your speed and the lighting. Last clear chance and gross negligence arguments depend on those details.
  • Calendar the three-year deadline, and the two-year deadline if the injured person has died.

faqs.answer: Only in medical malpractice, where the non-economic cap is $712,847 for 2026, with exceptions for reckless or malicious conduct causing serious harm. Other injury claims have no cap.

michigan.metaTitle: Michigan Personal Injury Laws 2026: No-Fault and Threshold
michigan.metaDescription: How Michigan no-fault PIP choices, the serious impairment threshold, the 51% rule, three-year deadline, $3,000 mini-tort and 2026 malpractice caps work.
michigan.excerpt: Michigan’s no-fault system pays your medical bills and most lost wages regardless of fault, but pain and suffering requires a serious impairment, and since 2020 drivers choose their PIP and liability limits. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
michigan.html:
How a Michigan injury claim is valued

Michigan splits most car crash claims in two. Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical expenses, a large share of lost wages and household help, whoever caused the crash. Then, separately, you can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering if the injury meets Michigan’s threshold, and for economic losses no-fault doesn’t cover. Claims that don’t involve a car, such as falls, dog bites and malpractice, follow ordinary negligence rules with Michigan’s own twists.

The 2019 no-fault reform, which took effect for policies issued or renewed after July 1, 2020, changed both halves of the system: it let drivers choose lower PIP medical limits, set a fee schedule for providers, raised the default liability limits and wrote the serious-impairment threshold into the statute. This guide explains how those rules work today, along with Michigan’s fault rule, deadlines and damage caps, with the statute or case behind each. Run your own figures with the Michigan car accident calculator, which applies no-fault and the threshold, or the Michigan personal injury calculator.

A Michigan crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is rear-ended on US-131 in Grand Rapids and tears a knee ligament that needs surgery and eight months off work. Medical costs of $60,000 are paid by the driver’s own PIP coverage, chosen at the $250,000 level. The driver earns $7,000 a month, so the lost income is $56,000; PIP pays 85% of it, leaving about $8,400 unpaid. The at-fault driver’s insurer argues the injured driver braked abruptly and was 25% at fault.

  • From PIP, regardless of fault: the $60,000 medical and 85% of wages, up to the monthly cap.
  • From the at-fault driver, economic losses PIP didn’t pay: about $8,400 of wage loss.
  • Surgery and months of restricted activity meet the serious-impairment threshold, so non-economic damages are available. At two to three times the total economic loss of $116,000: $232,000 to $348,000.
  • Tort claim after a 25% fault reduction: $180,300 to $267,300.

Whether that tort claim is collectible depends on the at-fault driver’s bodily injury limit. Policies default to $250,000 per person, but a driver can choose $50,000, and in that case your own underinsured motorist coverage, if you bought it, has to fill the gap. If the injured driver had been more than 50% at fault, the non-economic damages would be barred, though PIP benefits would still be paid.

PIP: what your own policy pays

Personal protection insurance (PIP) pays benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

  • Allowable expenses: reasonable and necessary medical care, rehabilitation, attendant care and other care costs, up to the medical limit you chose.
  • Work loss: 85% of gross income for up to three years after the crash, up to a monthly maximum that is adjusted every year.
  • Replacement services: up to $20 a day for household help such as chores and driving, for up to three years.
  • Survivor’s loss benefits for dependents if the injured person dies.

The PIP medical limit you chose

Since July 2, 2020, drivers choose a PIP medical limit (MCL 500.3107c): unlimited, $500,000, $250,000, $250,000 with some household members excluded because they have qualifying health coverage, $50,000 for Medicaid enrollees, or no PIP medical coverage for people with Medicare Parts A and B. Policies issued before the reform were unlimited. When PIP medical runs out, your health insurance and the at-fault driver become the sources for the rest. Choosing a low limit doesn’t change your right to sue the at-fault driver for medical costs above it.

The fee schedule and attendant care

The reform limited what providers can charge PIP insurers to percentages of Medicare rates (MCL 500.3157) and capped family-provided attendant care at 56 hours a week. In Andary v. USAA (2023), the Michigan Supreme Court held that those limits don’t apply to people injured before the reform took effect on June 11, 2019, who keep the benefits their policies promised. The no-fault and PIP calculator estimates what PIP pays.

Pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists

PIP follows a priority order that decides which insurer pays (MCL 500.3114 and 500.3115). A pedestrian or cyclist hit by a car usually claims PIP first from a policy in their own household, as the named insured, a spouse or a resident relative. If no household policy exists, the insurer of the vehicle involved pays, and if there is none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan assigns an insurer. Choosing a low PIP limit on your own car policy can therefore matter even when you are walking.

Motorcyclists are treated differently. A motorcycle isn’t a “motor vehicle” for no-fault purposes, so a rider gets PIP only when a car or truck is involved in the crash, and the insurer of that vehicle’s owner or driver is generally first in line to pay, ahead of the rider’s own auto policy. A rider hurt in a crash with no other vehicle involved gets no PIP and relies on health insurance and any medical payments coverage on the motorcycle policy. The motorcycle accident calculator and the pedestrian accident calculator apply these rules.

PIP deadlines: the one-year rules

PIP has its own deadlines, separate from the lawsuit deadline against the driver (MCL 500.3145):

  • You must give written notice of injury to the insurer, or have received a payment from it, within one year after the crash.
  • A lawsuit for unpaid PIP benefits can recover only losses incurred within one year before the suit was filed, the “one-year-back” rule. Since the reform, that period is paused from the time a specific claim is made until the insurer formally denies it.

If you don’t know which insurer is responsible, for example when no household policy exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan assigns one; the same one-year notice rule applies.

The serious-impairment threshold

You can sue the at-fault driver for non-economic damages, such as pain, suffering and lost enjoyment of life, only if the injury caused death, permanent serious disfigurement, or serious impairment of a body function (MCL 500.3135(1)). The 2019 reform wrote into the statute the test from McCormick v. Carrier (2010): a serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects the person’s general ability to lead their normal life (MCL 500.3135(5)). It doesn’t have to be permanent, and it doesn’t have to affect every part of the person’s life; the question is whether it affected the ability to lead their own pre-crash life, for however long it lasted.

Objective manifestation means the impairment can be observed or perceived by someone other than the injured person, often through imaging, surgery, measured loss of motion or a doctor’s documented restrictions. Pain alone, without a medically identifiable cause, usually isn’t enough.

Other claims against the at-fault driver

  • Excess economic loss. Medical costs above your PIP limit, wage loss beyond three years or above the monthly cap, and the 15% of wages PIP doesn’t pay can be claimed from the at-fault driver without meeting the threshold (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)).
  • Mini-tort. Up to $3,000 for damage to your vehicle that your own insurance didn’t cover, such as your collision deductible (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). Like other tort damages, it is reduced by your share of fault and isn’t available if you were more than 50% at fault or were driving without the required insurance.

Fault: the 51% rule for non-economic damages

Michigan reduces damages by the injured person’s percentage of fault. If you are more than 50% at fault, you can’t recover non-economic damages at all, though you can still recover economic damages reduced by your share (MCL 600.2959 and 500.3135(2)). PIP benefits aren’t affected by fault.

Not wearing a seat belt can be considered evidence of negligence in a car crash case, but it can’t reduce your recovery by more than 5% (MCL 257.710e). Michigan generally doesn’t make one defendant pay another’s share; each pays its own percentage, with exceptions such as some medical malpractice cases (MCL 600.2956). The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the result.

Michigan filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (MCL 600.5805).
  • Wrongful death: the underlying claim’s period, generally three years, with a saving provision that lets the personal representative file within two years after appointment, if no more than three years after the original period ended (MCL 600.5852).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the act, or six months from when the injury was or should have been discovered, with a six-year outer limit in most cases (MCL 600.5805 and 600.5838a). You must send a notice of intent and wait 182 days before filing (MCL 600.2912b), and file an affidavit of merit from a qualified expert with the complaint (MCL 600.2912d).
  • PIP benefits: notice within one year, and the one-year-back rule (above).
  • Road defects: written notice to the government agency within 120 days of the injury (MCL 691.1404).
  • Claims against the State: in the Court of Claims, with a notice of intention or the claim itself filed within six months for personal injury (MCL 600.6431).

The Michigan filing deadline calculator counts these dates.

Liability limits and UM/UIM coverage

Since the reform, bodily injury liability coverage defaults to $250,000 per person and $500,000 per crash. A driver can choose lower limits, down to $50,000 and $100,000, by signing a form (MCL 500.3009). Michigan no-fault also includes $1,000,000 of property protection insurance for damage your car does to other people’s property in Michigan, and $10,000 of property damage liability for crashes in other states.

Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is optional in Michigan. Because a driver can now pick $50,000 limits, UIM on your own policy is often what pays a serious claim. Check your declarations page. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how much the coverages can pay.

Trucks and commercial vehicles

A crash with a commercial truck often has more insurance behind it than any personal policy. Interstate freight carriers must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and the company can be liable for its own negligence in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance. In Michigan the injured person’s PIP benefits still come through the normal priority order, but the tort claim for pain and suffering and excess economic loss runs against the driver and the carrier. Send the carrier a written request to preserve its driver logs, electronic data and dashcam video early. The Michigan truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

How Michigan claims move

A Michigan crash often produces two claims on different tracks: a first-party claim against your own PIP insurer for benefits, and a third-party claim against the at-fault driver. PIP disputes, such as denied bills or cut-off wage benefits, are often litigated separately and sometimes by providers directly. The tort claim usually waits until treatment has progressed far enough to show whether the threshold is met. Many circuit courts send civil cases to case evaluation, where a panel of three lawyers places a value on the case that either side can accept or reject. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage, and the settlement offer checker compares an offer with your estimate.

Medical malpractice caps

Michigan caps non-economic damages in malpractice cases at amounts adjusted each year by the state Treasurer (MCL 600.1483). For 2026 the lower cap is $596,400. A higher cap of $1,065,000 applies when the patient was left paralyzed by a brain or spinal cord injury, with cognitive impairment so severe that they can’t make independent life decisions or care for themselves, or with permanent damage to a reproductive organ that prevents having children. Economic damages aren’t capped. The malpractice calculator applies the 2026 Michigan caps.

Claims against government

The Governmental Tort Liability Act gives government agencies broad immunity, with exceptions for defects in highways the agency is responsible for, negligent operation of government vehicles by employees, dangerous or defective public buildings, and proprietary functions (MCL 691.1402 to 691.1413). Individual employees are liable only for gross negligence that was the proximate cause of the injury (MCL 691.1407). The highway exception has the shortest fuse: a written notice describing the defect, the injury and the witnesses must reach the agency within 120 days. Potholes and broken sidewalks are common examples, and the agency often argues it had no notice of the defect.

Wrongful death

Michigan’s wrongful death act lets the personal representative recover medical, funeral and burial expenses, the person’s conscious pain and suffering before death, lost financial support and services, and the family’s loss of society and companionship (MCL 600.2922). The court divides the recovery among the family. In a car crash case, no-fault survivor’s loss benefits pay dependents separately, and the tort claim is subject to the same threshold rules, which are met by the death itself. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. For years Michigan owners could avoid liability by showing a hazard was “open and obvious.” In Kandil-Elsayed v. F & E Oil (2023), the Michigan Supreme Court changed that: whether a danger was open and obvious is now considered when deciding whether the owner breached its duty and how fault is shared, rather than wiping out the duty altogether. That has made more fall claims viable, with the injured person’s own carelessness reducing the award. See the Michigan slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable when their dog bites someone, without provocation, who is lawfully on public or private property (MCL 287.351), whether or not the dog had bitten before. See the Michigan dog bite calculator.

Bars. The dram shop act allows claims against a licensee that sold alcohol to a visibly intoxicated person or a minor, when that sale caused the injury (MCL 436.1801). You must give the bar written notice within 120 days after hiring a lawyer for the claim, and you must keep the intoxicated person in the lawsuit until it ends.

Interest, liens and what you keep

Michigan judgments earn interest from the date the complaint was filed (MCL 600.6013), which gives insurers a reason to settle cases that are likely to win. From the settlement itself come the lawyer’s contingency fee, typically one third for the tort claim, case costs, and any reimbursement claims from Medicare, Medicaid or a health plan for costs they paid that no-fault didn’t. If you chose coordinated coverage, your health insurer pays medical bills first and PIP is secondary, which affects who has a claim on the settlement. The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you. Settlements for children need court approval.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Send your auto insurer a written application for PIP benefits right away, and keep proof of when you sent it.
  • Find your declarations page and note your PIP medical limit, whether coverage is coordinated, and your UIM limits.
  • If a road defect caused the crash or fall, send the 120-day notice to the right agency.
  • Ask your doctors to document restrictions on work, driving, sleep and daily activities. That record is the threshold evidence.
  • Submit wage records to the PIP insurer, and track the 15% of income PIP doesn’t replace.

faqs.question: Can I sue for pain and suffering after a Michigan car accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the crash caused death, permanent serious disfigurement or a serious impairment of a body function: an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life (MCL 500.3135). It doesn’t have to be permanent.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Michigan?
faqs.answer: Three years from the injury for a claim against the at-fault party (MCL 600.5805). PIP claims need written notice within one year, and road defect claims need notice to the agency within 120 days.

faqs.question: What does Michigan PIP pay?
faqs.answer: Medical and care expenses up to the limit you chose, 85% of lost gross income for up to three years up to a monthly cap, up to $20 a day for replacement services, and survivor’s benefits.

faqs.question: What is the Michigan mini-tort?
faqs.answer: A claim for up to $3,000 against an at-fault driver for vehicle damage your insurance didn’t cover, such as your collision deductible (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). It is reduced by your share of fault and isn’t available if you were more than 50% at fault.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in Michigan?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your damages are reduced by your share. If you are more than 50% at fault you lose non-economic damages but can still recover reduced economic damages, and your PIP benefits are paid regardless.

faqs.question: What are Michigan’s medical malpractice caps for 2026?
faqs.answer: $596,400 for non-economic damages in most cases and $1,065,000 for certain catastrophic injuries, such as paralysis from a brain or spinal cord injury or severe permanent cognitive impairment (MCL 600.1483).

new-jersey.metaDescription: How New Jersey’s limitation on lawsuit threshold, PIP, 51% fault rule, two-year deadline, 90-day public notice and new 35/70/25 minimums shape a claim.
new-jersey.excerpt: In New Jersey, your own PIP pays medical bills first, the limitation on lawsuit option restricts pain and suffering claims, and other insurance is deducted from the award. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
new-jersey.html:
How a New Jersey injury claim is valued

A New Jersey injury claim recovers economic loss (medical care, lost income and other expenses) and non-economic loss (pain, suffering, disability, impairment and loss of enjoyment of life). The total is reduced by your share of fault, and you recover nothing if your fault is greater than that of the people you are suing. There is no cap on compensatory damages in New Jersey, including in medical malpractice cases.

What makes New Jersey different is the auto insurance system around a car crash claim. Your own personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills first, most drivers have chosen a “limitation on lawsuit” option that blocks pain and suffering claims for less serious injuries, and other insurance payments are taken out of the award. Those rules shape what a New Jersey car accident claim is worth more than any jury formula. This guide explains each of them, with the statute or court rule behind it.

Run your own figures with the New Jersey car accident calculator or the New Jersey personal injury calculator.

A New Jersey claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is broadsided at an intersection in Edison and suffers a displaced wrist fracture that needs surgery and a plate. Her policy has the limitation on lawsuit option and the $15,000 PIP option. Her medical bills reach $58,000: PIP pays the first $15,000 and her health insurance pays most of the rest, leaving $3,500 of deductibles and copays. She misses $24,000 of pay that PIP doesn’t cover. The other driver’s insurer says she was going a little too fast and assigns her 15% of the fault.

  • A displaced fracture meets the limitation on lawsuit threshold, so she can claim pain and suffering. A jury might value it at $175,000 to $325,000.
  • The medical bills PIP paid can’t be claimed from the other driver, and what her health insurance paid is deducted from any award. Her economic claim is the lost pay plus out-of-pocket costs: $27,500.
  • After the 15% reduction, the claim is worth about $172,125 to $299,625.
  • The other driver carries the standard minimum of $35,000 per person. Her own $100,000 underinsured motorist coverage can add up to $65,000, the difference between the two limits. Without other assets to collect from, about $100,000 is realistically available.

The example shows the two points that most often decide a New Jersey crash claim: whether the injury meets the threshold, and how much insurance is actually there to pay. The medical bills, which drive the value of claims in many other states, matter much less here because PIP and health insurance have already paid them.

Fault: the 51% rule and joint liability

Under the Comparative Negligence Act, you can recover if your negligence is not greater than the negligence of the person or people you are suing, and your damages are reduced by your percentage (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-5.1). At 50% you still recover half; at 51% you recover nothing.

When several defendants share fault, a defendant found 60% or more responsible is liable for the entire award. A defendant less than 60% responsible pays only its own percentage (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-5.3). If an uninsured driver is 55% at fault and a trucking company 45%, the trucking company pays only 45% of your damages, and your own UM coverage becomes the source for the rest. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

New Jersey filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury, with a discovery rule when the injury or its cause wasn’t reasonably knowable (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (N.J.S.A. 2A:31-3).
  • Medical malpractice: two years under the same statute, subject to the discovery rule. Claims for injuries a child suffered at birth can be filed until the child’s 13th birthday.
  • Public entities: a notice of claim within 90 days, then a lawsuit no sooner than six months after the notice and within two years (N.J.S.A. 59:8-8). A court can allow late notice up to one year after the claim arose for extraordinary circumstances (N.J.S.A. 59:8-9).
  • Bars and restaurants: two years under the dram shop act.

The 90-day notice is the deadline most often missed, because a pothole, a bus crash or a fall in a public building doesn’t look like a government claim at first. The New Jersey filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

PIP: your own insurance pays first

New Jersey is a no-fault state for medical bills. Personal injury protection on your own policy pays your medical expenses after a crash, whoever caused it. A standard policy includes $250,000 of PIP medical coverage unless you choose a lower option. The lowest option is $15,000 per person, except that up to $250,000 remains available for permanent or significant brain injury, spinal cord injury or disfigurement (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4.3). You can also choose to make your health insurance primary for these expenses.

PIP benefits can’t be claimed again from the at-fault driver (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-12). If you chose PIP below $250,000, the New Jersey Supreme Court held in Haines v. Taft (2017) that you can sue the at-fault driver for medical expenses between your PIP limit and $250,000 that you actually owe. That’s one reason the PIP option on your declarations page affects the value of your claim.

The uninsured driver rule

New Jersey takes away the right to sue for injuries from people who were driving their own uninsured car. An owner or registrant of a vehicle that didn’t have the required coverage has no cause of action for economic or non-economic loss from the crash. The same applies to a driver convicted of drunk driving in that crash and to someone who caused the crash on purpose (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4.5). Passengers aren’t affected by the owner’s failure to insure.

The limitation on lawsuit threshold

When you buy a standard New Jersey policy, you pick between two options. With “no limitation on lawsuit,” you can sue for pain and suffering after any injury. With “limitation on lawsuit,” the cheaper option and the one assigned if you don’t choose, you can claim non-economic damages only if the injury results in one of these (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-8(a)):

  • Death
  • Dismemberment
  • Significant disfigurement or significant scarring
  • A displaced fracture
  • Loss of a fetus
  • A permanent injury within a reasonable degree of medical probability, meaning a body part or organ hasn’t healed to function normally and won’t with further treatment

The threshold must be backed by a doctor’s certification, served within 60 days after the defendant files its answer. In DiProspero v. Penn (2005), the New Jersey Supreme Court held that a plaintiff who proves one of these injuries doesn’t also have to prove a serious impact on daily life. Soft tissue injuries such as neck and back strains are where most threshold disputes arise: the case usually depends on objective findings, such as an MRI showing a herniation together with a doctor’s opinion that it is permanent.

The threshold follows your policy. A family member covered by your policy is generally bound by your choice, and out-of-state drivers whose insurers do business in New Jersey are usually treated as having the limitation option under the “deemer” statute (N.J.S.A. 17:28-1.4). Economic losses such as lost wages above PIP can be claimed whatever option applies.

Liability limits and UM/UIM coverage

New Jersey raised its minimum liability limits in two steps. Standard policies issued or renewed since January 1, 2026 must carry at least $35,000 per person, $70,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, up from 25/50/25 in 2023 and 15/30/5 before that. The same law raised the minimum uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage. The increases don’t apply to the basic policy, a low-cost option with $15,000 of PIP, $5,000 of property damage coverage and only optional $10,000 bodily injury coverage. Basic policyholders are always subject to the limitation on lawsuit threshold.

Underinsured motorist coverage in New Jersey pays the difference between your UIM limit and the at-fault driver’s liability limit. With $100,000 of UIM against a driver with $35,000, the most the UIM insurer pays is $65,000. Before accepting the at-fault driver’s limits, you must notify your UIM insurer and give it the chance to pay that amount itself and pursue the driver, under the procedure from Longworth v. Van Houten (1988). Settling without that notice can forfeit the UIM claim.

Since January 2022, the Insurance Fair Conduct Act has let a policyholder sue their own insurer for unreasonably delaying or denying UM or UIM benefits, and recover actual damages, including trial verdicts of up to three times the coverage amount, plus interest and attorney fees (N.J.S.A. 17:29BB-3). The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay.

Rideshare companies must carry at least $1.5 million of coverage from the moment a driver accepts a ride until the passenger gets out, and lower limits while the driver is only logged in and waiting. The rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers. For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers; see the New Jersey truck accident calculator.

Other insurance: the collateral source rule

New Jersey reverses the usual rule about other insurance. After a verdict, the court deducts benefits you received from other sources, such as health insurance and disability benefits, from the award, except workers’ compensation and life insurance (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-97). The amount you paid in premiums for those benefits is credited back to you. In Perreira v. Rediger (2001), the Supreme Court held that because the award is reduced, a state-regulated health insurer can’t also take a lien on the recovery.

The practical effect is that a New Jersey award doesn’t pay you twice for the same medical bill, and in many cases you owe less back to insurers than injured people in other states. Self-funded employer health plans, Medicare and Medicaid are governed by federal or separate rules and often do have repayment rights. The medical lien calculator shows how a repayment claim affects the net.

Claims against government and charities

The New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J.S.A. 59:1-1 and following) allows injury claims against the state, counties, municipalities and other public entities, with significant limits. Beyond the 90-day notice, the most important is a threshold on pain and suffering: it can be recovered only for a permanent loss of a bodily function, permanent disfigurement or dismemberment, and only when medical treatment expenses exceed $3,600 (N.J.S.A. 59:9-2(d)). Public entities don’t pay punitive damages or prejudgment interest, and collateral benefits are deducted from the award.

Claims involving public property usually require proof that the property was in a dangerous condition, that the entity had notice of it, and that its failure to fix it was “palpably unreasonable” (N.J.S.A. 59:4-2). That is a higher standard than ordinary negligence.

Nonprofit organizations are immune from negligence claims by the people they serve, and nonprofit hospitals are liable up to $250,000 to their patients (N.J.S.A. 2A:53A-7 and 2A:53A-8). These limits don’t protect a charity from claims by people who aren’t its beneficiaries, such as a passing driver hit by a charity’s van.

Medical malpractice in New Jersey

New Jersey has no cap on medical malpractice damages. The main procedural hurdle is the affidavit of merit: within 60 days after the defendant’s answer, extendable once by 60 more days, the plaintiff must serve an affidavit from a qualified professional stating that there is a reasonable probability the care fell below accepted standards (N.J.S.A. 2A:53A-27). Missing the deadline usually means dismissal with prejudice. Courts hold an early conference, known as a Ferreira conference, to catch problems with the affidavit before time runs out. The malpractice calculator estimates a claim.

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with actual malice or with wanton and willful disregard of people who foreseeably might be harmed (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-5.12). They are capped at five times compensatory damages or $350,000, whichever is greater. The cap doesn’t apply in some cases, including injuries caused by a drunk driver, bias crimes and sexual abuse (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-5.14).

Wrongful death and survival claims

A New Jersey wrongful death claim is limited to the family’s pecuniary losses: lost financial support, the value of household services, and medical and funeral expenses (N.J.S.A. 2A:31-5). The family’s grief isn’t compensable. In Green v. Bittner (1980), the Supreme Court allowed juries to value the companionship, advice and guidance a person would have provided as services with a financial value, which matters most when a child or retired parent dies. Bills to allow damages for the family’s emotional loss have been introduced repeatedly, most recently in January 2026, but none had become law as of November 2026.

A separate survival action (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-3) recovers what the person could have claimed had they lived, including their pain and suffering before death. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. Businesses owe customers a duty to keep the premises reasonably safe and to inspect for hazards. In self-service settings where the way the business operates makes spills or dropped items likely, the “mode of operation” rule removes the need to prove the store knew about the specific hazard (Prioleau v. Kentucky Fried Chicken, 2015). Commercial property owners are responsible for the public sidewalks next to their property, which residential owners generally aren’t. Under the ongoing storm rule adopted in Pareja v. Princeton International Properties (2021), a commercial owner usually doesn’t have to clear snow and ice until the storm ends. See the New Jersey slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog owner is strictly liable when the dog bites someone in a public place or lawfully on private property, even if the dog never bit anyone before (N.J.S.A. 4:19-16). Injuries without a bite, such as being knocked over, follow the older rule that requires proof the owner knew of the dog’s dangerous tendencies or was negligent. See the New Jersey dog bite calculator.

Bars. Under the Licensed Alcoholic Beverage Server Fair Liability Act, a licensed server is liable only if it served a person who was visibly intoxicated, or a minor it knew or should have known was underage, and that service caused the injury (N.J.S.A. 2A:22A-5).

Hurt at work in New Jersey

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, except for an “intentional wrong.” The Supreme Court has read that to include conduct the employer knew was substantially certain to cause injury, such as removing a safety guard from a machine (Laidlow v. Hariton Machinery, 2002). A claim against a third party, such as a driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim. The employer or its insurer is repaid from the third-party recovery, after a share of the legal fees and costs (N.J.S.A. 34:15-40). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Interest, offers and timing

New Jersey adds prejudgment interest to tort judgments, running from the date the lawsuit was filed or six months after the claim arose, whichever is later (Court Rule 4:42-11(b)). Under the offer of judgment rule, if you make a written offer to settle that the defendant rejects and the verdict is at least 120% of your offer, the defendant pays your reasonable attorney fees and costs from the date of the offer. The rule works in reverse for a defendant’s offer when the verdict is 80% or less of it (Court Rule 4:58). Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, and the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes. The attorney fee calculator shows what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Find your declarations page and check two choices: your PIP medical limit and whether you have the limitation on lawsuit option.
  • Report the crash to your own insurer for PIP benefits promptly, and follow the PIP plan’s rules for treatment and precertification.
  • If a public road, vehicle or building was involved, file the notice of claim within 90 days.
  • Get imaging and a clear medical opinion on permanence for soft tissue injuries. The threshold depends on it.
  • Check your UIM limit before talking about settlement, and notify your UIM insurer in writing before accepting the other driver’s limits.
  • Keep pay stubs and records of time missed; lost income above PIP is part of the claim whatever threshold applies.

faqs.question: Can I sue for pain and suffering after a car accident in New Jersey?
faqs.answer: If your policy has the no limitation on lawsuit option, yes. With the limitation on lawsuit option, only for death, dismemberment, significant disfigurement or scarring, a displaced fracture, loss of a fetus, or a permanent injury (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-8(a)).

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in New Jersey?
faqs.answer: Two years for personal injury, wrongful death and medical malpractice. Claims against public entities need a notice of claim within 90 days.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in New Jersey?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fault isn’t greater than the fault of the people you sue; your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 51% or more you recover nothing (N.J.S.A. 2A:15-5.1).

faqs.question: What are New Jersey’s minimum car insurance limits in 2026?
faqs.answer: Standard policies issued or renewed since January 1, 2026 must carry $35,000 per person, $70,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage. The basic policy has lower limits.

faqs.question: Does New Jersey cap personal injury damages?
faqs.answer: No. There is no cap on compensatory damages, including in medical malpractice. Punitive damages are capped at five times compensatory damages or $350,000, with exceptions such as drunk driving.

faqs.question: Can I sue if I was driving without insurance in New Jersey?
faqs.answer: Generally no. An owner of an uninsured vehicle injured while driving it has no claim for economic or non-economic loss from that crash (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4.5). Passengers keep their claims.

virginia.title: Virginia Personal Injury Claims: Contributory Negligence, Deadlines and Insurance
virginia.metaTitle: Virginia Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps, Deadlines
virginia.metaDescription: How Virginia’s contributory negligence rule, two-year deadline, 50/100/25 minimums, add-on UIM, malpractice cap and $350,000 punitive cap affect a claim.
virginia.excerpt: Virginia bars any recovery if you were even slightly at fault, with narrow exceptions. Here is how that rule works, along with Virginia’s deadlines, insurance minimums, underinsured coverage, malpractice cap and government claim rules.
virginia.html:
How a Virginia injury claim is valued

A Virginia injury claim recovers medical expenses, lost earnings, future losses, and compensation for pain, inconvenience, disfigurement and mental anguish. There is no general cap on those damages, and Virginia lets the jury hear the full amount of the medical bills, not just what an insurer paid.

What sets Virginia apart is how it treats fault. Virginia is one of only a handful of jurisdictions that still apply pure contributory negligence: if you were even slightly at fault for your own injury, you can recover nothing. That rule shapes every negotiation, because an insurer that can point to any mistake by you has a defense to the entire claim. This guide explains that rule, its exceptions, and the other Virginia laws that decide what a claim is worth, with the statute behind each one.

Run your own figures with the Virginia car accident calculator or the Virginia personal injury calculator. Both apply the contributory negligence rule.

A Virginia claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver in Henrico County is hit by a car that ran a red light. She has a fractured ankle that needs surgery, medical bills of $42,000 and lost wages of $13,000, for economic loss of $55,000. The other driver’s insurer claims she was looking at her phone and could have braked in time.

  • A jury might value the pain, recovery and lasting limitation at two to four times the economic loss: $110,000 to $220,000.
  • If she is found free of fault, the claim is worth about $165,000 to $275,000.
  • If the jury finds that any carelessness on her part contributed to the crash, she recovers nothing. There is no reduction by percentage.
  • The other driver carries the 2025 minimum of $50,000 per person. Her own $100,000 underinsured motorist coverage pays on top of that, so up to $150,000 is available.

Two Virginia rules are at work. The first is the all-or-nothing fault rule, which makes evidence about her phone the most important issue in the case: phone records, the crash data from both cars and witness accounts decide whether she recovers anything. The second is the change Virginia made to underinsured coverage in 2023, which now adds to the at-fault driver’s limits instead of being reduced by them.

Contributory negligence: the all-or-nothing rule

Virginia has never adopted comparative fault. If the defendant proves that your own negligence was a proximate cause of your injury, you recover nothing, whether your share was 1% or 49%. The rule comes from Virginia common law and applies to every kind of negligence claim. There are a few important exceptions:

  • Willful and wanton conduct. Contributory negligence isn’t a defense when the defendant acted with conscious disregard of others’ safety, such as racing or driving while heavily intoxicated.
  • Last clear chance. If you were in a position of helpless peril, or unaware of the danger, and the defendant saw or should have seen you in time to avoid the harm, the defendant can be liable despite your negligence.
  • Young children. A child under seven can’t be contributorily negligent, and a child between seven and 14 is presumed incapable of it unless the defense proves otherwise.

The defense has the burden of proving your negligence, and it must have caused the injury, not just been present. A pedestrian outside a crosswalk isn’t automatically barred if the driver would have hit her anyway. Even so, the rule gives insurers leverage, and claims with any arguable fault on the injured person’s side often settle for less than full value to avoid the risk of a zero verdict. The fault calculator shows how Virginia’s rule compares with its neighbors’.

How the rule plays out in negotiation

Insurers adjusting Virginia claims look first for anything that suggests the injured person contributed: speed, distraction, a missed turn signal, footwear in a fall case, or a pedestrian’s choice of where to cross. When they find something, the offer often reflects the chance of a defense verdict rather than the value of the injury. A claim worth $200,000 on full liability might draw an offer of half that or less if the fault evidence is genuinely disputed. The answer is usually evidence rather than argument: event data recorder downloads, traffic camera or business security footage, phone records showing no use at the time, and independent witnesses. Because the stakes of a fault finding are total, these cases are also more likely than average to be decided by a jury, and the decision to try or settle often turns on how strong that evidence is.

Several defendants

Virginia keeps full joint and several liability. When two or more defendants cause one injury, you can collect the full judgment from any of them, and they sort out their shares among themselves (Va. Code § 8.01-443). If you settle with one defendant, your claim against the others is reduced by the amount paid (Va. Code § 8.01-35.1).

Seat belts

Not wearing a seat belt can’t be used as evidence of negligence or to reduce damages in a Virginia civil case (Va. Code § 46.2-1094(D)). Since July 2025 the law requires all adult occupants to buckle up, not only those in front, but the rule about evidence didn’t change.

Virginia filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (Va. Code § 8.01-243(A)).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (Va. Code § 8.01-244(B)). Since July 2025 the period is extended while a related criminal case is pending (Va. Code § 8.01-229(K)).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the act, with limited extensions for a foreign object left in the body, fraud or concealment, and a 10-year outer limit for most claims (Va. Code § 8.01-243(C)).
  • Property damage: five years (Va. Code § 8.01-243(B)).
  • The Commonwealth: a written notice of claim within one year (Va. Code § 8.01-195.6).
  • Cities, towns and counties: a written notice within six months for injuries from a negligent act of the locality (Va. Code § 15.2-209).

For a minor, the injury deadline generally doesn’t start until age 18. The Virginia filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Car insurance in Virginia

Virginia is an at-fault state. Since January 1, 2025, policies must carry at least $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, up from 30/60/20. The option to register a vehicle without insurance by paying a fee ended on July 1, 2024. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage must be included at limits at least equal to the liability minimums (Va. Code § 38.2-2206).

Underinsured coverage now adds to the other driver’s limits

For policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2023, Virginia UIM coverage pays in addition to the at-fault driver’s liability coverage, instead of being reduced by it. With $100,000 of UIM against a driver who has $50,000, up to $150,000 is available. Before the change, the same policies would have produced $100,000 in total. A policyholder can choose in writing to keep the older, reduced form of the coverage, so check your declarations page and any form you signed.

For a hit-and-run crash, an uninsured motorist claim usually requires that the crash be reported to the police promptly, and the lawsuit against the unknown “John Doe” driver must be served on your own UM insurer. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the coverage can pay.

Rideshare companies must carry at least $1 million of coverage while a ride is under way, and lower limits while the driver is only logged in and waiting. The rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers. Interstate trucking companies need federal minimums starting at $750,000; see the Virginia truck accident calculator.

Medical bills and other insurance

Virginia applies the collateral source rule in full. In Acuar v. Letourneau (2000), the Supreme Court of Virginia held that a defendant can’t reduce damages by the amounts a health insurer wrote off, so the full billed amount is the measure of medical expenses. Virginia also lets an injured person prove medical bills with an affidavit, which creates a presumption that the charges were reasonable and necessary (Va. Code § 8.01-413.01). The result is that medical damages in Virginia are often higher than in states that limit evidence to the amounts actually paid.

Hospitals, doctors and some other providers have a lien on an injury recovery for unpaid treatment, limited to a set dollar amount per provider (Va. Code § 8.01-66.2). Medicaid has its own lien (§ 8.01-66.9), and Medicare and self-funded employer plans have federal repayment rights. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Virginia

Virginia caps the total recovery in a malpractice case, including economic, non-economic and punitive damages. The cap is $2.7 million for malpractice between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026, and $2.75 million for malpractice between July 1, 2026 and June 30, 2027. It rises by $50,000 each July 1 until it reaches $3 million in 2031 (Va. Code § 8.01-581.15). The cap that applies is the one in effect on the date of the malpractice, not the date of the verdict. In 2026 the General Assembly considered raising it to $6 million, but the version it passed dropped the increase and focused on reporting of malpractice costs.

Before asking for the lawsuit to be served, the plaintiff must obtain a written opinion from a qualified expert that the provider breached the standard of care and caused the injury. Since July 2025, the plaintiff must also certify that in writing within 21 days after the defendant answers, and failure to comply can lead to dismissal (Va. Code § 8.01-20.1). The malpractice calculator applies the Virginia cap.

Claims against government in Virginia

Under the Virginia Tort Claims Act, the Commonwealth is liable for the negligence of its employees up to $100,000 per claim or the limits of any applicable insurance, whichever is greater (Va. Code § 8.01-195.3). The written notice of claim must go to the Director of the Division of Risk Management or the Attorney General within one year, and the lawsuit must be filed within 18 months of the notice. Punitive damages and prejudgment interest aren’t available.

Local governments are treated differently. Counties keep broad sovereign immunity. Cities and towns are immune for governmental functions such as police and fire protection, but can be liable for proprietary functions, which Virginia courts have held include routine maintenance of streets and sidewalks. Government employees can be personally liable for gross negligence, and often for ordinary negligence in routine driving that isn’t an emergency. Who employed the driver, and what they were doing, can decide whether there is a claim at all.

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require willful or wanton conduct, and Virginia caps them at $350,000 per case, whatever the jury awards (Va. Code § 8.01-38.1). A separate statute treats drunk driving as willful and wanton conduct that supports punitive damages when the driver’s blood alcohol was 0.15% or more, the driver knew or should have known their driving was impaired, and the intoxication caused the crash (Va. Code § 8.01-44.5). The $350,000 cap still applies.

Wrongful death in Virginia

A Virginia wrongful death action is brought by the personal representative for the statutory beneficiaries: the spouse, children and grandchildren of deceased children, or, if there are none, parents and siblings and other relatives in a set order (Va. Code § 8.01-53). The jury can award damages for the family’s sorrow, mental anguish and solace, including loss of society, companionship, comfort, guidance and advice; lost income and services; medical and funeral expenses; and punitive damages for willful or wanton conduct (Va. Code § 8.01-52). The jury decides how the award is divided among the beneficiaries. There is no cap outside malpractice and punitive damages. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. A business must use ordinary care to keep its premises reasonably safe for customers and to warn of hidden dangers it knows or should know about. Fall claims in Virginia are especially exposed to contributory negligence: if the hazard was open and obvious, the defense will argue the customer was negligent for not seeing it, which bars the claim. Proof of how long the hazard was there, and why it wasn’t visible, is the core of the case. See the Virginia slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Virginia has no statute making dog owners strictly liable. An owner is liable if they knew or should have known the dog was dangerous, or if they were negligent, and breaking a local leash or at-large law can itself be evidence of negligence. See the Virginia dog bite calculator.

Bars. Virginia doesn’t recognize dram shop liability. A bar that overserves a customer who then causes a crash generally can’t be sued for it (Williamson v. Old Brogue, Inc., 1986), so the claim runs against the driver and the driver’s insurance.

Hurt at work in Virginia

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer (Va. Code § 65.2-307). Virginia’s statutory employer rule extends that protection to some other companies: when you are injured doing work that is part of the trade or business of the owner or general contractor, that company may also be immune, which can rule out claims that would be allowed in other states (Va. Code § 65.2-302). Claims against true third parties, such as a negligent driver or an equipment maker, are allowed. The employer or its insurer has a lien on that recovery for benefits paid, reduced by its share of the attorney fees and costs (Va. Code §§ 65.2-309 and 65.2-311). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Interest, timing and settlement

Prejudgment interest is up to the judge or jury in Virginia rather than automatic (Va. Code § 8.01-382), and judgment interest generally runs at 6% a year (Va. Code § 6.2-302). Settlements for minors need court approval (Va. Code § 8.01-424). Since July 2025, a police report is required only for crashes with injuries or property damage of $5,000 or more, up from $1,500, so photos and witness details from the scene matter more in smaller crashes. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Be careful what you say about your own conduct. In a contributory negligence state, a casual admission such as “I didn’t see him” can end the claim.
  • Preserve evidence that rules out your fault: photos, dashcam video, witness contact details, and a request that the other driver’s vehicle data be preserved.
  • Check your policy for UIM coverage and whether it is the added-on form. Don’t sign an election that reduces it without reading it.
  • If a government vehicle or road was involved, identify the agency and send the written notice: six months for a locality, one year for the Commonwealth.
  • Keep every medical bill. Virginia juries can see the full billed amounts.
  • For a malpractice concern, talk to a lawyer well before the two-year deadline; the expert opinion has to be in hand before the lawsuit is served.

faqs.question: Can I recover in Virginia if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Virginia applies contributory negligence, so any negligence of yours that helped cause the injury bars recovery. Exceptions include the defendant’s willful and wanton conduct and the last clear chance doctrine.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Virginia?
faqs.answer: Two years for personal injury, wrongful death and medical malpractice (Va. Code §§ 8.01-243 and 8.01-244). Claims against a locality need written notice within six months, and against the Commonwealth within one year.

faqs.question: What are Virginia’s minimum car insurance limits?
faqs.answer: Since January 1, 2025: $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage. UM and UIM coverage must be at least equal to those limits.

faqs.question: Does Virginia underinsured coverage stack on top of the other driver’s insurance?
faqs.answer: For policies issued or renewed since July 1, 2023, yes, unless the policyholder elected otherwise in writing. UIM pays in addition to the at-fault driver’s liability limits.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on medical malpractice damages in Virginia?
faqs.answer: Yes. The cap is $2.7 million for malpractice from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 and $2.75 million from July 1, 2026, rising $50,000 a year to $3 million in 2031 (Va. Code § 8.01-581.15).

faqs.question: Does Virginia limit punitive damages?
faqs.answer: Yes. Punitive damages are capped at $350,000 per case (Va. Code § 8.01-38.1), including against drunk drivers.
