washington.title: Washington Personal Injury Claims: Pure Comparative Fault, No Caps and Deadlines
washington.metaTitle: Washington Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps, Deadlines
washington.metaDescription: How Washington’s pure comparative fault, three-year deadline, lack of damage caps and punitive damages, PIP and UIM rules and claim forms shape a claim.
washington.excerpt: Washington reduces damages by your share of fault but never bars them, has no cap on injury damages and generally allows no punitive damages. Here is how those rules and Washington’s insurance and deadline rules work, with the statute behind each.
washington.html:
How a Washington injury claim is valued

A Washington injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost earnings, loss of future earning capacity and other costs) and non-economic damages (pain, suffering, emotional distress, disability, disfigurement and loss of enjoyment of life). Washington uses pure comparative fault, so your damages are reduced by your share of fault but never eliminated, even if you were mostly to blame.

Two features set Washington apart. There is no cap on non-economic damages in any kind of case: the Washington Supreme Court struck down the state’s cap in 1989 as a violation of the right to a jury trial. And Washington generally doesn’t allow punitive damages at all, which makes it one of very few states without them. The jury’s compensatory award is therefore the whole case. This guide explains those rules and the others that shape a claim, with the statute behind each one.

Run your own figures with the Washington personal injury calculator or the Washington car accident calculator.

A Washington claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A cyclist in Spokane is hit by a driver turning right across the bike lane. He breaks his collarbone and pelvis, with medical bills of $60,000 and lost wages of $20,000, for economic loss of $80,000. The driver’s insurer argues that he was riding too fast for the conditions and assigns him 25% of the fault.

  • A jury might value the pain, months of recovery and lasting limitation at three to five times the economic loss: $240,000 to $400,000. Washington has no cap.
  • Under pure comparative fault, a 25% finding reduces the award by 25%. The claim is worth about $240,000 to $360,000.
  • The driver carries the state minimum of $25,000 per person. The cyclist’s own auto policy, which covers him on a bike too, has $100,000 of underinsured motorist coverage that pays damages above the driver’s limit, so about $125,000 is available.
  • His PIP coverage paid the first $10,000 of medical bills. Because his total recovery falls well short of his full damages, Washington’s made-whole rule generally prevents the PIP insurer from taking that money back.

The example shows how much a Washington claim depends on insurance. With no cap and pure comparative fault, the value of the injury is often far higher than the coverage available, and your own UIM and PIP coverage frequently decide what you actually receive.

Fault: pure comparative negligence

Under RCW 4.22.005, any fault of the injured person reduces the damages in proportion but doesn’t bar recovery. A plaintiff found 70% at fault still recovers 30% of their damages. The same rule applies to claims against several defendants and to people who weren’t parties, such as an unidentified driver, if the defense proves their fault.

When several defendants are at fault

Washington’s rule on paying for another defendant’s share depends on your own fault. If you were not at fault at all, the defendants who are found liable are jointly and severally liable for the sum of their shares, so you can collect the full amount from any of them. If you were partly at fault, each defendant pays only its own percentage (RCW 4.22.070). Fault assigned to a person who is immune, such as your employer in a workplace case, generally isn’t paid by anyone.

Seat belts

Failure to wear a seat belt isn’t admissible as evidence of negligence in a Washington civil case (RCW 46.61.688(6)), and Washington courts have long kept it out as a way to reduce damages as well. The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the result.

Washington filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (RCW 4.16.080(2)).
  • Wrongful death: three years from the date of death.
  • Medical malpractice: three years from the act or omission, or one year from when the patient discovered or reasonably should have discovered that the injury was caused by it, whichever is later (RCW 4.16.350). In Bennett v. United States (2023), the Washington Supreme Court struck down the eight-year outer limit for these claims.
  • Government claims: a claim form first. Before suing the state or a local government, you must file a standard tort claim form and wait 60 days. The deadline to sue is extended by the waiting period (RCW 4.92.110 for the state and RCW 4.96.020 for local governments).

For minors, the injury deadline generally doesn’t run until age 18. The Washington filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Car insurance in Washington

Washington is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry liability coverage of at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $10,000 for property damage (RCW 46.29.090), among the lower minimums in the country. A serious injury claim against a minimum-limits driver usually exhausts the policy quickly.

PIP and underinsured coverage

Insurers must offer personal injury protection, which pays at least $10,000 of medical and hospital expenses, plus funeral costs, income continuation and loss of services, regardless of fault (RCW 48.22.095). They must also offer underinsured motorist coverage, which pays the damages you are legally entitled to recover from an uninsured or underinsured driver, above what that driver’s liability insurance covers (RCW 48.22.030). Both are included unless you reject them in writing, so many Washington drivers have them without realizing it. Your UIM coverage usually follows you as a pedestrian or cyclist as well.

When your PIP insurer pays your bills and you later recover from the at-fault driver, Washington limits its repayment. Under Thiringer v. American Motors Insurance Co. (1978), the insurer can’t recover anything until you have been fully compensated for your damages. Under Mahler v. Szucs (1998), when it is repaid, it must pay its share of the legal fees and costs of the recovery. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the coverage can pay.

When your own insurer won’t pay

The Insurance Fair Conduct Act lets you sue your own insurer if it unreasonably denies a claim for coverage or payment of benefits, such as a UIM or PIP claim. The court can award up to three times the actual damages, plus attorney fees and costs. You must give written notice to the insurer and the Office of the Insurance Commissioner at least 20 days before filing (RCW 48.30.015).

Rideshare companies carry much higher limits from the moment a driver accepts a ride until the passenger gets out than while the driver is only logged in and waiting; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers. Interstate trucking companies need federal minimums starting at $750,000; see the Washington truck accident calculator.

Hit-and-run and phantom vehicles

UIM coverage also pays when the at-fault driver can’t be identified. For a “phantom vehicle” crash, the statute requires that the crash be reported to the police or the insurer within 72 hours. If there was no physical contact with the other vehicle, the facts must be corroborated by evidence other than your own testimony, such as an independent witness or video (RCW 48.22.030(8)). A prompt police report is therefore part of the claim.

No cap, and no punitive damages

In Sofie v. Fibreboard Corp. (1989), the Washington Supreme Court held that a statute limiting non-economic damages violated the state constitution’s guarantee of a jury trial. No cap has applied since, including in medical malpractice and wrongful death cases. Damages against the state and local governments aren’t capped either: Washington waived sovereign immunity for injury claims in 1961 for the state and 1967 for local governments, and treats government defendants like private ones, subject to the claim form requirement (RCW 4.92.090 and 4.96.010).

The other side of that rule is that Washington doesn’t allow punitive damages unless a statute specifically authorizes them, a principle the Supreme Court has applied since the 1890s. A drunk driver or a company that knowingly ignored a safety risk pays full compensatory damages but no additional punishment award. Juries can still hear the evidence of that conduct when it bears on liability and on the harm caused.

Claims against government in Washington

A claim against the state starts with the standard tort claim form filed with the Office of Risk Management. A claim against a city, county or other local government is filed with the agent that government has designated. The form must describe the conduct and circumstances, the injuries, and the amount of damages claimed, and the 60-day waiting period runs from filing. There are no damages caps, but the public duty doctrine limits some claims: a government generally isn’t liable for failing to perform a duty owed to the public at large, such as general law enforcement, unless an exception applies. The exceptions include a special relationship with the injured person, a statute meant to protect a particular class of people, a failure to enforce a known violation, and a voluntary rescue. Ordinary negligence, such as a government employee’s careless driving or a poorly maintained road, isn’t affected by the doctrine.

When the claim is worth more than the policy

With no cap and low minimum limits, many Washington claims are worth more than the at-fault driver’s insurance. Washington law requires insurers to act in good faith toward their insured (RCW 48.01.030). An insurer that unreasonably refuses a reasonable offer to settle within its policy limits can become liable for a verdict above those limits. When that happens, the at-fault driver often agrees to a stipulated or “covenant” judgment and assigns their bad faith claim against the insurer to the injured person, in exchange for a promise not to collect from the driver’s own assets. The Washington Supreme Court has held that a reasonable covenant judgment sets the presumptive measure of damages in the bad faith claim (Besel v. Viking Insurance Co., 2002). A clear, documented demand within the limits, with a reasonable deadline and the medical records to support it, is the usual starting point.

Medical bills and other insurance

Washington applies the collateral source rule: payments from your own health insurance, disability coverage or PIP don’t reduce what the at-fault party owes, and the jury decides the reasonable value of the medical care. Those insurers may have repayment rights, which are limited by the made-whole and fee-sharing rules above when they are state-regulated. Medicare, Medicaid and self-funded employer plans follow federal or separate rules. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Washington

Malpractice claims are governed by RCW chapter 7.70. The plaintiff must prove that the provider failed to follow the accepted standard of care and that the failure caused the injury, or that the provider failed to obtain informed consent (RCW 7.70.040 and 7.70.050). Washington has struck down several procedural hurdles that other states impose: the certificate of merit requirement in Putman v. Wenatchee Valley Medical Center (2009), the 90-day pre-suit notice in Waples v. Yi (2010), and the eight-year outer limit in Bennett. Claims usually go to mandatory mediation before trial (RCW 7.70.100). There is no damages cap. The malpractice calculator estimates a claim.

Wrongful death and survival claims

Washington rewrote its wrongful death statutes in 2019. A wrongful death action is brought by the personal representative for the spouse or domestic partner and children. If there are none, parents and siblings can recover, and since 2019 they no longer have to have been financially dependent on the person who died or live in the United States (RCW 4.20.020). The jury can award economic and non-economic damages for the beneficiaries’ losses, including loss of love, companionship and support. The estate’s own claims, including the person’s pain and suffering before death, survive under RCW 4.20.046 and 4.20.060.

Parents also have a separate claim for injury to or death of a minor child, or an adult child who depended on them, including loss of love and companionship and injury to the parent-child relationship (RCW 4.24.010). The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites, recreation and bars

Falls. A business owes customers a duty to keep the premises reasonably safe and must have known or should have known about the hazard. In self-service operations where hazards are reasonably foreseeable, such as produce sections, the plaintiff doesn’t have to prove notice of the specific hazard (Pimentel v. Roundup Co., 1983). See the Washington slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog owner is strictly liable for a bite to a person in a public place or lawfully on private property, including the owner’s, whether or not the dog was known to be dangerous (RCW 16.08.040). Provocation is a defense. Injuries without a bite follow the common law. See the Washington dog bite calculator.

Recreation. Landowners who open their land or water to the public for recreation without charging a fee are immune from injury claims except for known, dangerous, artificial conditions that weren’t conspicuously posted (RCW 4.24.210). The rule covers many parks, trails and boat launches, including public ones.

Bars. Washington allows negligence claims against a commercial seller that served alcohol to a person who was apparently under the influence, when that service caused the injury. The claim is based on the duty in RCW 66.44.200 and Washington case law rather than a separate dram shop statute.

Hurt at work in Washington

Washington is one of four states where most employers must get workers’ compensation coverage from a state fund, run by the Department of Labor and Industries; large employers can self-insure. An employee can’t sue the employer except for a deliberate intention to injure, which the Supreme Court has read to require actual knowledge that an injury was certain to occur and willful disregard of that knowledge (Birklid v. Boeing Co., 1995). Claims against third parties are allowed, and L&I or the self-insured employer is repaid from the recovery under a statutory formula that first deducts the legal fees and costs and guarantees the worker a share (RCW 51.24.060). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Interest, fees and settlement

Judgments on tort claims carry interest from the date of judgment at two percentage points above the prime rate (RCW 4.56.110(3)(b)). For claims of $10,000 or less, the prevailing party can recover attorney fees when a settlement offer was made and rejected under the statute’s procedure (RCW 4.84.250 through 4.84.280), which gives small claims real leverage. Settlements for minors need court approval. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Check your auto policy for PIP and UIM. Unless someone rejected them in writing, you probably have both, and they apply even if you were walking or cycling.
  • Open a PIP claim with your own insurer for medical bills and wage loss.
  • If a government agency, road or vehicle was involved, file the standard tort claim form, then wait 60 days before suing.
  • Don’t assume partial fault ends the claim. Under pure comparative fault, it only reduces it.
  • If your insurer delays or denies a UIM or PIP claim without a reason, the IFCA notice is the first step.
  • Keep a record of how the injury affects work, sleep and daily life. With no cap, that evidence drives the value of the claim.

arizona.title: Arizona Personal Injury Claims: Pure Comparative Fault, No Caps and Deadlines
arizona.metaTitle: Arizona Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps, Deadlines
arizona.metaDescription: How Arizona’s pure comparative fault, several liability, two-year deadline, 180-day government notice and constitutional ban on damage caps shape a claim.
arizona.excerpt: Arizona’s constitution bars damage caps, fault reduces but never bars recovery, and each defendant pays only its own share. Here is how those rules work, with Arizona’s deadlines, insurance minimums and government claim rules.
arizona.html:
How an Arizona injury claim is valued

An Arizona injury claim recovers medical expenses, lost earnings, loss of earning capacity and other economic losses, plus non-economic damages for pain, suffering, disfigurement, emotional distress and loss of enjoyment of life. Arizona uses pure comparative fault, so your share of fault reduces the award but never bars it.

Two parts of the Arizona Constitution shape every claim. Article 2, Section 31 forbids any law limiting the amount of damages for death or personal injury, and Article 18, Section 6 says the right to recover damages for injuries can never be abolished. As a result, Arizona has no cap on compensatory or punitive damages, including in medical malpractice. On the other side, Arizona has abolished joint liability in most cases, so each defendant pays only its own share of fault. This guide explains those rules and the deadlines, insurance and government claim rules around them, with the statute behind each.

Run your own figures with the Arizona personal injury calculator or the Arizona car accident calculator.

An Arizona claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver in Tucson is broadsided by a driver who ran a stop sign that was hidden by overgrown city landscaping. She has a fractured femur, medical bills of $70,000 and lost wages of $30,000. A jury values her total damages at $300,000, including $200,000 for pain and lasting limitation. It assigns 60% of the fault to the other driver, 25% to the city and 15% to her for not slowing at an intersection she knew was hard to see.

  • Under pure comparative fault, her 15% share, $45,000, comes off the award.
  • Because Arizona liability is several only, each defendant pays its own percentage: the driver owes $180,000 and the city owes $75,000. Neither pays the other’s share.
  • The driver carries the state minimum of $25,000 per person. Her own $100,000 of underinsured motorist coverage pays damages above that limit, so it pays $100,000 toward the driver’s share.
  • The city’s share is collectible, but only because she served a proper notice of claim within 180 days and sued within one year.
  • Total collected: about $200,000. About $55,000 of the driver’s share goes unpaid unless the driver has assets worth pursuing.

The example shows the two Arizona rules that most often decide a claim with more than one responsible party: several liability, which makes every defendant’s ability to pay matter separately, and the government notice of claim, whose 180-day deadline is far shorter than the two-year limit for ordinary claims.

Fault: pure comparative and several liability

Arizona reduces a plaintiff’s damages by their percentage of fault and never bars recovery entirely (A.R.S. § 12-2505). Fault is assigned to every person who contributed to the injury, including people who aren’t parties to the lawsuit, if the defense gives timely notice that it will blame them.

Each defendant is liable only for the damages matching its own percentage of fault, not for anyone else’s share (A.R.S. § 12-2506). The exceptions are defendants who acted in concert, a defendant responsible for another’s fault as an employer or principal, and certain federal environmental claims. So an employer remains fully liable for its employee’s driving, but a negligent bar, a road contractor and a speeding driver each pay only their own slice. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

Seat belts

Arizona allows a seat belt defense on damages. In Law v. Superior Court (1988), the Arizona Supreme Court held that evidence of not wearing a seat belt can reduce the damages for injuries a belt would have prevented, if the defense proves that connection with evidence.

Arizona filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (A.R.S. § 12-542).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death, under the same statute.
  • Medical malpractice: two years, measured from when the patient knew or reasonably should have known of the injury and its cause.
  • Public entities and public employees: a notice of claim within 180 days after the claim arises, and a lawsuit within one year (A.R.S. §§ 12-821.01 and 12-821).
  • Strict liability dog bite claims: one year, because the claim is created by statute (A.R.S. § 12-541(5)). A negligence claim for the same bite has the usual two years.

For minors, the two-year deadline usually doesn’t begin until age 18. The Arizona filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Claims against government in Arizona

The notice of claim under A.R.S. § 12-821.01 must be filed with the person authorized to accept service for the public entity or employee within 180 days. It must contain facts sufficient for the entity to understand the basis of its liability and a specific amount for which the claim can be settled, with the facts supporting that amount. In Deer Valley Unified School District v. Houser (2007), the Arizona Supreme Court held that a notice without a specific amount is invalid, which bars the claim. There is no cap on damages against public entities, but they don’t pay punitive damages (A.R.S. § 12-820.04).

Some government decisions are immune. Absolute immunity covers judicial and legislative acts and the exercise of fundamental governmental policy, such as deciding whether to build a road (A.R.S. § 12-820.01). Qualified immunity covers certain acts, such as failing to arrest someone or the issuance of licenses, unless the employee intended to cause injury or was grossly negligent (A.R.S. § 12-820.02). Ordinary negligence in carrying out a decision, such as maintaining a road or driving a city vehicle, generally isn’t immune.

Car insurance in Arizona

Arizona is an at-fault state. Since July 1, 2020, drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $15,000 for property damage (A.R.S. § 28-4009). Insurers must offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage in writing, and a policyholder who rejects it must do so on an approved form (A.R.S. § 20-259.01). Arizona UIM pays the damages above the at-fault driver’s liability limits, up to your UIM limit, which is why it was decisive in the example above.

Arizona doesn’t require PIP. Optional medical payments coverage pays your bills regardless of fault, and it doesn’t reduce what the at-fault driver owes. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay.

Rideshare companies carry much higher limits from the moment a driver accepts a ride until the passenger gets out than while the driver is only logged in and waiting; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers. Interstate trucking companies need federal minimums starting at $750,000, and Arizona’s interstate corridors make truck claims common; see the Arizona truck accident calculator.

No caps on damages

Because of Article 2, Section 31, the Arizona Legislature can’t limit the amount of damages for injury or death. That holds for economic, non-economic and punitive damages, and for medical malpractice. The jury’s valuation stands unless the court finds it the result of passion or prejudice. In practice, the limits on an Arizona claim come from fault allocation, several liability and the available insurance rather than from a statute.

When the claim is worth more than the policy

With no caps and a $25,000 minimum, many serious Arizona claims are worth far more than the at-fault driver’s policy. An insurer owes its policyholder a duty of good faith, which includes giving equal consideration to the policyholder’s interests when deciding whether to accept an offer to settle within the limits. An insurer that unreasonably refuses can be liable for a verdict above its limits.

Arizona has two well-known settlement tools built on that duty. In a Damron agreement, named for Damron v. Sims (1969), the at-fault party whose insurer refused to defend or settle agrees to a judgment and assigns their claims against the insurer to the injured person, who agrees not to collect from the at-fault party personally. In a Morris agreement, from United Services Automobile Ass’n v. Morris (1987), the same thing can happen when the insurer is defending under a reservation of its right to deny coverage, but the injured person must later prove that the settlement amount was reasonable. Both shift the dispute to the insurer. A clear demand within the limits, with a reasonable deadline and the records to support it, is usually what puts that pressure in place.

Settlements for minors and other people who can’t manage their own affairs generally need court approval, and the court may require that the money be placed in a restricted account or a structured settlement until the child turns 18.

Medical bills and other insurance

Arizona applies the collateral source rule. Payments from health insurance or medical payments coverage don’t reduce the at-fault party’s liability, and Arizona courts have allowed injured people to claim the full amount billed for their care, not only the discounted amount an insurer paid (Lopez v. Safeway Stores, Inc., 2006).

Hospitals, ambulance companies and other health care providers can record a lien on an injury recovery for their reasonable and customary charges (A.R.S. § 33-931). The lien attaches only to the recovery from the at-fault party, not your other assets, and it must be properly recorded and noticed to be enforceable. Courts have held that a provider that accepted payment from AHCCCS, Arizona’s Medicaid program, can’t also use a lien to collect its full charges from the patient’s recovery. The medical lien calculator shows how liens affect what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Arizona

There is no cap on malpractice damages. When a claim depends on expert testimony about the standard of care, the plaintiff must certify that when filing the complaint and serve a preliminary expert opinion affidavit with the initial disclosures (A.R.S. § 12-2603). The expert generally must practice in the same specialty as the defendant (A.R.S. § 12-2604). Missing or deficient affidavits are a common reason for dismissal. The malpractice calculator estimates a claim.

Punitive damages

Arizona allows punitive damages only on clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with an “evil mind”: an intent to injure, or a conscious pursuit of a course of conduct knowing it created a substantial risk of significant harm to others (Linthicum v. Nationwide Life Insurance Co., 1986). Gross negligence alone isn’t enough. There is no cap, but public entities and public employees acting within the scope of their employment aren’t liable for punitive damages.

Wrongful death and survival claims

A wrongful death action can be brought by the surviving spouse, child, parent or guardian, or the personal representative, for the benefit of the spouse, children and parents (A.R.S. § 12-612). The jury awards damages it finds fair and just for the injury to the survivors, including loss of love, affection, companionship and guidance, their emotional suffering, lost financial support and the medical and funeral costs (A.R.S. § 12-613). There is no cap.

The survival statute is narrower. The estate can recover the person’s medical expenses and lost earnings before death, but Arizona doesn’t allow survival damages for the person’s own pain and suffering (A.R.S. § 14-3110). The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites, recreation and bars

Falls. A business must keep its premises reasonably safe for customers and usually must have known or should have known about the hazard. Where the way a business operates makes certain hazards foreseeable, such as spills in a self-service grocery, Arizona’s mode-of-operation rule removes the need to prove notice of the specific hazard (Chiara v. Fry’s Food Stores, 1987). See the Arizona slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog owner is strictly liable for a bite to a person in a public place or lawfully in a private place, including the owner’s property, whether or not the dog had bitten before (A.R.S. § 11-1025). Provocation is a defense (A.R.S. § 11-1027). Remember the one-year deadline for the strict liability claim. See the Arizona dog bite calculator.

Recreation. Landowners, including public entities, who allow recreational use of their land without charge are generally liable only for willful, malicious or grossly negligent conduct (A.R.S. § 33-1551).

Bars. A liquor licensee is liable when it sold alcohol to a purchaser who was obviously intoxicated, or to someone under 21 without asking for identification, and that sale caused the injury (A.R.S. § 4-311). Social hosts are generally immune (A.R.S. § 4-301).

Hurt at work in Arizona

Arizona has an unusual feature: an employee can reject workers’ compensation in writing before being injured and keep the right to sue the employer instead (A.R.S. § 23-906). Few workers do. For everyone else, comp is the exclusive remedy against the employer unless the injury was caused by the employer’s willful misconduct, meaning an act knowingly and purposely done with the direct object of injuring someone (A.R.S. § 23-1022). Claims against third parties, such as another driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, are allowed, and the comp carrier has a lien on that recovery for benefits paid (A.R.S. § 23-1023). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Offers, interest and litigation funding

Arizona’s offer of judgment rule has real teeth. If a party rejects a written offer and then does no better at trial, it must pay the other side’s reasonable expert witness fees and double its taxable costs incurred after the offer. When the rejected offer came from the plaintiff, the defendant also owes prejudgment interest on the damages from the date of the offer (Ariz. R. Civ. P. 68(g)). Judgments otherwise carry interest at one percentage point above the prime rate (A.R.S. § 44-1201(B)).

A 2025 law, SB 1215, regulates litigation funding agreements, in which an outside company advances money against a future settlement. It bars funders from controlling legal strategy or settlement decisions, bans funding from foreign entities of concern, and requires disclosure of referral fees paid to attorneys or health care providers. Read the terms of any advance closely. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • If a city, county, state agency, school district or public employee may share responsibility, prepare the notice of claim now. It needs a specific settlement amount and supporting facts, and it is due within 180 days.
  • Identify every party that may share fault. Under several liability, each one’s insurance matters separately.
  • Check your policy for UM and UIM coverage and your medical payments limit.
  • Ask each at-fault party’s insurer for its policy limits in writing. Under several liability, the limits of every responsible party matter, not only the main one.
  • Don’t sign a release from one party without checking how it affects your claims against the others and against your own UIM coverage.
  • For a dog bite, keep the one-year deadline in mind.
  • Keep copies of every bill and any lien notices from hospitals or ambulance companies.
  • Write down how the injury affects your work and daily life. With no cap, that record drives the value of the claim.

tennessee.metaTitle: Tennessee Personal Injury Laws 2026: Deadlines, Caps, Fault
tennessee.metaDescription: How Tennessee’s one-year deadline, $750,000 and $1 million non-economic caps, 50% fault bar, several liability and 25/50/25 insurance minimums shape a claim.
tennessee.excerpt: Tennessee gives you one year to sue in most injury cases, caps non-economic damages at $750,000 or $1 million, and bars recovery at 50% fault. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
tennessee.html:
How a Tennessee injury claim is valued

A Tennessee injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, loss of earning capacity) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering, permanent impairment, disfigurement and loss of enjoyment of life). Your damages are reduced by your share of fault, and you recover nothing if your fault is 50% or more.

Three rules make Tennessee different. It has one of the shortest filing deadlines in the country: one year for most injury claims. It caps non-economic damages at $750,000, or $1 million for catastrophic injuries, under the Tennessee Civil Justice Act of 2011. And it abolished joint liability, so each defendant pays only its own share. This guide explains those rules and the others that shape a claim, with the statute behind each.

Run your own figures with the Tennessee personal injury calculator or the Tennessee car accident calculator. Both apply the Tennessee cap and fault rule.

A Tennessee claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver on I-40 near Nashville is struck by a tractor-trailer that changed lanes into her. She suffers a severe leg fracture and a back injury that requires fusion, with medical bills of $150,000 and lost wages of $50,000, for economic loss of $200,000. The trucking company argues she was speeding and is 20% at fault.

  • A jury might value her pain, permanent limitation and lost enjoyment of life at $1,200,000.
  • Tennessee’s cap limits non-economic damages to $750,000. Her claim before fault: $200,000 + $750,000 = $950,000.
  • After a 20% reduction: about $760,000.
  • If her injury were catastrophic under the statute, such as paraplegia, the cap would be $1,000,000 and the result about $960,000. If the truck driver had been impaired by alcohol or drugs, no cap would apply, and the result would be about $1,120,000.

Because the trucking company’s driver was cited under state traffic law at the scene, her deadline to sue is two years rather than one. Without that citation, she would have had one year from the crash. The deadline, the cap and its exceptions are the three things to check first in any serious Tennessee claim.

Tennessee’s one-year deadline

  • Personal injury: one year from the injury (Tenn. Code § 28-3-104(a)(1)).
  • Two years if criminal charges are brought against the person who caused the injury for the conduct that caused it, such as DUI, vehicular assault or a citation under state traffic law (§ 28-3-104(a)(2)). Tennessee courts have held that a citation under a city ordinance doesn’t trigger the extension.
  • Wrongful death: one year from the death, generally, under the same statute.
  • Health care liability: one year from discovery, with a three-year outer limit except for a foreign object or fraudulent concealment (Tenn. Code § 29-26-116). Giving the pre-suit notice extends the deadline by 120 days.
  • Local governments: one year under the Governmental Tort Liability Act (Tenn. Code § 29-20-305).
  • The State of Tennessee: written notice within one year to the Division of Claims and Risk Management.
  • Property damage: three years (Tenn. Code § 28-3-105).

The one-year deadline catches many people who are still being treated or negotiating with an insurer when it expires. Talks with an adjuster don’t extend it. The Tennessee filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Minors, nonsuits and the saving statute

For an injured child, the deadline generally doesn’t start running until the child turns 18 (Tenn. Code § 28-1-106), though a parent’s own claim for the child’s medical bills follows the regular deadline. Tennessee also has a saving statute: if a lawsuit filed on time is dismissed without a judgment on the merits, including a voluntary dismissal, the plaintiff can refile within one year of the dismissal (Tenn. Code § 28-1-105). That protects a claim that was filed in time, but it doesn’t help one that was never filed.

Fault: the 50% bar and no joint liability

Tennessee adopted modified comparative fault in McIntyre v. Balentine (1992). You can recover only if your fault is less than the combined fault of the defendants; at 50% you recover nothing, and below 50% your damages are reduced by your percentage. The jury can also assign fault to people who aren’t parties, such as an unidentified driver, if the defense identifies them.

McIntyre also abolished joint and several liability in most cases. Each defendant pays only the percentage of damages matching its own fault. The exceptions include defendants who acted in concert, an employer responsible for its employee’s conduct, and defendants in the chain of distribution of a defective product. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

Seat belts

Failure to wear a seat belt can’t be considered as comparative fault and isn’t admissible in a Tennessee civil case, except in some product liability cases (Tenn. Code § 55-9-604).

The cap on non-economic damages

Tennessee Code § 29-39-102 limits non-economic damages to $750,000 for each injured plaintiff, for all injuries and occurrences. Claims that derive from the injury, such as a spouse’s loss of consortium, fall under the same limit. The cap rises to $1 million for catastrophic losses, which the statute defines as:

  • A spinal cord injury resulting in paraplegia or quadriplegia
  • Amputation of two hands, two feet, or one of each
  • Third-degree burns over 40% or more of the body, or over 40% or more of the face
  • The wrongful death of a parent that leaves a surviving minor child for whom the parent had custody or support obligations

No cap applies when the defendant intended to injure, intentionally falsified or destroyed records to avoid liability, was under the influence of alcohol or drugs that substantially impaired their judgment, or was convicted of a felony for the conduct that caused the injury. Economic damages aren’t capped. The Tennessee Supreme Court upheld the cap in McClay v. Airport Management Services (2020). The jury isn’t told about it; the court applies it after the verdict.

How the cap plays out in negotiation

For serious injuries, the cap sets the insurer’s ceiling on non-economic damages, so the economic damages, the fault percentage and the exceptions carry the most weight. Evidence of impairment, such as a blood test after a crash, can remove the cap entirely, and evidence of catastrophic injury raises it by $250,000. For moderate injuries well below the cap, the cap doesn’t affect value at all.

Car insurance in Tennessee

Tennessee is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, or a $65,000 single limit (Tenn. Code § 55-12-102). Uninsured motorist coverage is included in every policy at the same limits as the bodily injury coverage unless the named insured rejects it or selects lower limits in writing (Tenn. Code § 56-7-1201). The same coverage applies to underinsured drivers: it is available when the at-fault driver’s limits are less than yours, and what the at-fault driver’s insurer pays is credited against it. To make a UM claim, you must serve your own insurer with the lawsuit against the at-fault driver (§ 56-7-1206).

The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay. Interstate trucking companies need federal minimums starting at $750,000, and Tennessee’s interstate network makes truck claims common; see the Tennessee truck accident calculator. For rideshare crashes, the company’s coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

When the claim is worth more than the policy

With a $25,000 minimum and a cap that can still allow $750,000 or more in non-economic damages, many serious Tennessee claims exceed the at-fault driver’s coverage. An insurer that fails in bad faith to accept a reasonable offer to settle within its policy limits can be liable to its own policyholder for the full verdict above those limits, and that claim is often assigned to the injured person in exchange for not collecting from the policyholder personally. A clear demand within the limits, with a reasonable deadline and the records to support it, puts that risk on the insurer.

For claims against your own insurer, such as an uninsured motorist claim, Tennessee adds a statutory bad faith penalty. If the insurer refuses to pay within 60 days after a formal demand and the refusal was not in good faith, it can be liable for an additional amount of up to 25% of the loss (Tenn. Code § 56-7-105). The formal demand starts that clock, so it is worth making in writing.

Medical bills: the full billed amount

In Dedmon v. Steelman (2017), the Tennessee Supreme Court held that in ordinary injury cases the plaintiff can introduce the full, undiscounted medical bills as evidence of reasonable medical expenses, and the defense can’t introduce the discounted amounts insurers paid to rebut them. The defense can still challenge whether the charges were reasonable or the care necessary, with expert testimony. Itemized bills can be admitted with an affidavit, creating a rebuttable presumption that they are reasonable (Tenn. Code § 24-5-113).

Health care liability cases are an exception. Under Tenn. Code § 29-26-119, damages in a malpractice case are limited to the economic losses actually paid or incurred, so the amounts insurers actually paid generally control. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment claims affect what you keep.

Health care liability claims

Tennessee calls malpractice claims health care liability actions. At least 60 days before filing, the plaintiff must send each provider written notice with a HIPAA-compliant medical records authorization (Tenn. Code § 29-26-121). The complaint must include a certificate of good faith stating that a qualified expert has reviewed the case and believes there is a good faith basis for it (§ 29-26-122). Defects in either step are a frequent reason for dismissal. The $750,000 and $1 million caps apply. The malpractice calculator applies the Tennessee rules.

Claims against government in Tennessee

Under the Governmental Tort Liability Act, counties, cities and other local governments are immune except where the Act removes immunity, such as negligent operation of a vehicle by an employee, dangerous or defective streets and public buildings they knew about, and some negligent acts of employees. Damages are limited to $300,000 per person and $700,000 per occurrence for bodily injury, unless the entity bought more insurance (Tenn. Code § 29-20-403). GTLA cases are tried by a judge without a jury (§ 29-20-307), and the one-year deadline applies.

Claims against the State of Tennessee go to the Tennessee Claims Commission after written notice to the Division of Claims and Risk Management, with damages limited to $300,000 per claimant and $1 million per occurrence (Tenn. Code § 9-8-307).

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted intentionally, fraudulently, maliciously or recklessly (Hodges v. S.C. Toof & Co., 1992). They are capped at the greater of twice the compensatory damages or $500,000 (Tenn. Code § 29-39-104). The cap doesn’t apply in the same circumstances that remove the non-economic cap, including impairment by alcohol or drugs.

Wrongful death in Tennessee

Tennessee’s wrongful death statutes keep the person’s own claim alive and pass it to the surviving spouse, or children or next of kin if there is no spouse (Tenn. Code §§ 20-5-106 and 20-5-107). Damages include the person’s medical and funeral expenses, their pain and suffering before death, and the pecuniary value of their life (Tenn. Code § 20-5-113). The Tennessee Supreme Court has held that the pecuniary value of a life includes the loss of consortium suffered by the spouse and children: their loss of attention, guidance, care, protection, companionship and love (Jordan v. Baptist Three Rivers Hospital, 1999). Non-economic damages are subject to the cap, which rises to $1 million when a parent dies leaving a minor child. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. A property owner must use reasonable care to keep the premises safe and must have created the hazard or known or should have known about it. A hazard being open and obvious doesn’t automatically defeat the claim; it is weighed in the comparative fault analysis (Coln v. City of Savannah, 1998). See the Tennessee slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. An owner is liable for injuries caused by a dog running at large or not under reasonable control, whether or not the dog was known to be dangerous. On the owner’s residential, farm or other noncommercial property, the injured person must prove the owner knew or should have known of the dog’s dangerous propensities (Tenn. Code § 44-8-413). See the Tennessee dog bite calculator.

Bars. Tennessee’s dram shop act sets an unusually high bar. A seller is liable only if a jury finds, beyond a reasonable doubt, that it sold alcohol to a visibly intoxicated person or to someone it knew was under 21, and that the sale was a proximate cause of the injury (Tenn. Code § 57-10-102). That is the criminal standard of proof, rarely seen in civil cases.

Hurt at work in Tennessee

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, with a narrow exception for an employer’s actual intent to injure (Tenn. Code § 50-6-108). A claim against a third party, such as a negligent driver or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim. The employer has a lien on that recovery for the benefits it paid, after a share of the legal fees and costs (§ 50-6-112). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Settling a Tennessee claim

Settlements for minors need court approval. Litigation funding, where an outside company advances money against a future settlement, is regulated by the Tennessee Litigation Financing Consumer Protection Act (Tenn. Code § 47-16-101 and following), which sets disclosure rules and limits on charges; read the terms of any advance closely. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Mark the one-year deadline on your calendar today. Check the police report for any criminal charge or state traffic citation, which can extend it to two years.
  • Check your policy for UM coverage and its limits. Unless someone rejected it in writing, it matches your liability limits.
  • If the other driver may have been impaired, make sure the police report and any blood or breath test results are preserved. Impairment removes the damages cap.
  • For a malpractice concern, plan for the 60-day pre-suit notice and the expert review before the deadline.
  • If a government vehicle or road was involved, identify the entity; the claim is tried by a judge and capped.
  • Keep every medical bill. Tennessee juries can see the full billed amounts in ordinary injury cases.
  • Before accepting the at-fault driver’s policy limits, notify your own UM insurer in writing so the settlement doesn’t put your UM claim at risk.
  • Write down how the injury affects work, sleep and daily life. The cap limits the non-economic number, but the jury still decides it.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Tennessee?
faqs.answer: One year in most cases (Tenn. Code § 28-3-104). It is two years if the person who caused the injury is criminally charged or cited under state law for the conduct, and three years for property damage.

faqs.question: Does Tennessee cap pain and suffering damages?
faqs.answer: Yes. Non-economic damages are capped at $750,000, or $1 million for catastrophic injuries such as paralysis, amputations, severe burns or the death of a parent of a minor child (Tenn. Code § 29-39-102). The cap doesn’t apply to an impaired or intentional wrongdoer.

faqs.question: Can I recover in Tennessee if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fault is less than 50%. Your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 50% or more you recover nothing (McIntyre v. Balentine, 1992).

faqs.question: What are Tennessee’s minimum car insurance limits?
faqs.answer: $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage, or a $65,000 single limit (Tenn. Code § 55-12-102).

faqs.question: Can a Tennessee jury see my full medical bills?
faqs.answer: In ordinary injury cases, yes. Dedmon v. Steelman (2017) allows the full billed amounts. In health care liability cases, damages are limited to amounts actually paid or incurred.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on claims against Tennessee cities and counties?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the GTLA, $300,000 per person and $700,000 per occurrence for bodily injury, unless the entity has more insurance, and the case is tried without a jury (Tenn. Code §§ 29-20-403 and 29-20-307).

massachusetts.title: Massachusetts Personal Injury Claims: PIP, Tort Threshold and 12% Interest
massachusetts.metaTitle: Massachusetts Personal Injury Laws 2026: PIP, Fault, Interest
massachusetts.metaDescription: How Massachusetts’s $8,000 PIP, $2,000 tort threshold, 51% fault rule, three-year deadline, 12% interest and new 25/50/30 minimums shape a claim.
massachusetts.excerpt: Massachusetts pays the first $8,000 of crash losses through PIP, limits pain and suffering claims to injuries over a threshold, and adds 12% interest to judgments. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
massachusetts.html:
How a Massachusetts injury claim is valued

A Massachusetts injury claim recovers medical expenses, lost wages and loss of earning capacity, plus non-economic damages for pain and suffering, disfigurement and loss of enjoyment of life. Your damages are reduced by your share of fault, and you recover nothing if your fault is greater than that of the people you are suing.

Several Massachusetts rules have an outsized effect on value. Car crash claims run through a no-fault system with $8,000 of personal injury protection and a threshold for pain and suffering claims. Court judgments carry prejudgment interest of 12% a year from the date the lawsuit is filed, which puts real pressure on insurers to settle. Chapter 93A lets you recover multiple damages from an insurer that handles a claim unfairly. And claims against public employers and charities are capped at amounts far below their value. This guide explains each rule with the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Massachusetts car accident calculator or the Massachusetts personal injury calculator.

A Massachusetts claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver in Worcester is rear-ended at a light and pushed into the car ahead. She fractures her wrist and needs surgery. Her medical bills come to $28,000 and she misses $12,000 of work. The other driver’s insurer argues that she stopped short and assigns her 10% of the fault.

  • A fracture meets the Massachusetts tort threshold, so she can claim pain and suffering. A jury might value it at $90,000 to $160,000.
  • Her PIP coverage paid $8,000 of her bills and lost wages. The at-fault driver is exempt from liability for what PIP paid, so her economic claim is the remaining $32,000.
  • After a 10% reduction, the claim is worth about $109,800 to $172,800.
  • If she sues and wins a judgment of $150,000 two years after filing, 12% simple interest adds about $36,000.

The interest is the reason Massachusetts insurers often improve their offers once a lawsuit is filed. A claim that might settle for its value before suit can carry a much larger exposure two or three years into litigation. The other key point in the example is the threshold: had her injury been a soft tissue strain with less than $2,000 of medical bills, she couldn’t have claimed pain and suffering at all.

Fault: the 51% rule and joint liability

Under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 231, § 85, your negligence doesn’t bar recovery if it is not greater than the total negligence of the people you are suing, and your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 50% you recover half; at 51% you recover nothing. Your fault is compared with the combined fault of all defendants, not with each one separately.

Massachusetts keeps joint and several liability: when two or more defendants cause one injury, you can collect the full judgment from any of them, and they divide the cost among themselves under the contribution statute (ch. 231B). That makes it worthwhile to identify every responsible party, including ones with more insurance. The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the result.

Seat belts

Not wearing a seat belt can’t be used as evidence of contributory negligence in a Massachusetts civil case (ch. 90, § 13A).

Massachusetts filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (ch. 260, § 2A), with a discovery rule when the injury or its cause wasn’t reasonably knowable.
  • Wrongful death: three years from the death, or from when the executor or administrator knew or should have known of the factual basis for the claim (ch. 229, § 2).
  • Medical malpractice: three years from discovery, with a seven-year outer limit except for a foreign object left in the body (ch. 260, § 4). A written notice must be sent to the provider at least 182 days before filing (ch. 231, § 60L).
  • Public employers: a written presentment within two years to the executive officer of the public employer, then a lawsuit within three years (ch. 258, § 4).
  • Defects in city and town roads: written notice within 30 days under the road defect statute (ch. 84, §§ 15 and 18).

For an injured child, the general deadline doesn’t start until age 18 (ch. 260, § 7). Malpractice claims for children are different: they must be brought within three years, except that a child injured before age six has until the ninth birthday, subject to the seven-year outer limit (ch. 231, § 60D). The Massachusetts filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

PIP and the tort threshold

Massachusetts is a no-fault state for the first $8,000 of loss. Personal injury protection on the policy covering the car you were in, or your own policy if you were a pedestrian, pays medical expenses, 75% of lost wages and replacement services up to $8,000 per person, whoever caused the crash (ch. 90, § 34A). If you have private health insurance, PIP pays only the first $2,000 of medical bills and then covers amounts your health plan doesn’t. The at-fault driver is exempt from liability to the extent PIP paid or was required to pay (ch. 90, § 34M).

To claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver, you must meet the tort threshold in ch. 231, § 6D. The threshold is met if your reasonable and necessary medical expenses exceed $2,000, or the injury:

  • Caused death
  • Caused the loss of a body member, in whole or in part
  • Caused permanent and serious disfigurement
  • Caused loss of sight or hearing
  • Consisted of a fracture

The $2,000 figure hasn’t changed since the 1980s, so most injuries that need ongoing treatment meet it. Soft tissue claims with only a few visits are where it matters.

Getting PIP paid

The PIP insurer can ask for an examination by a doctor it chooses and for records and wage information, and it can refuse benefits if you don’t cooperate. If it doesn’t pay benefits that are due within the statutory period, you can sue the PIP insurer, and a successful claimant can recover reasonable attorney fees and costs in addition to the benefits (ch. 90, § 34M). Keeping copies of every bill and wage form you send makes those disputes simpler.

Car insurance in Massachusetts

For policies written or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, compulsory coverage includes at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per crash for bodily injury to others, the same limits for injuries caused by uninsured drivers, and $30,000 for property damage, up from 20/40/5. PIP remains $8,000. It was the first increase in the compulsory limits since 1988.

Optional underinsured motorist coverage on your own policy can pay when the at-fault driver’s limits are lower than your UIM limits; check your declarations page for the amount. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the coverage can pay. For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers; see the Massachusetts truck accident calculator. Rideshare coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

12% prejudgment interest

In personal injury cases, Massachusetts adds interest of 12% a year to damages, running from the date the lawsuit was filed until the judgment (ch. 231, § 6B). The rate is fixed by statute, not tied to market rates, so it is far above what money earns elsewhere. Bills to change it are filed regularly, but the 12% rate still applied as of November 2026. The interest doesn’t apply to settlements, only to judgments, which is why it pushes insurers to resolve strong claims once a lawsuit is under way. Claims against public employers don’t carry prejudgment interest.

When an insurer handles a claim unfairly

Massachusetts regulates how insurers settle claims. Chapter 176D, § 3(9) lists unfair claim settlement practices, including failing to make a prompt, fair and equitable settlement once liability has become reasonably clear. Under ch. 93A, § 9, a claimant injured by those practices, including a third party claiming against someone else’s insurer, can sue for damages, and the damages are doubled or tripled if the insurer’s conduct was willful or knowing. In Rhodes v. AIG Domestic Claims, Inc. (2012), the Supreme Judicial Court held that the multiplied amount can be based on the underlying judgment, not just the harm from the delay. A ch. 93A claim generally must begin with a written demand letter sent at least 30 days before suing.

These rules give Massachusetts claimants leverage that doesn’t exist in most states. A clear demand, with the records that make liability and damages reasonably clear, is what starts the insurer’s obligation.

Medical bills and other insurance

Itemized medical bills are admissible as evidence of the fair and reasonable charge for the care when served with the required notice (ch. 233, § 79G). In Law v. Griffith (2010), the Supreme Judicial Court held that a defendant can offer evidence of the amounts actually accepted as payment to challenge whether the billed charges are reasonable, without telling the jury that insurance paid them. Payments from your own health insurance don’t otherwise reduce the award.

Hospitals have a lien on an injury recovery for reasonable charges (ch. 111, § 70A). Health insurers, Medicare and Medicaid (MassHealth) may also have repayment rights. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Massachusetts

Every malpractice claim first goes to a tribunal of a judge, a physician and a lawyer, which reviews the plaintiff’s offer of proof. If the tribunal finds it insufficient, the plaintiff can continue only by posting a $6,000 bond (ch. 231, § 60B). Non-economic damages are capped at $500,000 unless the jury finds a substantial or permanent loss or impairment of a bodily function, substantial disfigurement, or other special circumstances that make the cap unfair (ch. 231, § 60H). Economic damages aren’t capped. The 182-day pre-suit notice under § 60L also applies. The malpractice calculator applies the Massachusetts rules.

Claims against government and charities

Under the Massachusetts Tort Claims Act, a public employer is liable for the negligence of its employees acting within the scope of employment, but damages are limited to $100,000 per plaintiff, with no punitive damages or prejudgment interest (ch. 258, § 2). The individual employee isn’t personally liable for negligence. The Act excludes several categories of claims, including discretionary functions and many claims based on a failure to prevent harm caused by someone else (ch. 258, § 10). The written presentment within two years is a strict condition of the claim.

Road defects are handled separately. A claim for an injury caused by a defect in a city or town road must be brought under ch. 84, § 15, which requires written notice within 30 days and limits damages to $5,000. A bill filed in the 2025–2026 session would raise that limit to $50,000. Claims against the Commonwealth for defects in state highways are limited to $4,000 for personal injury.

Charitable organizations are liable for torts committed in carrying out their charitable purposes, but damages are capped at $20,000. For medical malpractice claims against nonprofit health care providers, the cap is $100,000 (ch. 231, § 85K). The cap doesn’t apply to activities that are primarily commercial, such as a charity’s for-profit business.

Wrongful death in Massachusetts

A wrongful death action is brought by the executor or administrator for the benefit of the family members who would inherit under the intestacy laws. The jury awards the fair monetary value of the person to those family members, including lost net income, services, protection, care, assistance, society, companionship, comfort, guidance, counsel and advice, plus funeral and burial expenses (ch. 229, § 2). Punitive damages of at least $5,000 are available when the death was caused by gross negligence or by willful, wanton or reckless conduct. The person’s conscious pain and suffering before death is recovered by the estate. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. Property owners owe lawful visitors a duty of reasonable care. In Papadopoulos v. Target Corp. (2010), the Supreme Judicial Court abolished the old rule that owners weren’t liable for natural accumulations of snow and ice, so the same reasonable-care standard now applies to winter conditions. See the Massachusetts slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog’s owner or keeper is strictly liable for any damage the dog causes to a person or property, unless the injured person was trespassing, committing another tort, or teasing, tormenting or abusing the dog. A child under seven is presumed not to have been doing any of those things (ch. 140, § 155). See the Massachusetts dog bite calculator.

Bars. Massachusetts allows negligence claims against a licensed seller that served alcohol to a person it knew or reasonably should have known was intoxicated, or to a minor, when that service caused the injury. Evidence that the person showed obvious signs of intoxication when served is the core of the claim.

Hurt at work in Massachusetts

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer (ch. 152, § 24). A claim against a third party, such as another driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim. The comp insurer has a lien on that recovery for the benefits it paid, after the legal fees and costs are deducted, and the worker keeps any excess (ch. 152, § 15). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Settling a Massachusetts claim

Timing matters more in Massachusetts than in most states. Before a lawsuit, an insurer weighs only the value of the claim. After filing, every year adds 12% interest to any judgment, and a well-documented ch. 93A demand adds the risk of multiple damages if the insurer fails to make a reasonable offer once liability is clear. Many claims are resolved after the medical treatment has ended and the lawsuit has been filed but before trial, when the claim’s value and the insurer’s exposure are both clear. MassHealth has a statutory lien on recoveries for the care it paid for (ch. 118E, § 22), and Medicare must be repaid from any settlement that covers care it paid for.

Settlements for minors usually need court approval. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • File a PIP claim with the insurer of the car you were in, or your own insurer if you were walking or cycling.
  • Keep a running total of medical bills. Crossing $2,000 matters for the tort threshold.
  • If a city or town road defect caused the injury, send written notice within 30 days.
  • For a claim against a public employer, send the written presentment to the right executive officer well before the two-year deadline.
  • Put your demand to the insurer in writing with the records that support it. That is the foundation for any later ch. 93A claim.
  • For a malpractice concern, plan for the 182-day notice and the tribunal review before the deadline.
