indiana.title: Indiana Personal Injury Claims: Fault, Deadlines, Caps and the Guest Statute
indiana.metaTitle: Indiana Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps, Deadlines
indiana.metaDescription: How Indiana’s 51% fault bar, several liability, two-year deadline, guest statute, $1.8 million malpractice cap and government notice rules shape a claim.
indiana.excerpt: Indiana bars recovery above 50% fault, makes each defendant pay only its own share and caps malpractice and government claims. Here is how those rules work, with the guest statute, insurance minimums and wrongful death rules.
indiana.html:
How an Indiana injury claim is valued

An Indiana injury claim recovers medical expenses, lost wages and loss of earning capacity, plus non-economic damages for pain, suffering, mental anguish, disfigurement and loss of enjoyment of life. Your damages are reduced by your share of fault, and you recover nothing if your fault is greater than the combined fault of everyone else who caused the injury.

Indiana has no general cap on injury damages, but several rules limit what particular claims can produce. Each defendant pays only its own share of fault. Medical malpractice claims are capped at $1.8 million and must go through a medical review panel. Claims against government are capped at $700,000 per person and need a notice within 180 or 270 days. Indiana’s guest statute bars some passengers from suing the driver at all, and the adult wrongful death statute caps damages for the loss of an adult without dependents. This guide explains each rule, with the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Indiana car accident calculator or the Indiana personal injury calculator.

An Indiana claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A woman riding in her brother’s car in Fort Wayne is hurt when another driver runs a red light. The jury values her damages at $200,000. The other driver blames the brother for speeding, and the jury assigns 60% of the fault to the other driver and 40% to her brother, who wasn’t a defendant.

  • Indiana’s guest statute bars a passenger from suing a driver who is her sibling, unless the driver’s conduct was wanton or willful. Ordinary speeding isn’t enough, so she has no claim for her brother’s 40% share.
  • Under several liability, the other driver owes only its 60% share: $120,000.
  • The other driver carries the state minimum of $25,000. Her own $100,000 of underinsured motorist coverage is reduced by that payment, so it pays up to $75,000.
  • Total realistically collected: about $100,000 on a claim valued at $200,000.

The example combines three Indiana rules that often surprise people: the guest statute, the allocation of fault to someone who isn’t being sued, and underinsured coverage that is reduced by what the at-fault driver pays. Each one can cut the recovery well below the value of the injury, which is why the facts about who was driving, and the coverage on every policy involved, matter early.

Fault: the 51% bar and several liability

Under Indiana’s Comparative Fault Act, you are barred from recovery if your fault is greater than the fault of all other people whose fault contributed to the injury. If your fault is 50% or less, your damages are reduced by your percentage (Ind. Code § 34-51-2-6).

Indiana has abolished joint and several liability under the Act. Each defendant is liable only for its own percentage of fault (Ind. Code § 34-51-2-8). A defendant can also name a nonparty, a person who caused or contributed to the injury but wasn’t sued, and the jury can assign fault to that nonparty, reducing what the defendants owe (Ind. Code § 34-51-2-14). The defendant must raise the nonparty defense within the statutory time, and the plaintiff can sometimes add the nonparty as a defendant in response. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

Seat belts

Evidence that you weren’t wearing a seat belt can’t be admitted in an Indiana civil case to reduce your damages (Ind. Code § 9-19-10-7).

Indiana filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (Ind. Code § 34-11-2-4).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the death (Ind. Code § 34-23-1-1).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the act or omission, not from discovery, with a limited exception when the patient couldn’t reasonably have discovered the malpractice within that period. A child injured before age six has until the eighth birthday (Ind. Code § 34-18-7-1).
  • Political subdivisions (cities, counties, school districts): a written notice within 180 days (Ind. Code § 34-13-3-8).
  • The State of Indiana: a written notice within 270 days to the Attorney General and the state agency involved (Ind. Code § 34-13-3-6).

For an injured child, the general two-year deadline usually doesn’t start until the child turns 18 (Ind. Code § 34-11-6-1), but the malpractice rule above has its own limit for young children.

Indiana’s malpractice deadline runs from the date of the care, which makes it shorter in practice than the same two years in most other states. The Indiana filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

The guest statute

Indiana is one of the few states that still has a guest statute. The owner or operator of a vehicle isn’t liable for injuries to, or the death of, a passenger who is the owner’s or operator’s parent, spouse, child or stepchild, or sibling, or a hitchhiker, unless the injury was caused by the driver’s wanton or willful misconduct (Ind. Code § 34-30-11-1). Friends, coworkers and other passengers aren’t covered by the statute and can sue a negligent driver in the ordinary way.

The statute doesn’t stop a family member from claiming against another driver who shared fault, or against their own uninsured or underinsured coverage when the other driver is underinsured. It also doesn’t apply to commercial transport such as a taxi or a rideshare trip.

Car insurance in Indiana

Indiana is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage (Ind. Code § 9-25-4-5). Insurers must provide uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage unless the named insured rejects it in writing (Ind. Code § 27-7-5-2). Indiana underinsured coverage applies when the at-fault driver’s limits are less than your UIM limits, and the amount the at-fault driver’s insurer pays is subtracted from your UIM limit, as in the example above (Ind. Code § 27-7-5-5).

The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay. For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers, and Indiana’s interstates carry heavy truck traffic; see the Indiana truck accident calculator. For rideshare crashes, the company’s coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

When the claim is worth more than the policy

Indiana doesn’t allow an injured person to sue the at-fault driver’s insurer directly. The claim is against the driver, and the insurer defends and pays within its limits. An insurer owes its own policyholder a duty to deal in good faith (Erie Insurance Co. v. Hickman, 1993). When it unreasonably refuses an offer to settle within the limits and a verdict comes in above them, the policyholder can have a claim against the insurer for the excess, which is sometimes assigned to the injured person as part of a settlement. The same duty of good faith applies when you claim against your own insurer for UM or UIM benefits.

In practice, Indiana insurers value claims with several liability and the nonparty defense in mind. If the insurer can point to a nonparty, such as a driver who left the scene or a family member protected by the guest statute, it will argue for a large share of fault there, because every percentage point assigned to a nonparty comes off what its own insured pays. Evidence that pins down who did what, from crash data, video and witnesses, protects the claim against that argument.

Medical bills and other insurance

Indiana partly modifies the collateral source rule. A defendant can introduce evidence of payments from collateral sources, except life insurance, insurance the plaintiff or their family paid for, and certain government benefits (Ind. Code § 34-44-1-2). In Stanley v. Walker (2009), the Indiana Supreme Court held that the discounted amounts actually accepted by providers are admissible to help the jury decide the reasonable value of medical care, as long as the jury isn’t told that insurance paid them. The medical figure in an Indiana verdict therefore often falls between the billed and paid amounts.

Hospitals have a lien on an injury recovery for their reasonable charges (Ind. Code § 32-33-4), and health plans, Medicare and Medicaid may also have repayment rights. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Indiana

Indiana’s Medical Malpractice Act applies to providers who qualify by carrying the required insurance and paying into the Patient’s Compensation Fund. For malpractice after June 30, 2019, the total recovery for an injury or death is capped at $1.8 million, including economic and non-economic damages (Ind. Code § 34-18-14-3). The provider or its insurer pays the first $500,000, and the Patient’s Compensation Fund pays the rest. Indiana last raised it in 2019. In 2026 a separate proposal to cap non-economic damages in all injury cases at $1 million was introduced and then withdrawn.

Before suing a qualified provider for more than $15,000, the patient must present the claim to a medical review panel of three health care providers, which gives an expert opinion on whether the standard of care was met (Ind. Code § 34-18-8-4). The panel’s opinion is admissible at trial but not binding. Attorney fees on the portion paid by the Fund are limited to 32% (Ind. Code § 34-18-18-1). The malpractice calculator applies the Indiana cap.

The Act and its cap apply only to providers who have qualified under it. If a provider wasn’t qualified when the care was given, the claim proceeds in court without the review panel and without the cap, so checking a provider’s status with the Department of Insurance is an early step in any Indiana malpractice case.

Claims against government in Indiana

The Indiana Tort Claims Act allows claims against the state and political subdivisions with conditions. The written notice must describe the facts, the extent of the loss, the time and place, the people involved, the amount claimed and the claimant’s address, and it must reach the right office within 180 days for a political subdivision or 270 days for the state. Damages are limited to $700,000 per person and $5 million per occurrence, and punitive damages aren’t allowed (Ind. Code § 34-13-3-4). The Act also lists immunities, including discretionary functions, the temporary condition of a public road caused by weather, and the adoption and enforcement of laws (Ind. Code § 34-13-3-3).

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require clear and convincing evidence of malice, fraud, gross negligence or oppressiveness that wasn’t the result of a mistake of fact or law, honest error, or ordinary negligence (Ind. Code § 34-51-3-2). They are capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $50,000 (§ 34-51-3-4). Indiana also takes most of the award: 75% of punitive damages goes to the state’s violent crime victims compensation fund, and the plaintiff keeps 25% (§ 34-51-3-6). Insurers know that, which is one reason punitive claims carry less settlement weight in Indiana than in many states.

Wrongful death in Indiana

Indiana has three wrongful death statutes, and which one applies changes the damages:

  • The general statute applies when the person who died left a spouse or dependents. Damages include lost earnings and support, medical and funeral expenses, and the loss of love, care and affection (Ind. Code § 34-23-1-1).
  • The adult wrongful death statute applies to an unmarried adult without dependents. Damages for the loss of love and companionship are capped at $300,000, not counting medical, hospital and funeral expenses, and punitive damages aren’t available (Ind. Code § 34-23-1-2).
  • The child wrongful death statute applies to a child under 20, or under 23 while enrolled in school, and allows the parents to recover for the loss of the child’s love and companionship, plus expenses (Ind. Code § 34-23-2-1).

The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. A business owes customers a duty of reasonable care, and liability usually depends on whether it knew or should have known of the hazard and failed to fix it or warn. Indiana applies comparative fault, so a hazard the customer should have noticed reduces the claim rather than ending it unless the customer’s fault exceeds 50%. See the Indiana slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Indiana’s strict liability statute protects people performing a duty required by state or federal law, such as mail carriers and meter readers, when they are bitten without provocation (Ind. Code § 15-20-1-3). For everyone else, Indiana courts start from a presumption that a dog is harmless, and an owner is liable only if they knew or should have known of the dog’s dangerous tendencies, such as earlier aggressive behavior, or were negligent in controlling it. See the Indiana dog bite calculator.

Bars. A person who furnishes alcohol is liable for injuries caused by the intoxication only if they had actual knowledge that the person was visibly intoxicated when served, and the intoxication was a proximate cause of the injury (Ind. Code § 7.1-5-10-15.5). The statute applies to anyone who furnishes alcohol, including social hosts, not only bars and stores.

Hurt at work in Indiana

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer (Ind. Code § 22-3-2-6). A claim against a third party, such as another driver or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and the employer or its insurer has a lien on that recovery for the benefits paid, reduced by its share of the legal fees and costs (Ind. Code § 22-3-2-13). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Interest, offers and settlement

Indiana’s Tort Prejudgment Interest Act lets the court add interest of 6% to 10% a year to a tort judgment, depending on the timing and terms of the parties’ written settlement offers (Ind. Code § 34-51-4). That gives a well-supported written demand made early in a lawsuit real value. Settlements for minors usually need court approval. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • If you were a passenger, note your relationship to the driver. The guest statute applies only to close family members and hitchhikers.
  • Identify every driver and company that may share fault, and ask each insurer for its policy limits. Under several liability, each one’s coverage matters separately.
  • Check your own policy for UM and UIM coverage. Unless someone rejected it in writing, it is there.
  • If a city, county, school or state agency may be involved, send the written notice within 180 days for local government or 270 days for the state.
  • For a malpractice concern, count two years from the date of the care, not the date you found out, and plan for the review panel.
  • Before accepting the at-fault driver’s policy limits, notify your UIM insurer in writing. Indiana gives it a chance to pay that amount itself and pursue the driver, and settling without notice can jeopardize the UIM claim.
  • Make a written settlement demand once your treatment has ended and the damages are documented; it can affect prejudgment interest later.

missouri.title: Missouri Personal Injury Claims: Five-Year Deadline, Fault and Damage Caps
missouri.metaTitle: Missouri Personal Injury Laws 2026: Deadlines, Fault, Caps
missouri.metaDescription: How Missouri’s five-year deadline, pure comparative fault, 51% joint liability rule, malpractice and government caps, and medical bill evidence shape a claim.
missouri.excerpt: Missouri gives you five years to sue in most injury cases, reduces but never bars damages for your own fault, and caps malpractice and government claims. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
missouri.html:
How a Missouri injury claim is valued

A Missouri injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, loss of earning capacity) and non-economic damages (pain, suffering, disability, disfigurement and loss of enjoyment of life). Missouri uses pure comparative fault, so your share of fault reduces the award but never bars it.

Missouri stands out for its long filing deadline: five years for most personal injury claims, one of the longest in the country. It has no general cap on injury damages, but medical malpractice and claims against government are capped at amounts that adjust every year. Since 2017, juries can also hear what was actually paid for medical care, not only what was billed. This guide explains those rules and the others that shape a claim, with the statute behind each.

Run your own figures with the Missouri personal injury calculator or the Missouri car accident calculator.

A Missouri claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A pedestrian in Kansas City is hit by a delivery van while crossing in the middle of a block. He has a broken pelvis and a shoulder injury. His providers billed $90,000, and his health insurer paid $48,000 to settle those bills. He lost $20,000 of wages. The jury values his non-economic damages at $250,000 and assigns him 30% of the fault for crossing outside a crosswalk.

  • Missouri juries can hear both the billed amount and the actual amount paid, and decide the value of the medical care. Using the billed figure, the claim after a 30% reduction is about $252,000.
  • Using the amount paid, it is about $222,600.
  • Because the van was being driven for work, the delivery company is liable for its driver’s negligence, and commercial auto policies commonly carry $1 million or more, so the policy limit isn’t the constraint here.
  • He has five years from the crash to sue, but the evidence of where he crossed and what the driver could see is best gathered in the first weeks.

Under Missouri’s pure comparative fault rule, the 30% finding reduces the award without ending it. In a state with a 50% or 51% bar, the same facts could produce nothing if the jury put his share a little higher.

Fault: pure comparative and joint liability above 51%

Missouri adopted pure comparative fault in Gustafson v. Benda (1983). Your damages are reduced by your percentage of fault, however large it is, and the rule is written into the statute for product liability cases (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.765).

A defendant found 51% or more at fault is jointly and severally liable for the whole judgment. A defendant less than 51% at fault pays only its own percentage (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.067). Punitive damages are always assessed against each defendant separately. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

Seat belts: a 1% limit

Missouri allows evidence that an injured person wasn’t wearing a seat belt, but only to reduce damages, and the reduction can’t be more than 1% of the damages awarded (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 307.178). In practice, seat belt use has almost no effect on the value of a Missouri claim.

Missouri filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: five years from the injury (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.120). Bills to shorten it to two years are filed nearly every session, and one passed the House in 2025, but as of November 2026 the five-year limit still applied.
  • Wrongful death: three years from the death (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.100).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the act of neglect, with a two-year discovery period for a foreign object left in the body and a 10-year outer limit. A child under 18 has until the 20th birthday (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.105).
  • Assault and battery: two years (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 516.140).
  • Cities: written notice within 90 days for injuries caused by defects in streets and sidewalks in many Missouri cities, under the statutes that govern each class of city.

The long injury deadline doesn’t apply to every claim in the same case. A wrongful death claim arising from the same crash has three years, and a claim against a city may need notice within 90 days. The Missouri filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

How insurers value Missouri claims

Missouri’s rules cut in different directions, and insurers price all of them in. Pure comparative fault means a claim with a disputed share of fault still has value, so insurers argue about percentages rather than refusing to pay at all. The actual-cost rule for medical bills gives the defense a lower medical figure to put in front of the jury, and adjusters often start from the amounts paid rather than billed. Joint liability for a defendant 51% or more at fault makes the share assigned to a well-insured defendant, such as a trucking company or a property owner, especially important, because crossing 51% makes that defendant responsible for the whole judgment.

The other pressure points are procedural. A demand that meets the time-limited demand statute, followed by an insurer’s unreasonable refusal, can expose the insurer to a judgment above its limits through a § 537.065 agreement. That risk is why serious Missouri claims often turn on how and when the demand is made.

Family members’ claims

A spouse of an injured person has a separate claim for loss of consortium, meaning the loss of the injured spouse’s companionship, services and support during recovery and afterward. It is usually brought in the same lawsuit and is reduced by the injured spouse’s share of fault. Parents can recover the medical expenses and lost services of an injured minor child. These claims add to the value of a case and should be included in any demand.

Car insurance in Missouri

Missouri is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 303.190). Uninsured motorist coverage of at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per crash is required on every policy (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 379.203). Underinsured motorist coverage is optional, and how it interacts with the at-fault driver’s limits depends on the policy’s wording, which Missouri courts read closely; ambiguous terms are read in the policyholder’s favor. Missouri courts have also allowed policyholders to stack uninsured motorist coverage from several vehicles on their policies in many cases.

The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay. For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers; see the Missouri truck accident calculator. For rideshare crashes, the company’s coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

Medical bills: what was actually paid

A 2017 law changed how Missouri juries see medical bills. Under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 490.715, the parties can introduce evidence of the actual cost of the medical care, meaning the amounts actually paid or needed to satisfy the charges, not only the amounts billed. The jury decides the value of the care, and the result often falls between the two figures, as in the example above. The rule doesn’t let the jury hear that the payments came from insurance.

Because both figures can be used at trial, ask early for itemized bills from each provider and the explanations of benefits from your health plan. Health plans, Medicare and Medicaid may have repayment rights from your recovery, and Missouri hospitals and other providers can assert liens on it (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 430.230 and following). The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

Medical malpractice in Missouri

Missouri caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases at amounts that rise 1.7% each year. For 2026 the caps are $481,493 for most injuries and $842,614 for catastrophic personal injuries, such as quadriplegia, paraplegia, loss of two or more limbs, a brain injury that leaves the person unable to live independently, or irreversible failure of a major organ system (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 538.205 and 538.210). Economic damages aren’t capped.

The Missouri Supreme Court struck down an earlier malpractice cap in Watts v. Lester E. Cox Medical Centers (2012), holding that it violated the right to a jury trial for a common-law claim. In 2015 the legislature replaced the common-law claim with a statutory one and reinstated caps, which the court upheld in Ordinola Velazquez v. University Physician Associates (2021). Within 90 days of filing, the plaintiff must file an affidavit stating that a qualified health care provider has given a written opinion supporting the claim, with one 90-day extension available (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 538.225). The malpractice calculator applies the Missouri caps.

Claims against government in Missouri

Missouri public entities are immune from most tort claims, with two waivers: injuries caused by a public employee’s negligent operation of a motor vehicle, and injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.600). Damages under those waivers are limited to amounts adjusted each January. For 2026 the limits are $532,148 per person and $3,547,658 per occurrence, and no punitive damages are allowed (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.610).

A 2026 law, SB 916, effective August 28, 2026, made three changes: private contractors doing Missouri Department of Transportation work to approved plans get the same immunity and limits as the state; the limit that applies is the one in effect on the date of the accident; and a political subdivision waives immunity through insurance only by buying coverage directly. A government agency can also waive immunity to the extent of insurance it buys for other kinds of claims.

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require clear and convincing evidence that the defendant intentionally harmed the plaintiff without just cause or acted with a deliberate and flagrant disregard for the safety of others. A punitive damages claim can’t be included in the first petition; the plaintiff must ask the court for permission to add it, with evidence (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 510.261). Punitive damages are capped at the greater of $500,000 or five times the net amount of the judgment, with exceptions such as claims by the state and some discrimination claims (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 510.265).

Wrongful death in Missouri

A Missouri wrongful death claim belongs first to the spouse, children, grandchildren of a deceased child, and parents; if there are none, to siblings; and if there are none of those, to a plaintiff ad litem appointed by the court (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.080). The jury awards damages for the funeral and medical expenses, the value of the services, consortium, companionship, comfort, instruction, guidance, counsel, training and support the family lost, and the person’s pain and suffering before death. It can also award damages for aggravating circumstances, which work like punitive damages (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.090). There is no cap outside malpractice and government claims. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Section 537.065 agreements and time-limited demands

When an at-fault party’s insurer won’t settle within its limits, Missouri allows the injured person and the at-fault party to agree that any judgment will be collected only from insurance, not from the at-fault party’s personal assets (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.065). Since 2017, the insurer must be notified and given 30 days before the agreement takes effect, and it can then step in to defend. These agreements often lead to bad faith claims against insurers that refused reasonable offers.

Missouri also regulates time-limited settlement demands to liability insurers. A demand must be in writing, include the information the statute requires, such as medical records and a release, and give the insurer the minimum time to respond (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.058). A demand that doesn’t meet the statute can’t be the basis for a later bad faith claim, so the details matter.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. A business owes customers reasonable care and is liable for a dangerous condition it knew or should have known about. Missouri follows the rule that an owner usually isn’t liable for a danger so open and obvious that visitors can be expected to protect themselves, unless the owner should anticipate harm anyway (Harris v. Niehaus, 1993). Otherwise, under pure comparative fault, a hazard the customer should have noticed reduces the claim rather than ending it. See the Missouri slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog owner is strictly liable for damages from a bite to a person in a public place or lawfully on private property, including the owner’s, without proof that the dog was known to be dangerous. Damages are reduced by the injured person’s own fault (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 273.036). See the Missouri dog bite calculator.

Bars. A licensed seller is liable only if it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the seller knew or should have known that it was serving a visibly intoxicated person, or a minor (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 537.053).

Hurt at work in Missouri

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 287.120). A co-worker can be sued only for an affirmative negligent act that purposefully and dangerously caused or increased the risk of injury. A claim against a third party, such as another driver or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and the employer has a lien on that recovery for the benefits paid, after a share of the legal fees and costs (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 287.150). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Interest and settlement

Missouri adds prejudgment interest in tort cases only if the claimant made a written settlement demand that met the statute’s requirements, the demand was left open for the required time, and the judgment exceeds the demand. Interest then runs from the date of the demand (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 408.040). A properly made demand therefore has value well beyond the negotiation. Settlements for minors need court approval. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • If you were partly at fault, don’t assume the claim is over. Under pure comparative fault, it is reduced, not barred.
  • Don’t let the five-year deadline make you wait. Witnesses, video and vehicle data disappear long before the deadline.
  • Check your policy for UM coverage, which is required, and UIM coverage, which isn’t, and note how many vehicles are on the policy.
  • Keep both the bills and the explanations of benefits. Missouri juries can see what was billed and what was paid.
  • If a city street or sidewalk caused the injury, find out whether written notice is due within 90 days.
  • If a government vehicle or property was involved, identify the entity and whether it has insurance beyond the statutory limits.
  • Make any settlement demand in writing and in the form the statutes require. It can affect prejudgment interest and any later bad faith claim.

maryland.title: Maryland Personal Injury Claims: Contributory Negligence, Damage Cap and Deadlines
maryland.metaTitle: Maryland Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps, Deadlines
maryland.metaDescription: How Maryland’s contributory negligence rule, $980,000 non-economic cap from October 2026, three-year deadline, PIP and enhanced UIM shape a claim.
maryland.excerpt: Maryland bars recovery if you were even slightly at fault and caps non-economic damages at an amount that rises every October 1. Here is how those rules work, with Maryland’s deadlines, insurance and government claim rules.
maryland.html:
How a Maryland injury claim is valued

A Maryland injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, loss of earning capacity) and non-economic damages (pain, suffering, inconvenience, physical impairment, disfigurement and loss of consortium). Two Maryland rules shape almost every claim. The first is contributory negligence: if you were even slightly at fault for your own injury, you generally recover nothing. The second is a cap on non-economic damages that rises by $15,000 every October 1.

Maryland’s highest court considered abandoning contributory negligence in 2013 and kept it, leaving any change to the legislature, which hasn’t made one. Maryland also caps malpractice damages separately, limits claims against local and state government, and requires $2,500 of personal injury protection unless you waive it. This guide explains each rule with the statute or case behind it.

Run your own figures with the Maryland car accident calculator or the Maryland personal injury calculator. Both apply the contributory negligence rule and the current cap.

A Maryland claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A pedestrian in Baltimore is hit in a crosswalk by a driver who turned left without looking. She suffers a fractured pelvis and a head injury, with medical bills of $180,000 and lost wages of $60,000, for economic loss of $240,000. A jury might value her non-economic damages at $1,400,000.

  • If she was injured between October 1, 2025 and September 30, 2026, the cap is $965,000, and the claim is worth up to $1,205,000. For an injury on or after October 1, 2026, the cap is $980,000 and the total $1,220,000.
  • If the driver’s insurer proves that she stepped into the crosswalk against the signal or while looking at her phone, and that contributed to the crash, she recovers nothing, unless an exception such as last clear chance applies.
  • The driver carries the state minimum of $30,000 per person. Her standard underinsured motorist coverage of $250,000 is reduced by that payment, so it adds up to $220,000. If she had bought enhanced underinsured coverage, it would pay its full $250,000 on top of the driver’s limit.

The example shows how far apart a Maryland claim’s value and its collectible amount can be. The cap limits what the jury’s number becomes, the fault rule decides whether there is a recovery at all, and the insurance decides how much of it can actually be paid.

Contributory negligence

In Coleman v. Soccer Ass’n of Columbia (2013), Maryland’s highest court declined to replace contributory negligence with comparative fault, so a plaintiff whose own negligence contributed to the injury is barred from recovering. There are limited exceptions:

  • Last clear chance. If the defendant had a fresh opportunity to avoid the harm after the plaintiff’s negligence put them in danger, and failed to take it, the plaintiff can still recover.
  • Young children. A child under five can’t be contributorily negligent, and older children are judged against the conduct of a reasonable child of the same age.
  • Intentional or reckless conduct. Contributory negligence is a defense to negligence, not to intentional wrongs.

Assumption of risk is a separate, related defense: if the plaintiff knew of and voluntarily accepted a specific danger, the claim is also barred. Together these rules make evidence about the plaintiff’s own conduct the first thing insurers look at. The fault calculator shows how Maryland’s rule compares with its neighbors’.

How the rule plays out in negotiation

Insurers adjusting Maryland claims start with the injured person’s own conduct: speed, distraction, where a pedestrian crossed, whether a cyclist had lights, or whether a customer was watching where they walked. When there is a credible argument, the offer tends to reflect the risk of a defense verdict rather than the value of the injury, and claims with genuinely disputed fault often settle well below their full value. Evidence that answers the argument, such as intersection video, phone records, vehicle data and independent witnesses, is what moves those claims. Because a fault finding ends the case entirely, Maryland cases with disputed fault are also more likely to be tried.

Several defendants

Maryland keeps joint and several liability. When two or more defendants cause one injury, you can collect the full judgment from any of them, and they share the cost under the Uniform Contribution Among Joint Tort-Feasors Act.

Seat belts

Not wearing a seat belt isn’t admissible as evidence of contributory negligence or to reduce damages in a Maryland civil case (Md. Code, Transp. § 22-412.3).

Maryland filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from when the claim arises (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-101), with a discovery rule.
  • Wrongful death: three years from the death (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-904(g)).
  • Medical malpractice: five years from the injury or three years from its discovery, whichever is shorter, with special rules for minors (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-109).
  • Local governments: written notice within one year of the injury under the Local Government Tort Claims Act (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-304).
  • The State of Maryland: a written claim to the State Treasurer within one year, and a lawsuit within three years, under the Maryland Tort Claims Act (Md. Code, State Gov’t § 12-106).

The Maryland filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

The cap on non-economic damages

Maryland Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 11-108 caps non-economic damages in personal injury and wrongful death cases. The cap began at $500,000 for claims arising on or after October 1, 1994 and rises by $15,000 each October 1. The cap that applies is the one in effect when the cause of action arose, generally the date of the injury:

  • $965,000 for injuries from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026
  • $980,000 for injuries on or after October 1, 2026

In a wrongful death case with two or more beneficiaries, the total non-economic award to all beneficiaries is limited to 150% of the cap, $1,470,000 for deaths on or after October 1, 2026. A survival claim for the person’s own pain and suffering before death has its own separate cap. The jury isn’t told about the cap; the court reduces the verdict after it is returned. Economic damages aren’t capped. A 2026 bill to repeal the cap didn’t pass and was sent for further study.

Car insurance in Maryland

Maryland is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $30,000 per person, $60,000 per crash and $15,000 for property damage (Md. Code, Transp. § 17-103). Policies must include $2,500 of personal injury protection, which pays medical bills and lost wages regardless of fault, unless the named insured waives it in writing (Md. Code, Ins. § 19-505). PIP benefits don’t reduce what the at-fault driver owes.

Uninsured motorist coverage is required at limits equal to the liability coverage unless the policyholder chooses lower limits (Md. Code, Ins. § 19-509). In its standard form, Maryland underinsured coverage is reduced by the at-fault driver’s liability limits. Since July 1, 2018, insurers must offer enhanced underinsured motorist coverage on new private passenger policies, which pays in addition to the at-fault driver’s limits. It is optional and costs more, but as the example shows, it can make a large difference after a serious crash. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what each form of coverage can pay.

For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers; see the Maryland truck accident calculator. For rideshare crashes, the company’s coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

Medical bills and other insurance

Maryland applies the collateral source rule in ordinary injury cases: payments from your own health insurance, PIP or disability coverage don’t reduce what the at-fault party owes, and the jury doesn’t hear about them. Malpractice cases are different. There, an award for past medical expenses is limited to the amounts actually paid by or on behalf of the patient and the amounts incurred but not yet paid, so write-offs aren’t recoverable (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-2A-09(d)). Health plans, Medicare and Medicaid may have repayment rights from the recovery, and the medical lien calculator shows how those affect what you keep.

Uninsured drivers and bad faith

When an uninsured or hit-and-run driver causes a crash, your own UM coverage is the first source of payment. If you have no UM coverage of your own, for example because you don’t own a car and don’t live with a relative who has a policy, the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund may pay a claim within statutory limits. Strict notice deadlines apply, so it is worth contacting the Fund early.

If your own insurer handles a UM, UIM or PIP claim in bad faith, Maryland Insurance Article § 27-1001 provides a remedy. You must first file a complaint with the Maryland Insurance Administration, which decides whether the insurer acted in good faith; you can then go to court. A finding of bad faith allows recovery of the amount owed plus interest, attorney fees and expenses. When an at-fault driver’s insurer unreasonably refuses to settle within its limits, it can be liable to its own policyholder for a verdict above those limits, a long-standing Maryland rule.

Medical malpractice in Maryland

Malpractice claims have their own non-economic cap, which rises by $15,000 each January 1. It is $905,000 for claims arising in 2025 and $920,000 for claims arising in 2026, and in a wrongful death case with two or more beneficiaries the total is limited to 125% of the cap (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-2A-09). Before filing in court, the claim must be filed with the Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office, and within 90 days the plaintiff must file a certificate from a qualified expert stating that the provider departed from the standard of care and caused the injury (§ 3-2A-04). The parties can then waive arbitration and proceed in court, which most do. The malpractice calculator applies the Maryland cap.

Claims against government in Maryland

Under the Local Government Tort Claims Act, counties, cities and other local governments must pay judgments against their employees for torts committed within the scope of employment, up to $400,000 per individual claim and $800,000 per occurrence (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-303). Written notice must be given within one year of the injury, to the county attorney or the equivalent official, stating the time, place and cause of the injury (§ 5-304). A court can excuse a late notice for good cause if the government wasn’t prejudiced.

Under the Maryland Tort Claims Act, the State is liable for the negligence of its personnel up to $400,000 per claimant for injuries from a single incident (State Gov’t § 12-104). The written claim must go to the State Treasurer within one year, and the Treasurer must deny it before you sue. State employees acting within the scope of their jobs without malice or gross negligence are immune personally. Neither act allows punitive damages against the government.

Punitive damages

Maryland requires clear and convincing evidence of actual malice: conduct characterized by evil motive, intent to injure, ill will or fraud, or actual knowledge of a defect combined with a conscious or deliberate disregard of the danger (Owens-Illinois, Inc. v. Zenobia, 1992). Gross negligence isn’t enough, even for drunk driving. Maryland doesn’t cap punitive damages. A 2026 bill to lower the standard to gross negligence didn’t pass.

Wrongful death and survival claims

A wrongful death action benefits the spouse, parents and children of the person who died. If there are none, relatives who were substantially dependent on the person can bring it (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-904). Damages include lost financial support and services and solatium: mental anguish, emotional pain and suffering, and loss of society, companionship, comfort, protection, care, attention, advice, counsel, training, guidance or education. Non-economic damages are subject to the cap and its 150% rule. The estate’s separate survival action recovers the person’s own pain and suffering, medical bills and funeral expenses up to a statutory limit. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. A business owes customers a duty of reasonable care to keep the premises safe and must have known or should have known of the hazard. Fall claims in Maryland are especially exposed to contributory negligence and assumption of risk: if the hazard was visible, the defense will argue that the customer should have avoided it. See the Maryland slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. In a claim against a dog’s owner, the law presumes that the owner knew or should have known of the dog’s dangerous propensities, and the owner can rebut that presumption. An owner is strictly liable when a dog running at large causes injury, unless the injured person was trespassing, committing a crime, or provoking the dog (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-1901). See the Maryland dog bite calculator.

Bars. Maryland doesn’t recognize dram shop liability. A bar that overserves a customer who then causes a crash generally isn’t liable to the people injured (Warr v. JMGM Group, LLC, 2013), so the claim runs against the driver and the driver’s insurance.

Hurt at work in Maryland

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, except when the employer deliberately intended to injure or kill the worker (Md. Code, Lab. & Empl. § 9-509). A claim against a third party, such as another driver or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and the employer or its insurer is repaid from that recovery for the benefits paid, after the costs of the recovery (§ 9-902). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Interest and settlement

Maryland judgments generally carry interest at 10% a year from the date of judgment (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-107). Settlements for minors usually need court approval. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Be careful what you say about your own conduct. In a contributory negligence state, a casual admission can end the claim.
  • Preserve evidence that rules out your fault: photos, video from nearby businesses, and the names of witnesses.
  • Check your policy for PIP, the UM limits, and whether you have standard or enhanced underinsured coverage.
  • If a county, city or state vehicle or property was involved, send the written notice within one year.
  • Note the date of injury. It decides which cap applies, and the cap changes every October 1.
  • Keep a record of how the injury affects work, family life and sleep. The jury still decides the non-economic number before the cap is applied, and in many cases the value falls below the cap.
  • Before accepting the at-fault driver’s policy limits, notify your own UIM insurer in writing; Maryland gives it a set time to decide whether to pay that amount itself and pursue the driver.
  • For a malpractice concern, plan for the filing with the Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office and the expert certificate.

colorado.title: Colorado Personal Injury Claims: New Damage Caps, Fault and Deadlines
colorado.metaTitle: Colorado Personal Injury Laws 2026: Caps, Fault, Deadlines
colorado.metaDescription: How Colorado’s $1.5 million non-economic cap, 50% fault bar, three-year crash deadline, 9% prejudgment interest and 182-day government notice shape a claim.
colorado.excerpt: Colorado raised its damage caps for lawsuits filed since 2025, bars recovery at 50% fault and adds 9% interest to injury awards. Here is how those rules work, with Colorado’s deadlines, insurance and government claim rules.
colorado.html:
How a Colorado injury claim is valued

A Colorado injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost earnings, loss of earning capacity) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering, inconvenience, emotional stress and impairment of quality of life), plus separate damages for physical impairment and disfigurement. Your damages are reduced by your share of fault, and you recover nothing if your fault is as great as the defendants’.

Colorado overhauled its damage caps in 2024. For lawsuits filed on or after January 1, 2025, the general cap on non-economic damages is $1.5 million, the wrongful death cap is $2.125 million, and the malpractice caps are rising each year through 2029. Colorado also adds 9% prejudgment interest, compounded annually, to injury awards, has a three-year deadline for car crashes, and requires a 182-day notice for claims against government. This guide explains each rule with the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Colorado car accident calculator or the Colorado personal injury calculator.

A Colorado claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver on I-25 in Denver is hit by a driver who changed lanes without looking. He has a shoulder injury that needs surgery and a back injury, with medical bills of $85,000 and lost wages of $25,000. A jury values his non-economic damages at $300,000 and assigns him 30% of the fault for speeding.

  • His 30% share reduces the award: ($110,000 + $300,000) × 70% = about $287,000. Had the jury put his fault at 50%, he would recover nothing.
  • Colorado adds 9% prejudgment interest, compounded annually, from the date of the crash. If the judgment comes two years later, that adds about $53,985; three years later, about $84,673.
  • The other driver carries the state minimum of $25,000. His own $250,000 of underinsured motorist coverage pays in addition to that limit, so up to $275,000 is available.
  • His medical payments coverage paid the first $5,000 of bills regardless of fault.

The interest is one reason Colorado claims tend to settle once the facts are clear: an insurer that delays a strong claim pays for the delay at 9% a year. The fault rule works the other way. The difference between 49% and 50% fault is the difference between a reduced recovery and none.

Fault: the 50% bar and several liability

Under C.R.S. § 13-21-111, a plaintiff can recover only if their negligence was less than the negligence of the person or people they are suing, and the damages are reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage. At 50% the claim is barred.

Colorado has abolished joint and several liability. Each defendant pays only the share of damages matching its own percentage of fault, except for defendants who consciously conspired to commit the wrong (C.R.S. § 13-21-111.5). A defendant can also designate a nonparty at fault within 90 days after the case begins, and the jury can assign fault to that nonparty, which reduces what the defendants owe. The comparative fault calculator shows how the percentages change the result.

Seat belts

Evidence that you weren’t wearing a seat belt can be used to reduce damages for pain and suffering, but not economic damages such as medical bills and lost wages, and it can’t be used to establish fault for the crash (C.R.S. § 42-4-237(7)).

Colorado filing deadlines

  • Motor vehicle injuries: three years (C.R.S. § 13-80-101(1)(n)).
  • Most other personal injuries: two years (C.R.S. § 13-80-102(1)(a)).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the death (C.R.S. § 13-80-102(1)(d)).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from when the injury and its cause were or should have been discovered, with a three-year outer limit except for a foreign object, concealment and some other situations (C.R.S. § 13-80-102.5).
  • Public entities: a written notice within 182 days after discovering the injury, under the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act (C.R.S. § 24-10-109).
  • Bars and liquor stores: one year from the sale or service of alcohol (C.R.S. § 44-3-801).

For a child, Colorado’s disability statute can extend the deadline until a legal representative is appointed or the child turns 18 (C.R.S. § 13-81-103), but the rules are technical and a parent’s own claim for the child’s medical bills follows the regular deadline, so families shouldn’t rely on the extension. A crash claim and a related claim against a bar or a public entity can have three different deadlines. The Colorado filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

The damage caps after HB24-1472

In 2024 the legislature passed HB24-1472, the first major increase in Colorado’s caps in decades. For civil actions filed on or after January 1, 2025:

  • General non-economic damages: $1.5 million, up from about $640,000, adjusted for inflation every two years starting January 1, 2028 (C.R.S. § 13-21-102.5).
  • Wrongful death non-economic damages: $2.125 million, with no cap when the death resulted from a felonious killing (C.R.S. § 13-21-203).
  • Medical malpractice non-economic damages: $415,000 for cases filed in 2025, $530,000 for 2026, $645,000 for 2027, $760,000 for 2028 and $875,000 for 2029, then adjusted for inflation (C.R.S. § 13-64-302).
  • Malpractice wrongful death: $555,000 for 2025, $810,000 for 2026, rising to $1.575 million in 2029.

Two features of the new law matter in practice. The caps now depend on the date the lawsuit is filed, not the date of the injury, so an injury in 2024 sued on in 2025 gets the new caps. And the old provision letting a court double the cap on clear and convincing evidence was eliminated, so the cap is now a fixed number. Damages for physical impairment and disfigurement remain outside the general non-economic cap. Economic damages aren’t capped.

How the caps play out in negotiation

Most injury claims are worth less than $1.5 million in non-economic damages, so for them the 2024 change makes little difference. It matters most for catastrophic injuries and wrongful death, where the old caps often set the insurer’s ceiling well below what a jury would award. For malpractice, the cap that applies depends on the year the lawsuit is filed, and it rises each January through 2029. That can affect timing within the deadline, but the two-year limit still controls, and waiting is rarely worth the risk.

Car insurance in Colorado

Colorado is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $15,000 for property damage (C.R.S. § 10-4-620). Insurers must offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, which applies unless rejected in writing, and since 2008 Colorado underinsured coverage pays in addition to the at-fault driver’s liability limits, covering the difference between those limits and your damages up to your UIM limit (C.R.S. § 10-4-609). Insurers must also offer at least $5,000 of medical payments coverage, which pays your bills regardless of fault unless you reject it in writing (C.R.S. § 10-4-635).

The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay. For commercial trucks, federal minimums start at $750,000 for interstate freight carriers; see the Colorado truck accident calculator. For rideshare crashes, the company’s coverage depends on whether a ride was accepted; the rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

When an insurer delays or refuses

Colorado gives policyholders a strong remedy against their own insurer. If an insurer unreasonably delays or denies payment of a covered benefit, such as UIM or MedPay benefits, the policyholder can recover two times the covered benefit plus reasonable attorney fees and costs (C.R.S. §§ 10-3-1115 and 10-3-1116). That is in addition to the benefit itself, and it applies to delay as well as outright denial.

When an at-fault driver’s insurer unreasonably refuses a reasonable offer to settle within its limits and a larger verdict follows, the insurer can be liable to its policyholder for the excess. Colorado allows the policyholder to assign that bad faith claim to the injured person in exchange for a promise not to collect the judgment from the policyholder personally, an arrangement approved by the Colorado Supreme Court in Nunn v. Mid-Century Insurance Co. (2010). A clear, documented demand within the limits is usually what puts that risk on the insurer.

Medical bills and other insurance

Colorado’s collateral source rule has two parts. Before trial, evidence of payments from insurance and other sources is generally kept from the jury, and the Colorado Supreme Court has held that the discounted amounts an insurer paid aren’t admissible to reduce the reasonable value of the medical care shown by the bills (Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Crossgrove, 2012). After the verdict, the court reduces the award for collateral payments, but not for benefits from insurance or other contracts the plaintiff or someone on their behalf paid for (C.R.S. § 13-21-111.6). In practice, health insurance and MedPay payments usually don’t reduce the award. Those insurers may have repayment rights, as may Medicare and Medicaid. The medical lien calculator shows how repayment affects what you keep.

9% prejudgment interest

In personal injury cases, Colorado adds interest of 9% a year, compounded annually, from the date the claim arose until the judgment (C.R.S. § 13-21-101). Interest applies to the damages awarded, and in long cases it can add a third or more to the judgment. It doesn’t apply to settlements, which is why it gives insurers a reason to resolve strong claims sooner. Colorado’s offer of settlement statute adds another incentive: a party that rejects a written offer and then does worse at trial loses the right to costs incurred after the offer and may have to pay the other side’s costs (C.R.S. § 13-17-202).

Claims against government in Colorado

Under the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act, public entities are immune from tort claims except in listed situations, including a public employee’s operation of a motor vehicle (with limits for emergency vehicles), a dangerous condition of a public building, road or highway, and the operation of public hospitals, jails, parks and utilities (C.R.S. § 24-10-106). A written notice of claim must be filed within 182 days after the injury is discovered, and the claimant must wait 90 days or until the claim is denied before suing (C.R.S. § 24-10-109). Missing the notice deadline bars the claim.

Damages are limited, with inflation adjustments every four years. For the 2026 to 2030 period, the limits are $505,000 per person and $1,421,000 per occurrence, and punitive damages aren’t allowed (C.R.S. § 24-10-114).

Punitive damages

Colorado calls them exemplary damages. They require proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the injury was attended by fraud, malice, or willful and wanton conduct (C.R.S. § 13-25-127(2)). A claim for them can’t be included in the original complaint; it can be added only after initial disclosures, with prima facie proof. They are generally limited to the amount of actual damages, and the court can increase them up to three times actual damages if the defendant continued the conduct during the case (C.R.S. § 13-21-102).

Wrongful death and survival claims

Colorado’s wrongful death statute limits who can sue and when. In the first year after the death, only the surviving spouse can bring the claim, or the heirs or a designated beneficiary with the spouse’s written consent. In the second year, the spouse, the heirs or a designated beneficiary can sue. If there is no spouse, heirs or a designated beneficiary can sue from the start, and if there are none of those, the parents (C.R.S. § 13-21-201). Since 2025, a sibling can bring the claim in some situations where no one else can. Damages include economic losses and the family’s grief and loss of companionship, subject to the $2.125 million non-economic cap. A survival action recovers the person’s own losses before death, but not their pain and suffering (C.R.S. § 13-20-101). The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites, skiing and bars

Falls. Claims against property owners are governed exclusively by the Premises Liability Act, which sets the duty by the visitor’s status. A customer, as an invitee, can recover for the owner’s unreasonable failure to use reasonable care against dangers the owner knew or should have known about. Social guests and trespassers have narrower rights (C.R.S. § 13-21-115). See the Colorado slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. A dog owner is strictly liable for economic damages when the dog causes serious bodily injury or death to a person lawfully on public or private property, with exceptions such as trespassing, provoking the dog, and some professional settings like veterinary care. Bites that cause less serious injuries, and non-economic damages, follow the ordinary negligence rules (C.R.S. § 13-21-124). See the Colorado dog bite calculator.

Skiing. The Ski Safety Act bars claims for injuries caused by the inherent dangers and risks of skiing, such as changing snow conditions, terrain and collisions with natural objects, and limits damages against ski area operators (C.R.S. § 33-44-112). Claims usually turn on an operator’s violation of a specific statutory duty or on another skier’s negligence.

Bars. A liquor licensee is liable only if it willfully and knowingly sold or served alcohol to a person under 21 or to a visibly intoxicated person, and the lawsuit is filed within one year of the sale. Damages are subject to a statutory limit that began at $150,000 and is adjusted for inflation (C.R.S. § 44-3-801).

Hurt at work in Colorado

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer (C.R.S. § 8-41-102). A claim against a third party, such as another driver or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and the comp insurer is repaid from that recovery for the benefits it paid (C.R.S. § 8-41-203). The construction accident calculator takes the lien into account.

Settling a Colorado claim

Settlements for minors usually need court approval. If Medicare or Medicaid paid for treatment, their repayment claims have to be resolved before the settlement money is distributed, and the same is true of many employer health plans. A written settlement demand that lists the medical bills, wage records and the evidence on fault gives the insurer what it needs to evaluate the claim and starts the clock on any later bad faith argument. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate, the settlement timeline calculator to see how long each stage usually takes, and the attorney fee calculator to see what a settlement leaves you.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Check your policy for UM and UIM coverage and MedPay. Unless someone rejected them in writing, you probably have them.
  • Note every deadline that might apply: three years for a crash, two for most other injuries, one year for a bar, and 182 days for a government claim.
  • Gather evidence on fault early. The 50% bar makes the fault percentage decisive.
  • If a government vehicle, road or building was involved, send the written notice of claim well before the 182-day deadline.
  • Keep a record of physical impairment and disfigurement as well as pain. Colorado treats them as a separate category of damages.
  • Make a written settlement offer once the damages are documented; it affects costs if the case goes to trial.
  • If your own insurer delays a UIM or MedPay payment without a good reason, raise the statutory remedy in writing.

faqs.question: What is the cap on pain and suffering damages in Colorado?
faqs.answer: For lawsuits filed on or after January 1, 2025, $1.5 million for non-economic damages in most injury cases and $2.125 million in wrongful death cases (C.R.S. §§ 13-21-102.5 and 13-21-203). Malpractice caps are lower and rising through 2029.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Colorado?
faqs.answer: Three years for motor vehicle injuries and two years for most other injuries and wrongful death. Claims against public entities need a written notice within 182 days.

faqs.question: Can I recover in Colorado if I was partly at fault?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fault is less than the defendants’; your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 50% or more you recover nothing (C.R.S. § 13-21-111).

faqs.question: What are Colorado’s minimum car insurance limits?
faqs.answer: $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $15,000 for property damage (C.R.S. § 10-4-620). Insurers must also offer UM/UIM coverage and $5,000 of medical payments coverage.

faqs.question: Does Colorado add interest to injury awards?
faqs.answer: Yes. Personal injury awards carry 9% interest a year, compounded annually, from the date the claim arose to the judgment (C.R.S. § 13-21-101).

faqs.question: What are the limits on claims against Colorado government?
faqs.answer: For 2026 to 2030, $505,000 per person and $1,421,000 per occurrence, with no punitive damages, and a written notice is due within 182 days (C.R.S. §§ 24-10-109 and 24-10-114).
